**How the definition helps.** Choosing the primary associate removes the unit factors that would spoil the symmetry. The cubic symbol does not change when the lower entry is replaced by an associate. But a unit factor on top can change it by a power of ω (our own). Reciprocity moves each number to the top once, so both must be normalized. The sign does not matter, because −1 is a cube, so α and −α give the same cubic symbols (our own). With primary numbers the law has no correction factor. The hard part is the proof, through Gauss and Jacobi sums or Eisenstein's elliptic functions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cubic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_reciprocity). It says: “A number is primary if it is coprime to 3 and congruent to an ordinary integer modulo (1−ω)², which is the same as saying it is congruent to ±2 modulo 3.”

**Sources:**

- [K. Ireland and M. Rosen, A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory, 2nd ed., Springer, 1990](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-2103-4)
- [F. Lemmermeyer, Reciprocity Laws: From Euler to Eisenstein, Springer, 2000](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-12893-0)

### Primary Gaussian primes make quartic reciprocity statable

**Remember:** Pick one associate out of four, and quartic reciprocity has no unit ambiguity.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 11R18. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In the Gaussian integers ℤ\[i\], the units are ±1 and ±i, and associates differ by a unit factor. A Gaussian integer is odd when 1 + i does not divide it. Gauss calls an odd number primary when it is ≡ 1 mod (1 + i)³.

**Problem.** Every odd Gaussian integer has exactly one primary associate. For distinct primary primes π and θ, quartic reciprocity relates the quartic residue symbols \[π/θ\] and \[θ/π\] by an explicit sign.

**How the definition helps.** The primary condition picks one associate out of four, just as positivity picks one of ±p in the ordinary integers. Reciprocity swaps the two numbers, so each appears once on top of a residue symbol (our own). On top, a unit factor such as i changes the value of the symbol (our own). So the law needs a fixed choice of associate, and the primary one makes it a single formula. Jacobi used a different choice, a ≡ 1 mod 4, and then the law takes another form. The hard part is the proof of the law, which Gauss never published. Jacobi gave proofs in lectures, and Eisenstein published the first ones.

**Wikipedia:** [Quartic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartic_reciprocity). It says: “In order to state the unique factorization theorem, it is necessary to have a way of distinguishing one of the associates of a number.”

**Sources:**

- [F. Lemmermeyer, Reciprocity Laws: From Euler to Eisenstein, Springer, 2000](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-12893-0)
- [G. Eisenstein, Lois de réciprocité, J. reine angew. Math. 28 (1844) 53–67](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1844.28.53)

### Weighting prime powers by log p makes prime counting match ζ′/ζ

**Remember:** Count primes with weight log p, and the zeros of ζ appear directly.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11N05, 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The von Mangoldt function Λ(n) equals log p when n is a power of a prime p, and 0 otherwise. Its sum ψ(x) = Σ Λ(n) over n ≤ x is the second Chebyshev function.

**Problem.** The Dirichlet series Σ Λ(n) n⁻ˢ equals −ζ′(s)/ζ(s). Off prime powers, ψ(x) = x − Σ (x to the power ρ)/ρ − log(2π) − ½ log(1 − x⁻²). The prime number theorem is equivalent to ψ(x) \~ x.

**How the definition helps.** With weight log p, the prime counting function is exactly the one whose Dirichlet series is −ζ′/ζ, the logarithmic derivative of the Euler product (our own). At a zero of ζ of multiplicity m, −ζ′/ζ has a simple pole with residue −m, so each zero ρ gives the clean term −(x to the power ρ)/ρ (our own). Riemann's weighted count Π(x) matches log ζ instead, which has logarithmic singularities at the zeros (our own). The hard part of the prime number theorem stays: ζ has no zeros on the line Re s = 1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Von Mangoldt function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Mangoldt_function). It says: “Von Mangoldt provided a rigorous proof of an explicit formula for ψ(x) involving a sum over the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. This was an important part of the first proof of the prime number theorem.”

**Sources:**

- [H. von Mangoldt, Zu Riemanns Abhandlung 'Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse', J. reine angew. Math. 114 (1895) 255–305](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1895.114.255)
- [T. M. Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory, Springer, 1976](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5579-4)

### Large characters locate repeated differences

**Remember:** Make the large Fourier terms agree to get a positive count.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B13 (Additive bases, including sumsets), 11B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A have density α &gt; 0 in a finite vector space over a prime field. Its large spectrum is the set of characters whose Fourier coefficient for A has magnitude at least √(α³/2). Take the common kernel, the vectors where all these characters equal 1.

**Problem.** The common kernel of the large spectrum is a subspace inside 2A − 2A, the set of sums a + b − c − d from A. Its codimension is at most 2/α².

**How the definition helps.** Selecting large coefficients lets us force their contributions to the representation count to have the same sign. In our own proof, Fourier inversion counts representations using fourth powers of the coefficient magnitudes, weighted by character values. On the common kernel every large term is nonnegative, and the constant term contributes α⁴. Parseval’s identity says the squared magnitudes sum to α. The threshold therefore bounds the combined magnitude of the small terms by α⁴/2 and the number of large terms by 2/α². The cited theorem gives a stronger codimension bound by a different argument.

**Paper or page:** [A bilinear Bogolyubov-Ruzsa lemma with poly-logarithmic bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04965v2). It says: “there exists a subspace V of 𝔽ⁿ of codimension O(log⁴ α⁻¹) such that V ⊆ 2A−2A.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Minimal growth controls repeated sums

**Remember:** Use the least expensive subset at every addition.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B13 (Additive bases, including sumsets), 11P70. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A and B be finite nonempty sets in an abelian group, and X + B the set of sums x + b. Choose a nonempty subset X of A that minimizes the growth ratio \|X + B\|/\|X\|. Write K for this minimum.

**Problem.** For every positive integer j, \|X + jB\| ≤ Kʲ\|X\|, where jB is the set of sums of j elements of B.

**How the definition helps.** Choosing X by its smallest growth ratio lets one bound every later addition using the same K. Starting with A itself only gives a bound for the first addition. Petridis proved that \|C + X + B\| ≤ K\|C + X\| for every finite C. The proof uses minimality to control overlaps between translates of X. In our own derivation, take C successively as {0}, B, B + B, and so on.

**Wikipedia:** [Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pl%C3%BCnnecke%E2%80%93Ruzsa_inequality). It says: “is a nonempty subset that minimizes the value of”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The stabilizer of a sumset extends Cauchy–Davenport to all abelian groups

**Remember:** Measure sumsets against their stabilizer, and subgroups stop being counterexamples.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B13 (Additive bases, including sumsets), 11P70. arXiv math.CO, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The sumset A + B is the set of all sums a + b. Its stabilizer Sym(A + B) is the subgroup K of elements g with A + B + g = A + B. The Cauchy–Davenport theorem says \|A + B\| ≥ min(p, \|A\| + \|B\| − 1) in a cyclic group of prime order p.

**Problem.** Kneser's theorem bounds \|A + B\| from below for finite nonempty sets A and B in any abelian group. With K the stabilizer, it says \|A + B\| ≥ \|A + K\| + \|B + K\| − \|K\|.

**How the definition helps.** The stabilizer absorbs the subgroups that would break the simple bound. Take A = B = H for a subgroup H with more than one element (our own example). Then \|A + B\| = \|H\|, which is less than 2\|H\| − 1. Kneser's bound gives equality there, because K = H. In a group of prime order, K is trivial or the whole group, and one recovers Cauchy–Davenport (our own remark). The proof of Kneser's theorem itself is still delicate.

**Wikipedia:** [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kneser%27s<sub>theorem</sub>\_(combinatorics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/https%3A//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kneser%2527s_theorem_%28combinatorics%29). It says: “They may be regarded as extensions of the Cauchy–Davenport theorem, which also concerns sumsets in groups but is restricted to groups whose order is a prime number.”

**Paper or page:** [On Lev's periodicity conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15174). It says: “If A, B are two finite nonempty subsets of an abelian group G and K=Sym(A+B), then \|A+B\| ≥ \|A+K\|+\|B+K\|−\|K\|.”

**Sources:**

- [Christian Reiher, On Lev's periodicity conjecture, arXiv:2408.15174 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15174)

### Balanced indicators expose missing progressions

**Remember:** Subtract the density before looking for missing patterns.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a cyclic group of prime order N, let A have density α&gt;0. Its balanced indicator is its indicator minus α. Measure this function with the Gowers norm of order k−1, which averages alternating products on additive cubes.

**Problem.** Fix k≥3, with N≥k and Nαᵏ⁻¹≥2. If A contains no k-term progression with nonzero difference, its balanced indicator has Gowers norm of order k−1 at least αᵏ/(2k).

**How the definition helps.** Centering turns a missing progression into a discrepancy from the count for the constant function α (our own argument). With only zero differences, the normalized count equals α/N, at most αᵏ/2. Replacing each indicator in turn by α expresses the discrepancy as k terms. The generalized von Neumann inequality bounds each term by the balanced indicator’s norm.

**Paper or page:** [An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014). It says: “Let k ≥ 3, let G be a finite additive group with (N,(k−1)!) = 1”

**Sources:**

- [Ben Green and Terence Tao, An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm, arXiv:math/0503014v4](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014)

### Centered Fourier uniformity counts three-term progressions

**Remember:** Remove the constant term so Fourier coefficients measure the counting error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A have density δ in a finite abelian group G of size n. For each homomorphism χ from G to the complex unit circle, average (1ₐ−δ) times the conjugate of χ. Here 1ₐ is the indicator of A. Call A Fourier ε-uniform if every such average has modulus at most ε.

**Problem.** Suppose n is odd and A is Fourier ε-uniform. The number of pairs (x,r) with x, x+r and x+2r in A differs from δ³n² by at most εn².

**How the definition helps.** Centering removes the constant Fourier coefficient, leaving only terms that measure the counting error (our own explanation). In the Fourier expansion, each nonconstant term uses frequencies χ, χ and χ⁻². Odd order makes χ⁻² nonconstant whenever χ is nonconstant. Uniformity bounds that factor by ε, and Parseval’s identity bounds the sum of the other squared moduli by one.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “Let G be an additive group of odd order and suppose A ⊆ G is Fourier ε-uniform.”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)

### Coset averages absorb large Fourier coefficients

**Remember:** A character survives coset averaging exactly when it is trivial on the subspace.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a subspace H of the vector space 𝔽ₚⁿ over the field of prime order p, define g(x) as the mean of f on x+H. This coset average preserves the range \[0,1\]. A normalized Fourier coefficient averages a function times the conjugate of a character, a homomorphism to the unit circle.

**Problem.** For every f from 𝔽ₚⁿ to \[0,1\] and ε&gt;0, there is a subspace H of codimension at most ε⁻². Every normalized Fourier coefficient of f minus its coset model has modulus at most ε.

**How the definition helps.** Coset averaging preserves selected frequencies while keeping the model bounded, which truncating a Fourier series need not do (our own explanation). Intersect the kernels of the characters whose coefficients exceed ε in modulus. Parseval bounds their number by ε⁻², so at most that many independent linear conditions define H. Character orthogonality shows that averaging preserves these coefficients and either preserves or kills every other coefficient.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “being a linear combination of at most 1/ε² characters with coefficients bounded in magnitude by 1”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)
- [Fox and Zhao, Removal lemmas and approximate homomorphisms, Combinatorics, Probability and Computing 31 (2022), Lemma 5.2](https://doi.org/10.1017/s0963548321000572)

### Cube products yield the triangle inequality

**Remember:** Expand the cube of a sum, then bound each mixed cube.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Choose a base point and d steps independently and uniformly in a finite abelian group. Each subset of steps gives a vertex by adding those steps to the base point. The cube average multiplies one function value per vertex, conjugates factors for odd subsets, and averages the product. Using f throughout and taking the 2ᵈ-th root gives its Gowers Uᵈ norm.

**Problem.** For d ≥ 2, the Gowers Uᵈ norm of f+g is at most the sum of their Gowers Uᵈ norms.

**How the definition helps.** Allowing different functions at the vertices gives one inequality for every mixed term in the expansion of f+g (our own explanation). Repeated Cauchy–Schwarz bounds each mixed average by the product of its vertex norms. Summing these bounds gives the binomial expansion of the sum of the two norms raised to 2ᵈ.

**Paper or page:** [Parseval-type identities for Gowers uniformity norms in finite abelian groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08968). It says: “Then we have ‖f₀+f₁‖(Uᴬ˒ˡ) ≤ ‖f₀‖(Uᴬ˒ˡ)+‖f₁‖(Uᴬ˒ˡ).”

**Sources:**

- [Martin Niepel, Parseval-type identities for Gowers uniformity norms in finite abelian groups, arXiv:2508.08968v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08968)

### Fourier moments expose large coefficients

**Remember:** A large fourth moment needs a large coefficient when the second moment is bounded.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be real on a finite abelian group. A character χ is a homomorphism to the complex unit circle. Its Fourier coefficient f̂(χ) is the mean of f times the conjugate of χ. Define the U² norm as the fourth root of the sum of \|f̂(χ)\|⁴ over all characters.

**Problem.** If \|f\| ≤ 1 and its U² norm is at least δ, some character χ has \|f̂(χ)\| ≥ δ².

**How the definition helps.** The fourth moment directly bounds the largest coefficient when the second moment is bounded (our own argument). Indeed, the fourth moment is at most the largest squared modulus times the second moment. Parseval’s identity makes the second moment equal to the mean of \|f\|². The usual definition averages products over parallelograms, and character orthogonality proves the two formulas agree.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “‖f‖(U²(G)) = ‖f̂‖(ℓ⁴(Ĝ)).”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)

### Independence keeps entropic distance nonnegative

**Remember:** An independent difference cannot have less entropy than either summand.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite distribution with positive probabilities p, its entropy H is the sum of −p log p over its outcomes. Draw independent samples X′ and Y′ from two given distributions on an abelian group. Their entropic Ruzsa distance is H(X′ − Y′) − (H(X′) + H(Y′))/2.

**Problem.** Entropic Ruzsa distance is nonnegative for any two finitely supported distributions on an abelian group.

**How the definition helps.** Independent sampling rules out cancellation caused by using the same draw twice. In our own example, set Y = X for a fair bit on the two-element group. Their actual difference has entropy zero, giving distance −log 2. With independent draws, fixing either draw leaves the entropy of the other in the difference. Conditioning cannot increase entropy, so the difference has at least the larger individual entropy.

**Paper or page:** [Marton's Conjecture in abelian groups with bounded torsion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02244v2). It says: “if X,Y are independent, then H\[X\], H\[Y\] are both at most H\[X ± Y\].”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Multiplicative differences expose Fourier structure

**Remember:** A large cube average forces many differences with large Fourier coefficients.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a complex function f on a finite abelian group, its multiplicative difference Δₕf(x) is f(x+h) times the conjugate of f(x). Define ‖f‖ᵤ₃⁸ as the mean over h of ‖Δₕf‖ᵤ₂⁴. For any g, ‖g‖ᵤ₂⁴ sums the fourth powers of its normalized Fourier coefficient moduli.

**Problem.** Let \|f\|≤1 and ‖f‖ᵤ₃≥η&gt;0. For at least a fraction η⁸/2 of the shifts h, some normalized Fourier coefficient of Δₕf has modulus at least η⁴/√2.

**How the definition helps.** The recursive definition exposes an average of Fourier moments directly (our own argument). Each moment is at most one, so a fraction at least η⁸/2 of the shifts must reach η⁸/2. Parseval bounds the sum of squared coefficient moduli by one. The fourth moment therefore forces one coefficient to reach η⁴/√2.

**Paper or page:** [An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014). It says: “Let G be an arbitrary finite additive group, and let f : G → 𝒟 be a bounded function”

**Sources:**

- [Ben Green and Terence Tao, An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm, arXiv:math/0503014v4](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014)

### Quadratic phases preserve cube norms

**Remember:** A quadratic phase cancels across the eight cube vertices.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An additive difference replaces P(x) by P(x + h) − P(x) for a chosen step h. Call exp(2πiP) a quadratic phase if P takes values modulo 1 and every third additive difference vanishes. The eighth power of the Gowers U³ norm averages products over x and three independent uniform steps. Include all eight subset sums of the steps added to x, conjugating the function values from odd-sized subsets.

**Problem.** On a finite abelian group, multiplying a function by a quadratic phase does not change its Gowers U³ norm.

**How the definition helps.** Defining quadratic phases by differences makes their eight factors cancel inside the norm. In our own calculation their product is the exponential of a signed third difference, hence equals 1. This avoids choosing coefficients for a quadratic formula. The cited representation theorem identifies these difference-defined phases with explicit quadratic formulas on groups of odd order.

**Paper or page:** [An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014v4). It says: “Conversely, all such functions x ↦ Mx · x + ξ · x + c are globally quadratic phase functions.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regular Bohr sets absorb small shifts

**Remember:** Small changes in radius control small shifts.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a finite abelian group, a character sends sums to products on the unit circle. A Bohr set B contains the elements that d chosen characters all send within distance r of 1. Call B regular if scaling r by 1 + t changes its size by at most 100d\|t\| times its original size. Require this for d ≥ 1 and \|t\| ≤ 1/(100d).

**Problem.** Take 0 &lt; ρ &lt; 1 and a shift x from the Bohr set with radius ρr. The uniform probabilities on B and B + x differ by at most 200ρd when we sum their absolute differences.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity controls points gained by enlarging B, which an arbitrary radius need not do. In our own proof, both B and B + x fit inside the set of radius (1 + ρ)r. Their sizes agree, so their symmetric difference contains at most twice the number of added points. Regularity gives the bound for 100ρd ≤ 1. Otherwise the total difference between two probability distributions is at most 2. Finding a regular radius near a prescribed radius takes a separate lemma.

**Paper or page:** [Sparse graph counting and Kelley-Meka bounds for binary systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12248v5). It says: “If B is a regular Bohr set of rank d”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Zero extension removes the ambient modulus

**Remember:** Divide by the interval’s cube norm to cancel the ambient group.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Choose integers d ≥ 2 and M &gt; 2ᵈN. Extend f on \[1,N\] by zero modulo M. Average the product of f over x plus every subset sum of d steps, conjugating factors from odd subsets. Take the 2ᵈ-th root and divide by the same quantity for the interval indicator.

**Problem.** For d ≥ 2, this normalized interval norm is independent of the choice of M &gt; 2ᵈN.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing by the indicator’s norm cancels the proportion of cubes inside the interval (our own explanation). Without that division, the average includes zeros from cubes outside the interval. Each surviving step lifts to the integer difference between its endpoint and the base point. The bound on M ensures that every lifted vertex agrees with its interval representative.

**Wikipedia:** [Gowers norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gowers_norm). It says: “This definition does not depend on Ñ, as long as Ñ &gt; 2ᵈN.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Discrete logarithms build Sidon sets

**Remember:** Equal exponent sums give equal products of monic linear factors at θ.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B75 (Other combinatorial number theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let q be a prime power and h ≥ 2. Choose a generator θ of the multiplicative group of the field with qʰ elements. For each λ in its subfield with q elements, record the exponent a modulo qʰ − 1 such that θᵃ = θ − λ.

**Problem.** The q exponents form a Sidon set of order h in the cyclic group of order q raised to h minus 1. This means an h-term sum, with repeats allowed, determines its summands up to order.

**How the definition helps.** Taking exponents replaces a search for repeated sums by a polynomial identity. In our own proof, equal sums modulo qʰ − 1 give equal products at θ. Subtract the two monic degree-h products. Their difference has degree below h and vanishes at θ. Only the zero polynomial can do this because θ has degree h over the smaller field. Unique factorization then recovers the summands, including repetitions.

**Paper or page:** [The Bose-Chowla argument for Sidon sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12711v3). It says: “is a classical Sidon set of order h modulo qʰ − 1 and cardinality q.”

**Sources:**

- [Melvyn B. Nathanson, The Bose–Chowla argument for Sidon sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12711v3)

### Positive genus makes Siegel's theorem on integral points exclude Pell equations

**Remember:** Genus at least one, or three points at infinity, means finitely many integer points.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11D45 (Counting solutions of Diophantine equations), 14G05, 14H25. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The genus of a smooth algebraic curve counts its holes as a complex surface (our own). The points at infinity of an affine curve are the points added when one closes it up to a projective curve. An integral point has coordinates in the ring of integers of the number field.

**Problem.** A smooth affine curve over a number field has finitely many integral points when its genus is positive. The same holds for genus zero with at least three points at infinity. Siegel proved this in 1929.

**How the definition helps.** The conditions remove the curves whose integral points come from a group that can be infinite (our own). The affine line has genus zero and one point at infinity, and every integer is a point on it. The Pell curve x² − dy² = 1, with d &gt; 0 not a square, has genus zero, two points at infinity and infinitely many integral points. The hard part is Siegel's proof, which combines Diophantine approximation with the Mordell–Weil theorem.

**Wikipedia:** [Siegel's theorem on integral points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel%27s_theorem_on_integral_points). It says: “The condition is sharp. A curve of genus zero with one or two points at infinity can have infinitely many integral points”

**Sources:**

- [C. L. Siegel, On some applications of Diophantine approximations, trans. C. Fuchs, ed. U. Zannier, Quaderni/Monographs 2, Edizioni della Normale, 2014 (German original 1929)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-88-7642-520-2)

### Degree at least 3 and irreducibility make Thue equations finite

**Remember:** Quadratic forms allow Pell's infinitely many solutions; cubic irreducible forms do not.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11D57 (Multiplicative and norm form equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Thue equation is f(x, y) = r, where f is a homogeneous polynomial in two variables. The polynomial f must be irreducible over the rationals and have degree at least 3, and r must be nonzero.

**Problem.** Thue proved in 1909 that a Thue equation has only finitely many integer solutions. Later work gives explicit bounds for the solutions.

**How the definition helps.** Each condition removes a known infinite family of solutions. In degree 2, x² − 2y² = 1 is a Pell equation with infinitely many solutions (our own). A reducible form can also fail: (x − y)³ = 1 holds whenever x = y + 1 (our own). With the conditions, f(x, y) = r would give rational numbers x/y very close to a root of f(t, 1). Thue's theorem on rational approximation shows that this can happen only finitely often. The hard part is that approximation theorem, later improved by Siegel and Roth.

**Wikipedia:** [Thue equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thue_equation). It says: “where f is an irreducible bivariate homogeneous polynomial of degree at least 3 over the rational numbers, and r is a nonzero rational number.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Thue, Über Annäherungswerte algebraischer Zahlen, J. reine angew. Math. 135 (1909) 284–305](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1909.135.284)
- [E. Bombieri and W. M. Schmidt, On Thue's equation, Invent. Math. 88 (1987) 69–81](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01405092)

### Hilbert symbols complete local classification

**Remember:** The determinant counts factors, and the Hasse invariant pairs them.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11E08 (Quadratic forms over local rings and fields), 11E95. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over the p-adic numbers ℚₚ, write a nonsingular quadratic form as a sum of squares with nonzero coefficients. The Hilbert symbol (a,b) equals 1 if z² = ax² + by² has a nonzero solution over ℚₚ, and −1 otherwise. The Hasse invariant multiplies these signs over all unordered pairs of distinct coefficient positions.

**Problem.** Two nondegenerate quadratic forms over ℚₚ are isometric exactly when their dimensions, determinant square classes, and Hasse invariants agree.

**How the definition helps.** The extra sign retains the interactions between coefficients that the determinant loses (our own). Over ℚ₃, the diagonal triples (1, 1, 1) and (1, 3, 3) have equal determinant square classes (our own). Their Hasse invariants differ because the symbol of (3, 3) is −1 over ℚ₃ (our own). The local classification theorem does the work of proving that no further invariant is needed (our own).

It says: “This is independent of the choice of diagonal form.”

### The Hilbert symbol turns quadratic reciprocity into one product formula

**Remember:** At each place, the Hilbert symbol asks whether a conic has a point.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E08 (Quadratic forms over local rings and fields), 11S31, 11A15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A place v of ℚ is either a prime p or the real place ∞. The completion ℚᵥ is then the p-adic numbers ℚₚ or the real numbers ℝ. For nonzero a and b, the Hilbert symbol (a,b)ᵥ is 1 if ax² + by² = z² has a nonzero solution in ℚᵥ. Otherwise it is −1.

**Problem.** For nonzero rationals a and b, (a,b)ᵥ = 1 at all but finitely many places, and the product of (a,b)ᵥ over all places v is 1. This one formula contains quadratic reciprocity and its two supplementary laws.

**How the definition helps.** The symbol is defined at every place, including the real place and the prime 2, so the whole law fits into one symmetric formula. In words, the conic ax² + by² = z² fails to have a point at an even number of places. The supplementary laws come from the factors at 2 and at the real place. The definition makes the law easy to state, not easy to prove: over ℚ the usual proof of the product formula uses quadratic reciprocity itself.

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_symbol). It says: “Therefore, the following product formula ∏ᵥ (a,b)ᵥ = 1 makes sense. It is equivalent to the law of quadratic reciprocity.”

- [J. Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, Springer (1999), p. 334](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-03983-0)

### Hyperbolic planes localize Witt indices

**Remember:** Split one plane and repeat the local test.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E12 (Quadratic forms over global rings and fields), 11E81. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A hyperbolic plane is the quadratic form xy. The Witt index counts the most such planes that split off in disjoint pairs of variables after a change of coordinates.

**Problem.** For a nonsingular quadratic form over a number field, its Witt index equals the smallest of its Witt indices over all completions of the field.

**How the definition helps.** Counting planes lets us repeat the local test for a single nonzero zero (our own). If every completion has one, the Hasse–Minkowski theorem gives one over the number field (our own). It supplies a hyperbolic plane, which splits off over the number field and every completion (our own). Witt cancellation lowers all the indices by one, so induction gives the minimum formula (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The density of integral quadratic forms having a k-dimensional totally isotropic subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10495v1), [The density of integral quadratic forms having a k-dimensional totally isotropic subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10495v1). It says: “If (V₁,Q) and (V₂,Q) are regular and isometric, then (V₁⊥,Q) and (V₂⊥,Q) are also isometric.”

### Spinor genera classify indefinite forms

**Remember:** A spinor genus remembers which local rotations lift.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E12 (Quadratic forms over global rings and fields), 11E41. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix integral lattices in one nonsingular rational quadratic space. A rotation is a linear map preserving the form with determinant one. Two lattices share a proper spinor genus if a rational rotation followed by local rotations matches them over every ring of p-adic integers. Each local rotation must lift to the spin group, the algebraic double cover of the rotation group.

**Problem.** A proper spinor genus of a nondegenerate indefinite integral form of rank at least three has exactly one proper integral isometry class.

**How the definition helps.** The spinor genus restricts local rotations to ones that strong approximation can match on the lattices (our own). Indefiniteness makes the real spin group noncompact (our own). Strong approximation supplies one rational spin rotation with all the required local lattice images (our own). The resulting rational rotation identifies the integral lattices because their local images agree at every prime (our own).

**Remember:** Compose with the inverse and look for a square.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms), 11E41. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a negative fundamental discriminant, the discriminant of an imaginary quadratic field. For primitive positive definite binary quadratic forms of that discriminant, proper classes identify forms under determinant-one integer changes of variables. Gauss composition multiplies these classes. Genus characters are sign-valued homomorphisms whose joint values distinguish genera, the classes of forms equivalent over ℝ and every p-adic integer ring.

**Problem.** Two classes are in the same genus exactly when the first composed with the inverse of the second is a square in the class group.

**How the definition helps.** Genus characters replace separate local comparisons with homomorphisms from the class group to signs (our own). Equal signs mean that the quotient of the classes lies in their common kernel (our own). Gauss’s principal genus theorem identifies the common kernel with the subgroup of squares (our own).

### Letting the middle coefficient be odd matches form discriminants with fields

**Remember:** Allow odd middle coefficients, and every quadratic field has its forms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Gauss studied forms ax² + 2bxy + cy² with an even middle coefficient. Eisenstein's convention allows every integer form ax² + bxy + cy², with discriminant b² − 4ac. A fundamental discriminant is a square-free D ≡ 1 mod 4, or 4m with m square-free and ≡ 2 or 3 mod 4.

**Problem.** For each fundamental discriminant D ≠ 1 there is exactly one quadratic field of discriminant D. Its narrow class group is isomorphic to the class group of primitive forms of discriminant D. For D &lt; 0 one uses only positive definite forms.

**How the definition helps.** With odd middle coefficients allowed, the norm forms of all quadratic fields are integer forms of the field's own discriminant (our own). For example, the ring of integers of ℚ(√−3) has norm form x² + xy + y², which Gauss's even convention does not allow (our own). Under that convention no discriminant D ≡ 1 mod 4 has any forms at all (our own). The hard part is the correspondence between forms and ideals, where composition of forms becomes multiplication of ideals.

**Wikipedia:** [Binary quadratic form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_quadratic_form), [Discriminant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant). ### Proper equivalence makes Gauss's classes of quadratic forms a group

**Remember:** Gauss counted only orientation-preserving changes of variable, and got a group.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Two binary quadratic forms are properly equivalent if one turns into the other by an integer change of variables with determinant 1. Lagrange also allowed determinant −1.

**Problem.** Composition makes the proper classes of primitive forms of discriminant Δ a finite abelian group. For fundamental Δ, it is isomorphic to the narrow class group of ℚ(√Δ).

**How the definition helps.** Proper equivalence keeps a form apart from its mirror image, and the mirror image is the inverse class. With determinant −1 allowed, the form ax² + bxy + cy² is equivalent to ax² − bxy + cy² (our own). Under composition these two classes are inverses, so Lagrange's classes would merge each class with its inverse (our own). The page does not give this reason, but says that the Lagrange definition is inferior. The match with the narrow class group explains the factor of two for positive discriminants. Dedekind's ideals later made composition plain multiplication of ideals (our own).

It says: “Lagrange used a different notion of equivalence, in which the second condition is replaced by αδ − βγ = ±1. ### Even self-dual lattices give modular symmetry

**Remember:** Evenness gives translation and self-duality gives inversion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E45 (Analytic theory (Epstein zeta functions; relations with automorphic forms and functions)), 11H06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a positive definite lattice, its theta series sums exp(πiz‖v‖²) over all lattice vectors v, where z has positive imaginary part. An even lattice has even integer squared lengths. A self-dual lattice equals the set of vectors whose dot products with all lattice vectors are integers.

**Problem.** The theta series of an even self-dual positive definite lattice of rank n is a modular form of weight n/2 for the full modular group. This means it satisfies the translation and inversion laws and is holomorphic on the upper half-plane and at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** The two lattice conditions match the two generators of the modular group (our own). Evenness fixes every exponential under z replaced by z + 1 (our own). Poisson summation turns inversion into the theta series of the dual, so self-duality closes the formula (our own). The analytic work goes into Poisson summation and the Fourier transform of a Gaussian (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Leech lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leech_lattice). It says: “the theta function of an even unimodular lattice of rank n is actually a modular form of weight n/2 for the full modular group”

### Dimension parity survives Witt equivalence

**Remember:** A hyperbolic plane changes dimension by two.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E81 (Algebraic theory of quadratic forms; Witt groups and rings). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Start with nonsingular quadratic forms over a field of characteristic different from two. Two forms represent the same Witt class if adding copies of the plane xy to each makes them equal after a change of variables. The Witt ring adds classes by summing forms in separate variables and multiplies classes by taking tensor products.

**Problem.** Dimension modulo two is a surjective ring map from the Witt ring to the field with two elements. Its kernel, the fundamental ideal, is maximal.

**How the definition helps.** Every discarded plane has even dimension, so parity descends to classes. It respects sum and product because dimensions add and multiply before taking the quotient (our own). The quadratic-form work is proving the stable equivalence agrees with having isometric anisotropic parts, the parts with no nonzero zeros (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Witt group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_group). It says: “Although classes may contain spaces of different dimension, the parity of the dimension is constant across a class”

### Isotropic Pfister forms split completely

**Remember:** One zero makes the whole Pfister form split.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11E81 (Algebraic theory of quadratic forms; Witt groups and rings). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a field of characteristic other than two, a Pfister form is a tensor product of binary forms x² − ay² with each a nonzero. In contrast, an arbitrary quadratic form of the same dimension need not have this tensor structure.

**Problem.** A Pfister form that vanishes at a nonzero vector is hyperbolic. That is, it is an orthogonal sum of planes with form xy.

**How the definition helps.** The tensor definition splits a Pfister form into two scaled copies φ and −aφ of a shorter Pfister form φ (our own). If φ has no nonzero zero, isotropy makes a a ratio of nonzero values of φ (our own). Pfister’s roundness theorem then takes aφ to φ, and the form pairs each square with its negative, giving hyperbolic planes (our own). The real form x² + y² + z² − t² has a nonzero zero but cannot split into two such planes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Pfister form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pfister_form). It says: “every isotropic Pfister form is in fact hyperbolic”

### Nondegeneracy lets an isotropic vector split off a plane

**Remember:** Pair an isotropic vector with a second vector to split off a plane.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11E81 (Algebraic theory of quadratic forms; Witt groups and rings). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Q be a quadratic form on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic different from two. Two vectors u and v pair by B(u,v) = Q(u + v) − Q(u) − Q(v). Nondegeneracy means every nonzero vector pairs nontrivially with some vector. An isotropic vector is a nonzero vector where Q vanishes.

**Problem.** A nondegenerate quadratic form has an isotropic vector exactly when it splits as xy plus a form in separate variables.

**How the definition helps.** Nondegeneracy gives an isotropic vector u a partner v, which we scale so B(u,v) = 1 (our own). Replacing v by v − Q(v)u makes its value zero and preserves the pairing (our own). On their span the form is xy, so the span splits off by orthogonality (our own). The degenerate form Q(x,y) = x² vanishes at (0,1) but contains no such plane (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The density of integral quadratic forms having a k-dimensional totally isotropic subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10495v1). It says: “A regular quadratic space (V,Q) is isotropic if and only if V has a subspace V₀ such that the quadratic space (V₀,Q) is a hyperbolic plane.”

### Defining j on elliptic curves makes modular transformations preserve it

**Remember:** Changing the lattice basis does not change the elliptic curve or its j-invariant.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F03 (Modular and automorphic functions), 14H52. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define j on isomorphism classes of complex elliptic curves, identifying curves when their lattices differ by a nonzero complex scale. A lattice is the integer span of two real-linearly independent complex numbers. In lattice coordinates use j = 1728g₂³/(g₂³ − 27g₃²). Here g₂ and g₃ are 60 times the sum of λ⁻⁴ and 140 times the sum of λ⁻⁶ over nonzero lattice points, respectively.

**Problem.** Let j(τ) be the j-invariant of ℂ/(ℤ + ℤτ), where Im τ &gt; 0. Then j((aτ + b)/(cτ + d)) = j(τ) for integers a, b, c and d with ad − bc = 1.

**How the definition helps.** The isomorphism-class definition makes invariance under a lattice basis change automatic. For τ′ = (aτ + b)/(cτ + d), multiplying ℤ + ℤτ′ by cτ + d gives ℤ + ℤτ, so the two parameters describe the same curve. The formula is a well-defined invariant because its numerator and both terms of its denominator scale by α⁻¹² (our own). The work goes into constructing the invariant and showing the denominator is nonzero on the upper half-plane.

**Wikipedia:** [Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form). It says: “For example, the j-invariant j(z) of an elliptic curve, regarded as a function on the set of all elliptic curves, is a modular function.”

### Bounding modular forms at the cusp makes each space finite-dimensional

**Remember:** No poles at the cusp, so only finitely many forms fit.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A modular form of weight k for a group G is a holomorphic function f on the upper half-plane. It satisfies f((az+b)/(cz+d)) = (cz+d)ᵏ f(z) for the matrices of G. It must also stay bounded as Im z → ∞, after each such change of variable. This growth condition is called being holomorphic at the cusps.

**Problem.** For a subgroup G of finite index in SL₂(ℤ), the space Mₖ(G) of modular forms of weight k is finite-dimensional. For the full modular group, its dimension is about k/12, with an explicit formula.

**How the definition helps.** The growth condition forbids poles at the cusp, and a compact curve has only finitely many functions with bounded poles (our own). Without it, E₄jⁿ satisfies the weight 4 law for every n ≥ 0, where E₄ is the Eisenstein series of weight 4 and j is the modular j-function (our own). These functions are linearly independent, so the space would be infinite-dimensional (our own). With the condition, the Riemann–Roch theorem on the compact modular curve gives the dimension.

**Wikipedia:** [Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form). It says: “For example, the spaces Mₖ(G) and Sₖ(G) are finite-dimensional, and their dimensions can be computed thanks to the Riemann–Roch theorem in terms of the geometry of the G-action on H”

- [J.-P. Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 7, Springer, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4684-9884-4)

### Lattice homogeneity gives Eisenstein series their modular transformation law

**Remember:** Scaling the lattice scales every term, while choosing another basis changes nothing.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In the lattice definition, a modular form of weight k is a function F on lattices with F(αΛ) = α⁻ᵏF(Λ) for every α ≠ 0. A lattice is the integer span of two real-linearly independent complex numbers. The function f(τ) = F(ℤ + ℤτ) must be holomorphic for Im τ &gt; 0 and bounded as Im τ tends to infinity.

**Problem.** For even k &gt; 2, let Gₖ(τ) sum (m + nτ)⁻ᵏ over all integer pairs except (0, 0), with Im τ &gt; 0. It satisfies Gₖ(−1/τ) = τᵏGₖ(τ) and Gₖ(τ + 1) = Gₖ(τ).

**How the definition helps.** The lattice definition makes the transformation law a direct consequence of scaling each summand. The sum is over nonzero lattice points, so choosing another basis leaves it unchanged. Replacing τ by τ + 1 keeps the lattice, and replacing τ by −1/τ scales it by 1/τ (our own checks). The work is to justify absolute convergence, check holomorphy at infinity, and prove the lattice and matrix definitions agree.

**Wikipedia:** [Modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_form). It says: “The key idea in proving the equivalence of the two definitions is that such a function F is determined, because of the second condition, by its values on lattices of the form ℤ + ℤτ, where τ ∈ H.”

### Newforms give a Hecke eigenbasis including primes that divide the level

**Remember:** Throw out forms inherited from lower levels, and all Hecke operators diagonalize.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight), 11F25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The group Γ₀(N) consists of integer matrices of determinant 1 whose lower left entry is divisible by N, and its forms have level N. The oldforms of level N are spanned by the forms g(dz). Here g is a cusp form of a smaller level M dividing N, and d divides N/M. The newforms are the cusp forms orthogonal to all oldforms.

**Problem.** On the space of newforms of level N, all Hecke operators commute and are self-adjoint. This includes the operators Tₚ for primes p that divide N. So the newforms have a basis of eigenforms for the full Hecke algebra.

**How the definition helps.** Removing the oldforms removes the copies of lower-level forms, which the Hecke operators cannot separate. An oldform g(z) and its shift g(pz) have the same eigenvalues for the operators at primes not dividing N (our own). On the full cusp space, the operators at primes dividing N need not be self-adjoint (our own). The real work is Atkin and Lehner's study of the operators that move forms between levels (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Atkin–Lehner theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atkin%E2%80%93Lehner_theory). It says: “the algebra of operators on newforms they generate is a finite-dimensional C\*-algebra that is commutative; and by the spectral theory of such operators, there exists a basis for the space of newforms consisting of eigenforms for the full Hecke algebra.”

- [A. O. L. Atkin and J. Lehner, Hecke operators on Γ₀(m), Math. Ann. 185 (1970) 134–160](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01359701)

### Vanishing at the cusps makes the Petersson inner product finite

**Remember:** Forms that die at the cusp have finite length.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F11 (Holomorphic modular forms of integral weight), 11F25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A modular form of weight k is a holomorphic function f on the upper half-plane with f((az+b)/(cz+d)) = (cz+d)ᵏ f(z) for the modular group. It must stay bounded as Im z grows. It has a Fourier expansion Σ aₙ qⁿ with q = e to the power 2πiz. A cusp form is one with a₀ = 0, so it vanishes at the cusp.

**Problem.** The Petersson integral of f ḡ yᵏ dx dy / y² over a fundamental domain converges when f or g is a cusp form. The Hecke operators, natural averaging operators Tₙ on modular forms, are self-adjoint for it. So the cusp forms have a basis of common Hecke eigenforms with real Fourier coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** A cusp form decays like e to the power −2πy high up in the fundamental domain, so the integral converges there (our own). Eisenstein series tend to a nonzero constant at the cusp, so for two of them the integrand grows like yᵏ⁻² and the integral diverges (our own). With a finite inner product, the spectral theorem for commuting self-adjoint operators gives an eigenbasis at once. The size of the eigenvalues is the separate Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture, which Deligne proved (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cusp form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cusp_form), [Petersson inner product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersson_inner_product). It says: “Cuspidality is what is required to make this integral finite.”

**Remember:** Constant terms become residues when the cusp is filled in.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F23 (Relations with algebraic geometry and topology), 11F11. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use a torsion-free subgroup of finite index in the determinant-one integer matrices. Assume that, after moving each cusp to infinity by an integral modular substitution, its stabilizer consists of translations. The cusp is a boundary point, and its width h is the least positive translation in this stabilizer. A weight two form f gives the invariant differential f(τ)dτ.

**Problem.** At each cusp, expand the transformed form in exp(2πiτ/h). The sum of its constant coefficients, each multiplied by its own cusp width, is zero.

**How the definition helps.** Each weighted constant coefficient equals 2πi times the residue of the differential at that cusp (our own). Writing q = exp(2πiτ/h) gives dτ = h dq/(2πiq) (our own). Holomorphy of the form leaves at most a simple pole there (our own). The residue theorem on the compact curve gives the result (our own).

### Normalizing eigenforms by a(1) = 1 makes coefficients equal Hecke eigenvalues

**Remember:** Set the first coefficient to one, and the coefficients become eigenvalues.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F30. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Hecke operators Tₘ are natural averaging operators on modular forms of a fixed weight k. A Hecke eigenform is a nonzero cusp form f = Σ a(n) qⁿ with Tₘ f = λₘ f for every m. It is normalized when a(1) = 1.

**Problem.** For a normalized Hecke eigenform, Tₘ f = a(m) f for all m. The coefficients satisfy a(m)a(n) = Σ dᵏ⁻¹ a(mn/d²), summed over d dividing gcd(m,n). So the coefficients are multiplicative, and the L-function of f has an Euler product.

**How the definition helps.** Once a(1) = 1, the eigenvalue equation read at the first coefficient says a(m) = λₘ. The first coefficient of Tₘ f is a(m), so λₘ a(1) = a(m), and a(1) is not 0 for a nonzero eigenform (our own). The multiplication rule of the Hecke operators then becomes a rule for the coefficients. For Ramanujan's Δ, the cusp form of weight 12, this gives τ(mn) = τ(m)τ(n) for coprime m and n.

**Wikipedia:** [Hecke operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_operator). It says: “Thus for normalized cuspidal Hecke eigenforms of integer weight, their Fourier coefficients coincide with their Hecke eigenvalues.”

### Quasimodularity preserves derivatives

**Remember:** Allow the extra chain-rule term instead of losing derivatives.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F37. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a determinant-one integer matrix with bottom row (c,d), remove the usual weight factor from the transformed holomorphic function f. A quasimodular form allows the result to be a polynomial in c/(cτ + d) with constant term f. Its coefficient functions are holomorphic, including in the Fourier coordinate at the cusp.

**Problem.** Differentiation maps a weight k quasimodular form to a weight k + 2 quasimodular form. The ordinary modular forms are not closed under differentiation, as the derivative of E₄ shows.

**How the definition helps.** The polynomial allows exactly the extra factors that the chain rule introduces (our own). Differentiation raises the weight by two and the polynomial degree by at most one. The ordinary weight-four Eisenstein series E₄ has a nonzero extra term, so its derivative fails the ordinary modular law (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Almost holomorphic modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_holomorphic_modular_form). It says: “Ramanujan observed that the derivative of any quasimodular form is another quasimodular form.”

**Paper or page:** [Quasimodular forms and modular differential equations which are not apparent at cusps: I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.04890v1). It says: “of quasimodular forms on Γ is closed under differentiation.”

**Sources:**

- [Don Zagier, Elliptic Modular Forms and Their Applications](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-74119-0_1)

### Refinements select Hecke eigenlines

**Remember:** A root chooses a direction in the two old copies.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F25 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (one variable)), 11F85. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Start with a normalized cusp eigenform f of weight k and level N, so its first Fourier coefficient is one. For simplicity take trivial character and a prime p outside N. Write a for its pth Fourier coefficient. A refinement chooses one root α of the polynomial X² − aX + pᵏ⁻¹.

**Problem.** At level Np, Uₚ replaces each nth Fourier coefficient by the coefficient at pn. If the roots differ, the span of f(τ) and f(pτ) has two Uₚ eigenlines. Each refinement labels the line with the chosen eigenvalue.

**How the definition helps.** The chosen root specifies one eigenvalue and hence one line (our own). If β is the other root, the line with eigenvalue α is generated by f(τ) − β f(pτ) (our own). The work is computing Uₚ on this span and showing that its characteristic polynomial is the original pth Hecke polynomial (our own).

**nLab:** [eigenvariety](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/eigenvariety). It says: “α is a root of the p-th Hecke polynomial.”

### Even self-dual lattices give modular theta series

**Remember:** Even norms give translation and self-duality gives inversion.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F27 (Theta series; Weil representation; theta correspondences), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L be a positive definite lattice with integer inner products. Call L even if every squared length is even. Call it self-dual if it contains exactly the vectors in its real span having integer inner products with every lattice vector. Its theta series sums exp(πiτ⟨v,v⟩) over v in L for τ in the upper half-plane.

**Problem.** For such a lattice of rank 8m with m a positive integer, the theta series is a scalar modular form of weight 4m for SL₂(ℤ). The odd self-dual lattice ℤ⁸ fails the translation rule.

**How the definition helps.** Evenness fixes every summand under τ ↦ τ + 1, while self-duality returns the same lattice under inversion (our own). For ℤ⁸, translation changes the sign of the terms from vectors of squared length one (our own). Gaussian Poisson summation proves the inversion formula at −1/τ with weight 4m (our own). Translation and inversion generate the modular group, and positive definiteness gives holomorphy at infinity (our own).

**nLab:** [Jacobi theta function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+theta+function). It says: “By the Poisson summation formula the number-theoretic theta function θ(0,z) satisfies the following functional equation”

### Distinct indices become orthogonal

**Remember:** As level grows, the nonzero moduli in the formula grow too.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F30 (Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms), 11F72. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix even weight k ≥ 4 and positive Fourier indices m,n. Let Γ₀(q) consist of determinant-one integer matrices with lower-left entry divisible by q. Use a Petersson-orthonormal basis of holomorphic weight k forms with trivial character vanishing at all ends. Sum the conjugate mth times the nth Fourier coefficient and multiply by Γ(k−1) divided by (4π√(mn)) to the power k−1.

**Problem.** As the positive integer q grows, this sum tends to one for equal indices and zero otherwise. The error is O(q to the power 1−k), with k,m,n fixed.

**How the definition helps.** The normalization fixes the diagonal contribution, while every other term has a modulus c divisible by q. In our own estimate, the Petersson formula writes each such term with a Kloosterman-type exponential sum of size at most c and a Bessel function of order k−1 at an argument proportional to 1/c. This gives terms of order c to the power 1−k. Summing over positive multiples of q gives the error bound.

**Paper or page:** [On the Density of Low Lying Zeros of a Large Family of Automorphic L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.09050v2). It says: “where δ(m,n) = 1 when m=n and 0 otherwise and S denotes a Kloosterman sum.”

### Harmonic weights normalize Petersson diagonals

**Remember:** Weight each form by the reciprocal of its squared norm.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F30 (Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms), 11F72. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix even k ≥ 4 and positive integer q. Use holomorphic cusp forms of weight k and trivial character for Γ₀(q), the determinant-one integer matrices with lower-left entry divisible by q. These forms obey the weight k transformation law and vanish at every cusp, or end. Give each orthogonal basis vector f weight Γ(k−1) divided by (4π) to the power k−1 and by its squared Petersson norm.

**Problem.** Divide the nth Fourier coefficient by n to the power (k−1)/2 and call the result a(n). For positive m and n, the Petersson formula writes the weighted sum of conjugate a(m) times a(n) as a diagonal term plus other terms. The diagonal term equals one for m = n and zero otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** The reciprocal squared norm cancels any rescaling of a basis vector, and the common factor sets the diagonal coefficient to one. The Petersson norm integrates \|f(z)\|² times y to the power k against hyperbolic area on the quotient. In our own derivation, expanding a sum of translates of one Fourier mode in the orthogonal basis supplies the reciprocal norm. Computing its other Fourier coefficients gives the remaining terms in the formula.

**Wikipedia:** [Petersson trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petersson_trace_formula). It says: “a kind of orthogonality relation between coefficients of a holomorphic modular form.”

**Paper or page:** [Trace formula and functional equation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16921v2). It says: “δ(m=n) + 2π i⁻ᵏ ∑₍c&gt;0, c≡0 (D)₎ Sχ(m,n;c)/c J₍k−1₎(4π√(mn)/c).”

### Poincaré series extract coefficients

**Remember:** Average one mode to recover one coefficient.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F30 (Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For the full modular group and even weight k &gt; 2, start with the Fourier mode exp(2πinτ), where n is a positive integer. Sum its weight k transforms over left cosets of the subgroup that fixes infinity. This subgroup consists of integer translations together with the central sign. The resulting cusp form is the nth Poincaré series.

**Problem.** Pair a cusp form with this series using the Petersson integral, linear in the cusp form, without dividing by the domain’s area. The result is its nth Fourier coefficient times Γ(k − 1) divided by (4πn) to the power k − 1. These series span the space of cusp forms.

**How the definition helps.** Averaging one Fourier mode turns the integral over a modular domain into a strip integral against that mode (our own). This replaces integrating a general product by Fourier orthogonality, which selects one coefficient (our own). A cusp form orthogonal to every series then has all coefficients zero (our own). Absolute convergence justifies unfolding the sum for k &gt; 2 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Poincaré series (modular form)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincar%C3%A9_series_%28modular_form%29). It says: “In general, the Poincaré series is, for n ≥ 1, a cusp form.”

### Dual isogenies make Fricke involutive

**Remember:** Dualize the isogeny twice to recover it.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F32 (Modular correspondences, etc.), 14G35. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over ℂ, a point of Y₀(N) represents an elliptic curve and a quotient map φ with cyclic kernel of order N. Its dual is the reverse map whose composite with φ multiplies points by N. Define the Fricke map by sending φ to its dual.

**Problem.** The Fricke map on Y₀(N) is an involution. It extends to an involution of its smooth compactification X₀(N).

**How the definition helps.** Dualizing twice recovers φ, so the Fricke map squares to the identity (our own). The dual isogeny theorem gives this identity and preserves cyclic kernels (our own). The cited proposition identifies dualization with the classical map τ ↦ −1/(Nτ). An automorphism of a smooth curve extends to its smooth projective compactification (our own).

**nLab:** [Hecke correspondence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hecke+correspondence). It says: “sending (E,E′) to E and E′ respectively”

### Factorial powers isolate ordinary forms

**Remember:** Factorial powers keep units and kill the rest.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F33 (Congruences for modular and \\(p\\)-adic modular forms), 11F85. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let U be a Hecke operator preserving a finite free module over the p-adic integers. Its ordinary part is the largest direct summand on which U acts invertibly and whose complementary summand has powers tending to zero. Define the ordinary projector by taking the limit of the powers with exponents n!.

**Problem.** The limit exists and is idempotent. Its image is the ordinary part, and it commutes with every operator that commutes with U.

**How the definition helps.** Factorial exponents eventually select the identity on the invertible part and zero on the nilpotent part modulo each power of p (our own). This constructs the projector without factoring a characteristic polynomial (our own). The finite-module decomposition supplies those two parts, and reduction preserves the resulting projectors (our own). Every operator commuting with U commutes with the powers and their limit (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Twisted Triple Product p-adic L-function for Finite Slope Families of Hilbert Modular Forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13230v2). It says: “is the ordinary projector $e<sub>n.o</sub> = \\lim <sub>n\\to \\infty </sub> U<sup>n!</sup>$.”

### Completions preserve quasimodular products

**Remember:** Multiply the completions, then take the constant coefficient.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F37 (Forms of half-integer weight; nonholomorphic modular forms), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At level one, let τ lie in the upper half-plane. A completion of weight k transforms with weight k and is a polynomial in 1/Im(τ) with holomorphic coefficients. Require these coefficients to extend holomorphically in the Fourier coordinate at infinity. Its constant coefficient defines a quasimodular form of weight k, and its degree is called the depth.

**Problem.** The product of level-one quasimodular forms of weights k and ℓ is quasimodular of weight k + ℓ. Its depth, the degree of the completion, is at most the sum of the depths.

**How the definition helps.** The constant coefficient of a product is the product of the constant coefficients (our own). The product of the two completions is modular and has degree at most the sum (our own). The work is the completion theorem, which identifies this definition with the polynomial transformation law (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Almost holomorphic modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_holomorphic_modular_form). It says: “An almost holomorphic modular form is determined by its holomorphic part”

### Half-integral weights compose

**Remember:** Keep the square root in the group element.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F37 (Forms of half-integer weight; nonholomorphic modular forms), 11F27. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let γ be a real determinant-one matrix with bottom row (c,d), acting on the upper half-plane by fractional linear substitutions. Lift γ to a pair (γ,φ), where φ is holomorphic and φ(τ)² = cτ + d. Multiply (γ,φ) by (δ,ψ) using the root φ(δτ)ψ(τ). These pairs form the metaplectic double cover, with two lifts per matrix.

**Problem.** For each integer k, transform f by evaluating it at γτ and dividing by φ(τ) to the power 2k + 1. These transformations give a right group action of weight k + ½.

**How the definition helps.** The group law already multiplies the chosen roots in the order that a slash action needs (our own). Raising that factor to the odd power 2k + 1 preserves the law (our own). The work is identifying the group of pairs with the metaplectic cover (our own).

### Quadratic indices rule out negative terms

**Remember:** A negative direction produces arbitrarily negative traces in its orbit.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F46 (Siegel modular groups; Siegel and Hilbert-Siegel modular and automorphic forms). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Siegel modular form of degree g depends on a symmetric g-by-g complex matrix Z with positive definite imaginary part. Label its Fourier terms exp(2πi tr(TZ)) by symmetric matrices T with integer diagonal and half-integer off-diagonal entries. This groups the frequencies of the separate entries of Z into a quadratic form.

**Problem.** Take a level-one holomorphic function that obeys the Siegel modular law in degree at least two. Its Fourier terms indexed by matrices with a negative direction vanish. In degree one, the modular function j has a pole at infinity.

**How the definition helps.** The quadratic form groups frequencies into integral change-of-basis orbits whose coefficients have the same absolute value (our own). If T has a negative direction, rational approximation gives a primitive integer vector of negative value (our own). Extend it to an integer basis, then add large multiples of it to another basis vector (our own). The resulting traces tend to minus infinity, although the coefficient magnitudes stay fixed (our own). Boundedness on a period cell at imaginary part I forces those coefficients to vanish (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Siegel modular form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_modular_form). It says: “Corollary to this theorem is the fact that Siegel modular forms of degree g &gt; 1 have Fourier expansions and are thus holomorphic at infinity.”

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F50 (Jacobi forms), 11F46. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A classical Jacobi form is holomorphic in two variables τ and z, with τ in the upper half-plane. Its weight controls modular substitutions in τ, and its index controls the exponential factor when z shifts by integer combinations of τ and one. For index m, a Fourier term with frequencies n and r can occur only if 4mn ≥ r².

**Problem.** A degree-two Siegel modular form depends on a symmetric two-by-two complex matrix with positive definite imaginary part. For a level-one form of weight k, expand in the last diagonal entry ω. For each integer m &gt; 0, the coefficient of exp(2πimω) is a Jacobi form of weight k and index m.

**How the definition helps.** The Jacobi definition packages exactly how one Fourier slice transforms under the subgroup preserving the expansion direction (our own). A translation contributes the exponential for that slice's index (our own). The work is restricting the Siegel transformation law to this subgroup and checking the resulting Fourier support (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Jacobi form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_form). It says: “Examples in two variables include Jacobi theta functions, the Weierstrass ℘ function, and Fourier–Jacobi coefficients of Siegel modular forms of genus 2.”

*True by definition.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be a holomorphic level-one cusp form that is an eigenvector of all Hecke averaging operators. Use the normalization with functional equation centered at ½. **Problem.** The resulting L-functions satisfy L(s,f×f̃) = ζ(s)L(s,Ad f), where f̃ denotes the dual. The adjoint function has a finite, nonzero value at 1.

Conjugation fixes that one-dimensional space, so its prime factor is 1/(1−p⁻ˢ). Multiplication over primes gives ζ(s). The Rankin–Selberg pole theorem gives a simple pole at 1 for the full product. Dividing by the simple pole of ζ proves the final claim.

It says: “a\_{\\mathrm{Sym}<sup>j</sup>(\\pi )\\times \\mathrm{Sym}<sup>j</sup>(\\widetilde{\\pi })}(v<sup>\\ell </sup>)&amp; =1+\\sum <sub>r=1</sub><sup>j</sup> a\_{\\mathrm{Sym}<sup>2r</sup>(\\pi )\\otimes \\omega <sub>\\pi </sub><sup>-r</sup>}(v<sup>\\ell </sup>)”

### Root numbers fix vanishing parity

**Remember:** A negative sign allows only odd central Taylor powers.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an automorphic L-function, completion multiplies the series by the exponential and gamma factors in its functional equation. In the self-dual case, the same completed function Λ occurs on both sides. Its root number is the sign ε in Λ(s) = εΛ(1−s).

**Problem.** Suppose Λ is holomorphic at ½ and does not vanish identically. Its vanishing order there is even for ε = 1 and odd for ε = −1. The original series has the same order if its completing factor is holomorphic and nonzero there.

**How the definition helps.** In our own argument, completion makes reflection multiply each central Taylor term by a sign. A term of degree j acquires the factor (−1)ʲ. The first nonzero term must therefore have the parity prescribed by ε. Proving the functional equation supplies the symmetry this argument needs.

**Wikipedia:** [Functional equation (L-function)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_equation_%28L-function%29). It says: “Λ the L-function multiplied by a gamma-factor, and ε a complex number of absolute value 1”

### Unfolding reads the Petersson pairing

**Remember:** The constant residue of E leaves precisely the inner product.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f and g be weight-k cusp forms for SL₂(ℤ), and put h(z) = yᵏ f(z) ḡ(z), with z = x + iy and ḡ the complex conjugate of g. Define I(s) by integrating h(z)E(z,s) over a fundamental domain with measure dx dy/y². The Eisenstein series E sums (Im γz)ˢ over matrices γ modulo the stabilizer of infinity.

**Problem.** Write a(n) and b(n) for the Fourier coefficients of f and g. For Re s &gt; 1, I(s) equals Γ(s+k−1)(4π)<sup>(−(s+k−1))</sup> times the sum of a(n)b̄(n)/nˢ⁺ᵏ⁻¹. Its residue at s = 1 is 3/π times the Petersson inner product of f and g.

**How the definition helps.** The Eisenstein series puts a known constant residue inside the integral defining the pairing. Unfolding integrates each summand over a translated domain and joins these domains into a strip. Integration across the strip keeps exactly the matching Fourier indices. In our own normalization, the remaining gamma integral gives the stated factor, and the residue of E is 3/π.

**Wikipedia:** [Rankin–Selberg method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankin%E2%80%93Selberg_method). It says: “The integral was identified with the convolution L-function by a technique called "unfolding”

### Cusp divisors add periods

**Remember:** Shared endpoints cancel as terms of a divisor.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F67 (Special values of automorphic \\(L\\)-series, periods of automorphic forms, cohomology, modular symbols), 11F75. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A degree-zero divisor of rational cusps is a formal integer sum of points in ℚ ∪ {∞} whose coefficients sum to zero. A weight two modular symbol is an additive map from these divisors to complex numbers, invariant when the modular group under consideration moves the cusps. It assigns the pair (α,β) the value on β − α.

**Problem.** For a weight two cusp form, write its period from α to β as P(α,β). Then P(α,β) + P(β,γ) = P(α,γ). These periods define a linear symbol invariant under the congruence subgroup.

**How the definition helps.** Addition of endpoint divisors cancels the middle cusp, giving the path addition formula immediately (our own). The usual analytic description integrates the differential of a cusp form along paths between cusps (our own). Vanishing at the cusps gives convergence, and simple connectivity of the upper half-plane gives path independence (our own). Invariance of the differential gives invariance of the resulting symbol (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Modular symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_symbol). It says: “Informally, {α,β} represents a homotopy class of paths from α to β in the upper half-plane.”

### Satake makes convolution commutative

**Remember:** Turn convolution into multiplication of symmetric Laurent polynomials.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F70 (Representation-theoretic methods; automorphic representations over local and global fields), 11F25. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be the invertible integral matrices inside GLₙ over a p-adic field. The spherical Hecke algebra consists of compactly supported complex functions invariant under K on both sides, with convolution as multiplication. The Satake transform averages such a function along upper triangular matrices with diagonal entries one, after translation by a diagonal matrix. A factor depending on the diagonal matrix normalizes the average.

**Problem.** The spherical Hecke algebra of GLₙ(F) is commutative.

**How the definition helps.** The transform replaces convolution of functions by ordinary multiplication of symmetric Laurent polynomials, which allows negative exponents (our own). Directly comparing the two convolution integrals is unnecessary (our own). The Satake isomorphism proves that the transform preserves products and detects equality.

**How the definition helps.** One integral converts the chosen modulus weight into a weight for every spectral parameter t. The spectral sum uses Fourier coefficients of cusp eigenfunctions, and the integral uses the Eisenstein series. In our own specialization, compact support gives the required derivative bounds and leaves only finitely many moduli. The equality itself is the Kloosterman summation theorem.

### Centralizers combine conjugate terms

**Remember:** One orbit of conjugate elements needs one quotient integral.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Γ be a discrete group acting freely by orientation-preserving hyperbolic isometries with compact quotient X. Fix γ in Γ and let C contain exactly the elements commuting with γ. For a smooth compactly supported distance weight k, integrate k(d(z,γz)) over C∖ℍ with hyperbolic area. Here ℍ is the hyperbolic plane and d measures distance.

**Problem.** This single integral equals the sum of the diagonal kernel integrals over X indexed by conjugates of γ.

**How the definition helps.** Integrating over C∖ℍ replaces a sum over conjugates with one integral. In our own derivation, the cosets Cg label the conjugates g⁻¹γg exactly once. Translating one fundamental region for Γ by those representatives covers a fundamental region for C up to null sets. Changing variables in each integral gives the equality. Evaluating the resulting integral is a separate step.
