### Completed factors make scattering unitary

**Remember:** On the critical line the scattering quotient divides conjugates.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11M36. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, normalize the Eisenstein eigenfunction so its horizontal average is yˢ + φ(s)y¹⁻ˢ at height y. The coefficient φ(s) measures scattering at the narrowing end. Complete the Riemann zeta function by setting Λ(w) = Γ(w/2)ζ(w) divided by π to the power w/2.

**Problem.** The scattering coefficient equals Λ(2s−1)/Λ(2s). It has absolute value one on Re(s) = ½, including its limiting value −1 at s = ½.

**How the definition helps.** Completion turns the numerator into the conjugate of the denominator on this line. Our own deduction uses the functional equation Λ(w) = Λ(1−w) and conjugation. Away from s = ½ the denominator is nonzero because ζ has no zeros on Re(w) = 1. At the midpoint the simple poles at zero and one have opposite residues. Computing the horizontal average of the Eisenstein series supplies the quotient formula.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_zeta_function). It says: “In this case the determinant of the scattering matrix is given by: φ(s) = π¹ᐟ² Γ(s−1/2) ζ(2s−1) / (Γ(s) ζ(2s)).”

### Congruence gives Selberg’s spectral gap

**Remember:** Finite area alone cannot prevent a small positive eigenvalue.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Call a subgroup of SL(2,ℤ) a congruence subgroup if it contains every matrix congruent to the identity modulo some positive integer. Each such subgroup acts on the upper half-plane by fractional linear transformations.

**Problem.** For congruence subgroups, every positive discrete Laplace eigenvalue on the quotient is at least 3/16. General finite-index subgroups can have arbitrarily small positive eigenvalues.

**How the definition helps.** The congruence condition rules out finite covers on which functions can vary very slowly between sheets, and Selberg’s theorem supplies the uniform bound. Our own counterexample cuts the once-punctured torus, the quotient by the commutator subgroup of PSL(2,ℤ), along a nonseparating closed curve and joins n copies in a ring. A function with sheet values cos(2πj/n), smoothed inside fixed collars, has mean zero and energy divided by squared norm O(1/n²). Below the continuous spectrum starting at ¼, this forces a small positive discrete eigenvalue.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg's 1/4 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg%27s_1/4_conjecture). It says: “Selberg showed that the eigenvalues are at least 3/16.”

### Cusp truncation gives finite norms

**Remember:** Cut the two power terms, not the whole cusp.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, let E(z,s) be the Eisenstein series describing the continuous spectrum. At height y its horizontal average is yˢ + φ(s)y¹⁻ˢ, where φ is the scattering coefficient. In the narrowing end above height Y &gt; 1, subtract this average from E. Use E itself below the cutoff.

**Problem.** For fixed real t ≠ 0 and s = ½+it, the truncated series is square integrable for hyperbolic area. Its squared norm equals 2 log Y + O(1) as Y grows, with the error bound depending on t.

**How the definition helps.** Subtracting the average removes exactly the two waves responsible for the divergent integral. The remaining Fourier modes decay exponentially with height. In our own calculation, each wave contributes log Y below the cutoff since \|φ(s)\| = 1. Their cross term has bounded integral because t ≠ 0. The Maass–Selberg relation gives the full norm formula.

**Wikipedia:** [Maass–Selberg relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maass%E2%80%93Selberg_relations). It says: “However the integral defining the inner product does not converge, so the Eisenstein series first have to be truncated.”

**Sources:**

- [Henryk Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, second edition (2002).](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/053)

### Free compact quotients simplify traces

**Remember:** No fixed points or cusps means only closed geodesics remain.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Γ be a discrete group of orientation-preserving isometries of the hyperbolic plane. Require Γ to have no nonidentity element of finite order and to have compact quotient.

**Problem.** In Selberg’s trace formula, the geometric sum contains only the identity and terms indexed by oriented closed geodesics.

**How the definition helps.** The two conditions exclude rotations about interior points and transformations that produce cusp ends. In our own examples, the modular group contains both the rotation z ↦ −1/z and the translation z ↦ z + 1. Every remaining nonidentity element translates along a geodesic, which closes on the quotient. The trace formula supplies the contribution of each class.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “the group Γ has no parabolic or elliptic elements (other than the identity).”

### Kuznetsov signs select odd forms

**Remember:** Subtracting the two signs cancels every even contribution.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11F30. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use the level one Kuznetsov formula, which relates Fourier coefficients on the modular surface to finite exponential sums. For positive integers m,n, take half the difference of its identities for (m,n) and (m,−n). Use the same even analytic test function with the decay required by the formula in both identities.

**Problem.** Only odd cusp forms contribute on the spectral side. These are Laplace eigenfunctions that change sign under x ↦ −x and have zero horizontal average. Each product of normalized coefficients carries the test weight divided by L(1,ad f), the adjoint L-function of the form evaluated at one.

**How the definition helps.** The difference assigns weight (1−ε)/2 to a form whose reflection sign is ε. This gives weight one to odd forms and zero to even forms. The continuous integrals in the two identities agree and cancel. Our own subtraction uses the signed coefficient formulas proved by Kuznetsov summation.

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ-Norm Bounds for Automorphic Forms via Spectral Reciprocity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.05613v3). It says: “ε₍f₎⁽¹ ∓ ¹⁾⁄² λ₍f₎(m) λ₍f₎(n)/L(1, ad f)”

### Length weights recover primitive counts

**Remember:** Subtract the shorter repeats before counting the new geodesics.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, call an oriented closed geodesic primitive if it traverses its path only once. For each primitive length ℓ, counting multiplicity, place mass ℓ/(2 sinh(mℓ/2)) at mℓ for each positive integer m. Add masses at equal lengths.

**Problem.** The Laplace eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, determine how many primitive oriented geodesics have each length.

**How the definition helps.** The masses record repeated trips with known weights, so shorter geodesics explain part of the mass at every later length. In our own reconstruction, Weyl’s eigenvalue counting law first gives the area. Selberg’s trace formula then determines the masses by integration against smooth even functions. At length ℓ, subtract repeats of all shorter geodesics and divide by ℓ/(2 sinh(ℓ/2)). Only finitely many lengths occur below any bound, so this procedure determines every count.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “so the lengths of primitive closed geodesics are spectral invariants.”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

**Remember:** Remove constants before asking the heat flow to decay.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Γ be a subgroup of SL(2,ℤ) containing every matrix congruent to the identity modulo some positive integer. On its upper half-plane quotient, take square integrable functions whose integral against hyperbolic area is zero.

**Problem.** At time t ≥ 0, heat flow on this space has operator norm at most exp(−3t/16).

**How the definition helps.** The zero integral removes the constant functions, which heat flow leaves unchanged. Selberg proved that every positive discrete Laplace eigenvalue here is at least 3/16. The continuous spectrum begins at ¼. In our own deduction, heat flow multiplies a spectral component at λ by exp(−tλ), giving the bound.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg's 1/4 conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg%27s_1/4_conjecture). It says: “Selberg showed that the eigenvalues are at least 3/16.”

### Odd reflection removes Eisenstein spectrum

**Remember:** Reflection makes the average at the only cusp vanish.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, determinant-one integer matrices identify points z = x+iy of the upper half-plane by fractional linear transformations. Call a square integrable function odd if f(−x+iy) = −f(x+iy) almost everywhere.

**Problem.** On the odd subspace the Laplacian has an orthonormal eigenbasis with finite multiplicities and no finite accumulation of eigenvalues.

**How the definition helps.** Oddness makes the horizontal average vanish at every height where the integral exists. In our own proof, integrate over the period from −½ to ½ and pair x with −x. The surface has just one narrowing end, or cusp, so this average tests the entire cuspidal condition. The Laplacian commutes with reflection, and its spectrum on the cuspidal subspace is discrete.

**Wikipedia:** [Maass wave form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maass_wave_form). It says: “A Maass form f is called even, if i(f)=f and odd if i(f)=−f.”

**Remember:** Opposite nonzero frequencies cannot match on the diagonal.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11F30. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the modular surface, pair Fourier modes of frequencies m and −n for positive integers m,n. Use an even test function h analytic in the strip \|Im(t)\| ≤ ½+δ for some δ &gt; 0. Require h to decay there at least as fast as (1+\|t\|) to the power −2−δ.

**Problem.** In the Kuznetsov formula relating Fourier coefficient averages to exponential sums, these pairs have zero diagonal contribution, even when m = n.

**How the definition helps.** Opposite signs forbid equality of the actual frequencies. In our own derivation, the identity transformation contributes the integral of exp(2πi(m+n)x) over one period. That integral vanishes, whereas equal signed frequencies give an integral of one. The Kuznetsov formula evaluates the remaining contributions.

### Resolvent differences have finite traces

**Remember:** Subtract before tracing to cancel the slow spectral tail.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11M36. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, let Δ be the nonnegative Laplacian. For real a &gt; ½ define its shifted inverse R(a) = (Δ − ¼ + a²)⁻¹. For distinct a,b &gt; ½ take D = R(a) − R(b).

**Problem.** The singular values of D have finite sum, so D has a trace. Neither shifted inverse alone has this property. After subtracting the identity contribution in Selberg’s trace formula, the trace equals F(a) − F(b), where F(a) = Z′(½+a)/(2a Z(½+a)).

**How the definition helps.** Subtraction cancels the leading reciprocal eigenvalue term. In our own proof, Weyl’s law makes the nth eigenvalue grow proportionally to n. The individual inverse eigenvalues decay like 1/n, while their differences decay like 1/n². For the trace identity, the Fourier weight of the single inverse at length u is exp(−a\|u\|)/(2a). Selberg’s trace formula then identifies the closed geodesic sum with the logarithmic derivative of Z, Selberg’s product over primitive geodesics.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “The trace formula is also central to the analytic theory of the Selberg zeta function.”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Short Fourier support removes orbit terms

**Remember:** If the weight cannot reach a length, that orbit cannot contribute.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let X be a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, and let L be its shortest closed geodesic length. Choose a smooth even function g supported in a compact subset of (−L,L). Define h(r) = ∫ℝ g(u) exp(iru) du.

**Problem.** Write each Laplace eigenvalue as ¼ + r², counting multiplicity. Then ∑ h(r) = area(X)/(4π) times ∫ℝ r h(r) tanh(πr) dr.

**How the definition helps.** The support condition kills every closed geodesic term because each length is at least L. In our own application of Selberg’s trace formula, only the identity contributes. An even weight positive at L would retain the shortest geodesics.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_trace_formula). It says: “∑ₙ₌₀∞ h(rₙ) = μ(X)/(4π) ∫₋∞∞ r h(r) tanh(πr) dr + ∑₍{T}₎ log N(T₀)/(N(T)¹ᐟ² − N(T)⁻¹ᐟ²) g(log N(T)).”

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Weighted counts control unweighted errors

**Remember:** Count repeats with their primitive length, then remove them.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 11M36. arXiv math.NT, math.SP. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, call a closed geodesic primitive if it makes one circuit. For each oriented primitive geodesic P of length ℓ, set N(P) = exp(ℓ). Count each positive integer m with mℓ ≤ log X using weight ℓ, and sum over P to obtain Ψ(X).

**Problem.** Fix ½ &lt; θ &lt; 1 and suppose Ψ(X) = X + O(X raised to θ). Then the number of primitive P with N(P) ≤ X differs from ∫₂ˣ du/log u by O((X raised to θ)/log X).

**How the definition helps.** The primitive length weight stays the same on every repeat, so one can remove repeats before removing weights. In our own deduction, double circuits contribute O(√X) by the assumed bound on Ψ. Longer repeats contribute O(X¹ᐟ³ log X), since the shortest length bounds the number of possible exponents by O(log X). Partial summation, the sum version of integration by parts, removes the length weight log N(P). The spectral estimate for Ψ is a hypothesis.

**Wikipedia:** [Prime geodesic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_geodesic). It says: “weighted counting functions analogous to the Chebyshev function”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Zero cusp averages give discrete spectra

**Remember:** Remove the constant Fourier term to remove the continuous part.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F72 (Spectral theory; trace formulas (e.g., that of Selberg)), 58J50. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The modular surface identifies points z = x+iy of the upper half-plane under determinant-one integer matrices acting by fractional linear transformations. A square integrable function belongs to the cuspidal subspace when its periodic lift satisfies ∫₀¹ f(x+iy) dx = 0 for almost every y &gt; 0.

**Problem.** On this subspace the nonnegative Laplacian has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Each eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, and only finitely many lie below any fixed bound.

**How the definition helps.** The zero average removes the horizontally constant mode that can extend far into the narrowing end, called the cusp. In our own proof, the circle Poincaré inequality bounds a zero-average function by its horizontal derivative. With bounded energy, this makes the squared integral above height Y uniformly small as Y grows. Compactness on the remaining bounded region gives discrete spectrum.

**Wikipedia:** [Maass wave form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maass_wave_form). It says: “Then Δₖ operates on C(Γ∖ℋ,k) and has a discrete spectrum.”

- [Henryk Iwaniec, Spectral Methods of Automorphic Forms, second edition (2002).](https://doi.org/10.1090/gsm/053)

### Cyclotomic determinants detect abelian quotients

**Remember:** Over ℚ, the full determinant sees every abelian quotient of the image.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Combine an elliptic curve’s Galois actions on all points of finite order into one representation, called its adelic representation. Its matrices have entries in the profinite integers, which record compatible residues modulo every positive integer. The closed commutator subgroup is the smallest closed normal subgroup with abelian quotient.

**Problem.** For an elliptic curve over ℚ, the kernel of the determinant on its adelic image equals the closed commutator subgroup of that image.

**How the definition helps.** Taking all torsion orders together makes the determinant record the action on every root of unity (our own). At each order the Weil pairing identifies the determinant with the exponent of the action on roots of unity (our own). Kronecker–Weber identifies the field generated by all these roots with the maximal abelian extension of ℚ (our own). Its fixing subgroup is therefore the closed commutator subgroup, and its image remains the closed commutator subgroup in the adelic image (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Degrees of points with rational j-invariant on X₀(n) and X₁(n)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13199v1). It says: “Let $E$ be an elliptic curve defined over $\\Q$. Then, we have $\\cG<sub>E</sub> \\cap \\SL(\\Zhat) = \[\\cG<sub>E</sub>, \\cG<sub>E</sub>\]$.”

### Monodromy isolates infinite inertia

**Remember:** Finite inertia is exactly the part left when monodromy vanishes.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11F85. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a finite extension of ℚₚ and let ℓ be a different prime. Inertia is the subgroup of the Galois group acting trivially on the residue field. A Weil–Deligne description separates a continuous ℓ-adic representation into an action with finite inertia image and a compatible nilpotent operator N. The action uses the Weil group, consisting of elements inducing integer powers of Frobenius on residues.

**Problem.** The original representation has finite inertia image exactly when N is zero.

**How the definition helps.** The Weil–Deligne description puts the potentially infinite part of inertia into one operator (our own). On an open inertia subgroup the matrices are exp(tN), where the parameter t ranges over an open subgroup of ℤℓ (our own). Nilpotence makes the exponential a finite sum (our own). In characteristic zero its logarithm recovers tN, so a nonzero N gives infinitely many matrices (our own). Grothendieck’s monodromy theorem supplies this description of the original Galois action (our own).

**nLab:** [Weil-Deligne representation](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Weil-Deligne+representation). It says: “N is a nilpotent monodromy operator”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Residual semisimplification removes lattice dependence

**Remember:** Every stable lattice gives the same simple factors after reduction.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A stable lattice is a free module over the coefficient field’s valuation ring that spans the representation and is preserved by Galois. Reduce its matrices modulo the maximal ideal. Semisimplification replaces that reduction by the direct sum of its irreducible factors.

**Problem.** For a continuous representation over a finite extension of ℚₚ, all stable lattices have isomorphic semisimplified reductions. Their reductions can differ before this step.

**How the definition helps.** Semisimplification keeps precisely the factors detected by characteristic polynomials (our own). The polynomials agree before reduction, so the Brauer–Nesbitt theorem gives the same irreducible factors afterwards (our own). For example, let each t in ℤₚ fix e and send f to f + te on a basis e, f (our own). This gives a local Galois action through its unramified ℤₚ quotient (our own). The lattice generated by e and f reduces to a nontrivial action (our own). On the lattice generated by e/p and f, every matrix reduces to the identity (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer–Nesbitt theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer%E2%80%93Nesbitt_theorem). It says: “the characteristic polynomials of ρ₁(g) and ρ₂(g) coincide for all g ∈ G, then ρ₁ and ρ₂ are isomorphic representations.”

**Paper or page:** [Stable free lattices in residually reducible Galois deformations and control theorem of Selmer groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03608v2). It says: “the semi-simplification (T/ϖT)ˢˢ of the residual representation is decomposed into two distinct characters”

### Semisimplification makes Frobenius traces decisive

**Remember:** Traces remember the simple pieces and forget how they fit together.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A representation describes a group action by linear maps. Choose a chain of invariant subspaces whose successive quotients have no proper nonzero invariant subspaces. Semisimplification takes the direct sum of those quotients.

**Problem.** Consider two continuous representations of a number field’s Galois group over the same finite extension of ℚℓ. Suppose inertia, the group acting trivially on the residue field, acts trivially outside finitely many primes. Equal Frobenius traces outside finitely many primes imply isomorphic semisimplifications.

**How the definition helps.** Semisimplification discards how the pieces fit together, which traces cannot detect (our own). The cited example has three representations with the same traces, but only one is a direct sum. At an unramified prime, Frobenius acts on residues by raising them to the residue field size (our own). Chebotarev density and continuity extend trace equality to the whole group (our own). In characteristic zero, traces determine a direct sum of simple representations up to isomorphism (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer–Nesbitt theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer%E2%80%93Nesbitt_theorem). It says: “Then the representation is uniquely determined by the values of the traces of ρ(Frobₚ)”

**Paper or page:** [Eisenstein degeneration of Euler systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02078v2). It says: “there are exactly three isomorphism classes of continuous Galois representations”

### The Weil pairing gives the determinant

**Remember:** On the determinant line, Galois acts on roots of unity.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write E\[n\] for the geometric points of an elliptic curve killed by a positive integer n. The Weil pairing pairs two such points with an nth root of unity. It is bilinear, alternating, and perfect, meaning that pairing with a point determines that point uniquely.

**Problem.** For an elliptic curve over a number field, the determinant of each Galois element acting on E\[n\] gives its exponent on nth roots of unity.

**How the definition helps.** Defining the determinant as the action on the exterior square lets the Weil pairing identify that action directly (our own). The exterior square records alternating bilinear products of two vectors (our own). In coordinates, pairing the images of two basis points raises their original pairing value to the matrix determinant (our own). Perfection makes this value a primitive root of unity (our own). The geometric work is constructing the pairing and proving it commutes with Galois action (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weil pairing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_pairing). It says: “With this definition it can be shown that w is alternating and bilinear,”

### Defining L-factors by ℓ-adic cohomology makes isogenous elliptic curves share them

**Remember:** An isogeny preserves the whole rational representation, including its inertia-fixed part.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 14G10. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an elliptic curve over a number field, take its first ℓ-adic étale cohomology with rational coefficients, for ℓ prime to the residue characteristic. At a prime p, inertia is the subgroup of the local Galois group acting trivially on the residue field, which has N(p) elements. The L-factor is the inverse of det(1 − Frob·N(p)⁻ˢ) on the inertia-fixed part, where Frob raises residues to the power N(p). The older recipe uses point counts at good primes and the reduction type at bad primes.

**Problem.** Elliptic curves that are isogenous over a number field have the same L-factor at every prime, good or bad.

**How the definition helps.** The cohomological definition depends only on the Galois representation, and an isogeny makes the two representations isomorphic. With rational coefficients the isogeny is invertible, since its dual composed with it is multiplication by its degree (our own). Isomorphic representations have isomorphic inertia-fixed parts, with the same Frobenius determinants (our own). With the older recipe, one must check separately that isogenous curves have the same reduction type at bad primes (our own). The work goes into proving that the cohomological factors agree with the older recipe (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse–Weil zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Weil_zeta_function). It says: “A more refined definition became possible with the development of étale cohomology”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre and John Tate, Good reduction of abelian varieties (1968)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970722)

### Local-condition Selmer groups sit between rational points and Tate–Shafarevich torsion

**Remember:** The local test leaves exactly the everywhere locally trivial torsors.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11R34. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let E be an elliptic curve over a number field K, and n ≥ 2. The n-Selmer group is the set of classes in H¹(K, E\[n\]) whose image in H¹(Kᵥ, E) is zero at every completion Kᵥ. Here E\[n\] is the group of points killed by n, with its Galois action. Classical descent instead tests whether certain equations have solutions everywhere locally.

**Problem.** There is an exact sequence 0 → E(K)/nE(K) → n-Selmer group → Ш\[n\] → 0. Here Ш, the Tate–Shafarevich group, classifies torsors that have a point over every completion. A torsor is a curve on which E acts freely and transitively over an algebraic closure.

**How the definition helps.** The local-condition definition makes the sequence come from a diagram chase. Multiplication by n gives 0 → E(K)/nE(K) → H¹(K, E\[n\]) → H¹(K, E)\[n\] → 0, and the same sequence over each Kᵥ (our own). Rational points die in H¹(Kᵥ, E), so E(K)/nE(K) lies in the Selmer group (our own). The image of the Selmer group is the part of H¹(K, E)\[n\] that is zero at every Kᵥ, which is Ш\[n\] (our own). The work is to identify H¹(K, E) with torsors (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selmer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selmer_group). It says: “More generally one can define the Selmer group of a Galois module”

**Sources:**

- [Joseph H. Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, Chapter X, §4 (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-09494-6)

### Quadratic twists split odd torsion

**Remember:** The twist supplies the minus part of the torsion.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L/K be a quadratic extension of number fields and let σ be its nonidentity automorphism. The quadratic twist of an elliptic curve becomes isomorphic to the original curve over L. Under this identification σ acts on L-rational points by applying the original action and then negating the result.

**Problem.** For any odd positive integer n, the points killed by n over L split as a direct sum. The two groups are the K-rational points killed by n on the original curve and on its quadratic twist.

**How the definition helps.** The twist identifies its rational points with the points over L satisfying σP = −P (our own). The original curve supplies the points satisfying σP = P (our own). Since two is invertible modulo n, half the sum and half the difference of P and σP give the two components (our own). At n = 2 the signs agree (our own). All four points killed by two on y² = x³ − x remain rational over ℚ on every quadratic twist (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The Effect of Quadratic Base Change on Torsion of Elliptic Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03709v2). It says: “If n is an odd positive integer we have E(K(√d))\[n\] ≃ E(K)\[n\] ⊕ Eᵈ(K)\[n\].”

### Requiring y ≠ 0 makes congruent numbers the curves of positive rank

**Remember:** Ignore the three points with y = 0; any other point proves A congruent.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11D25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A positive rational number A is congruent if it is the area of a right triangle with three rational sides. Equivalently, the curve y² = x³ − A²x has a rational point with y ≠ 0. The condition y ≠ 0 removes the points (0, 0), (A, 0) and (−A, 0), which lie on the curve for every A.

**Problem.** A rational point with y ≠ 0 on the curve has infinite order: no multiple of it in the group law is zero. So A is congruent exactly when the curve has positive rank, which means infinitely many rational points.

**How the definition helps.** The condition y ≠ 0 removes exactly the points that every curve of this family has (our own). These three points have order 2 and correspond to no triangle (our own). The paper's Theorem 1 says every remaining rational point has infinite order, so one triangle gives infinitely many triangles. Deciding whether a given A is congruent stays hard (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruent<sub>number</sub>](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/https%3A//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congruent_number). It says: “the only torsion points on this elliptic curve are those with y equal to 0, hence the existence of a rational point with y nonzero is equivalent to saying the elliptic curve has positive rank.”

**Paper or page:** [A Theorem of Fermat on Congruent Number Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09604). It says: “Equivalently, A is a congruent number if and only if the congruent number curve y²=x³−A²x has a rational point (x,y)∈ℚ² with y≠0.”

**Sources:**

- [Lorenz Halbeisen, Norbert Hungerbühler, A Theorem of Fermat on Congruent Number Curves, arXiv:1803.09604 (2018)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09604)

### Scheme kernels retain inseparable degrees

**Remember:** Kernel rank counts geometric points with their multiplicities.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 14K02. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An isogeny is a surjective homomorphism of elliptic curves with finite kernel. Its kernel as a group scheme is the entire fiber over zero, including multiplicities. Its rank counts that fiber by the dimension of its coordinate algebra over the base field.

**Problem.** Over a global function field, the kernel rank equals the isogeny degree. This includes inseparable isogenies, where some fiber multiplicities exceed one.

**How the definition helps.** Counting the full fiber retains the multiplicities that counting geometric points loses (our own). Relative Frobenius, the map given locally by taking pth powers in characteristic p, has degree p and only one geometric kernel point (our own). An isogeny is finite and flat, so every fiber has the same total multiplicity as the generic fiber (our own). The cited factorization uses the full subgroup scheme when constructing the quotient.

### Squarefree conductors exclude additive reduction

**Remember:** Smooth contributes zero, a node contributes one, and a cusp contributes more.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11G40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At each finite prime of a number field, choose an integral equation of the elliptic curve with smallest possible discriminant valuation. The curve is semistable if each such equation reduces to a smooth cubic or a cubic with an ordinary crossing. These cases are called good and multiplicative reduction. The remaining case is additive reduction.

**Problem.** An elliptic curve over a number field is semistable exactly when its conductor ideal has no repeated prime factor.

**How the definition helps.** Semistability allows exactly the reduction types with conductor exponent zero or one, in our own explanation. The conductor records ramification, the action of inertia on division points. The local conductor formula gives zero for good reduction and one for multiplicative reduction. Additive reduction contributes two plus a nonnegative term measuring wild ramification. In our own example, y² = x³ + 5 reduces to a cusp at five. Its conductor exponent there is two because the residue characteristic exceeds three.

**Wikipedia:** [Conductor of an elliptic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_of_an_elliptic_curve). It says: “ε=0 for good reduction, ε=1 for multiplicative reduction and ε=2 for additive reduction.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The conductor of an elliptic curve is the level of its newform

**Remember:** Bad primes of the curve become the level of its modular form.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11F11. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The conductor of an elliptic curve E over ℚ is a positive integer N built from the primes where E has bad reduction. A prime appears once when the curve mod p has a node, and more often when it has a cusp. A newform is a cusp form of level N that does not come from a lower level.

**Problem.** Every elliptic curve over ℚ of conductor N comes from a normalized newform of weight 2 and level exactly N, with integer coefficients. For a good prime p, its coefficient aₚ is p + 1 minus the number of points of E mod p.

**How the definition helps.** The conductor comes from the curve alone, and the level from the modular side alone, so the theorem can say the two numbers are equal (our own). For example, y² + y = x³ − x has conductor 37 and matches a form of level 37. Using newforms removes the copies of this form that appear at every multiple of 37 (our own). The hard part is the modularity theorem itself, and the page calls the step from level to conductor particularly delicate.

**Wikipedia:** [Modularity theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modularity_theorem). It says: “is the smallest integer for which such a parametrization can be found (which by the modularity theorem itself is now known to be a number called the conductor)”

### Torsors encode local failure

**Remember:** No rational origin means a nonzero torsor class.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 11R34. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A torsor for an elliptic curve E is a curve with an E-action that becomes free and transitive over an algebraic closure. The Tate–Shafarevich group consists of torsor classes that have points over every completion of the base field. The identity class is E acting on itself by translation.

**Problem.** A smooth projective geometrically integral genus-one curve over a number field has an associated elliptic curve, its Jacobian. If the curve has points everywhere locally but none globally, it gives a nonzero Tate–Shafarevich class of its Jacobian.

**How the definition helps.** Using torsors makes triviality a point test because choosing a point identifies the curve with its acting group (our own). Local points place the class in the group, while the missing global point makes the class nonzero (our own). The work connects this description to the kernel of restriction in Galois cohomology and constructs the Jacobian action (our own). Selmer’s projective cubic in the quotation gives an example.

**Wikipedia:** [Tate–Shafarevich group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate%E2%80%93Shafarevich_group). It says: “3x³ + 4y³ + 5z³ = 0”

### Weil pairings identify Galois determinants

**Remember:** Pair two basis vectors and watch the determinant act on roots of unity.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G05 (Elliptic curves over global fields), 14H52. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The division points of an elliptic curve are the points killed by multiplication by a given integer. The Weil pairing pairs two such points to give a root of unity. For a prime ℓ, the Tate module records compatible division points at successive powers of ℓ.

**Problem.** For an elliptic curve over a number field, each field automorphism fixing that field acts on the Tate module. Its determinant gives its exponent of action on the compatible roots of unity of ℓ-power order.

**How the definition helps.** Pairing a basis converts a change of basis into raising a root of unity to the determinant, in our own explanation. At each finite level the pairing is bilinear and alternating, so expanding on two transformed basis vectors gives that exponent. The theorem behind this calculation says the pairing is perfect, respects field automorphisms, and agrees across levels. Perfection makes the value on a basis a primitive root, so its exponent determines the action.

### Inertia detects good reduction

**Remember:** Good reduction means inertia fixes the entire prime-to-residue-characteristic Tate module.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G07 (Elliptic curves over local fields), 11G40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An elliptic curve has good reduction at a prime if it extends there to a smooth family of elliptic curves. Inertia consists of local field automorphisms that act trivially on the algebraic residue field. Choose a prime ℓ different from the residue characteristic. The ℓ-adic Tate module records compatible points killed by successive powers of ℓ.

**Problem.** For an elliptic curve over a number field, its conductor ideal contains a prime factor exactly where the curve has bad reduction.

**How the definition helps.** The inertia test describes good reduction using the same action that defines the conductor, in our own explanation. The conductor exponent adds the dimension lost to inertia and a nonnegative term measuring wild ramification. Both vanish when inertia acts trivially. Conversely, a zero exponent forces every vector to be fixed. The Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich theorem identifies this test with good reduction.

### Tate quotients reveal triangular actions

**Remember:** Roots of unity form the invariant line in Tate curve torsion.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G07 (Elliptic curves over local fields), 14G22. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

The kernel consists of the ℓth roots of unity. These roots give the first basis direction, and the quotient action is trivial. Tate’s uniformization theorem supplies this quotient presentation of the original curve.

**Remember:** Roots of unity give the submodule, and roots of q give the quotient.

An nth root of q lifts the class of one, so its Galois conjugates describe the extension (our own). Tate’s uniformization theorem identifies the multiplicative quotient with the elliptic curve (our own).

### Unramified tests can miss points

**Remember:** Good reduction lets the Kummer test forget inertia.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G07 (Elliptic curves over local fields), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an elliptic curve over a local field of odd residue characteristic, consider Galois cohomology classes on its points killed by two. The unramified test requires a class to vanish on inertia, the subgroup acting trivially on the residue field. The Kummer test requires the class to come from halving a local curve point.

**Problem.** The two tests agree at good reduction, where the reduced curve stays smooth. They can differ at bad reduction even if inertia fixes every point killed by two.

**How the definition helps.** The good reduction condition lets the unramified test detect exactly the classes obtained by halving points (our own). Doubling is invertible on the kernel of reduction, and Lang’s theorem gives vanishing first cohomology for the reduced curve over the residue field (our own). For a counterexample, choose an element π of valuation one and use the Tate curve with parameter π² (our own). Its multiplicative quotient identifies elements differing by powers of π², so its two-torsion is rational (our own). Halving the class of π requires a square root of an element of odd valuation and thus a ramified extension (our own).

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G50 (Heights), 11G10. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

Its canonical height measures arithmetic size and scales by n² when a point is multiplied by n.

**Problem.** For points defined over a number field, the canonical height vanishes exactly at points of finite order.

**How the definition helps.** Ampleness makes points of bounded height finite over the chosen number field, in our own explanation. This uses comparison with projective height and Northcott’s finiteness theorem. Every multiple of a point of height zero also has height zero, so two multiples must coincide. Conversely, the scaling law forces a point of finite order to have height zero. For our own counterexample, pull an ample symmetric bundle back from the first factor of a product of elliptic curves. Its height vanishes on the whole second factor, which can contain points of infinite order.

The logarithm of their product is the subspace height.

**Problem.** A subspace and its annihilator have the same height in dual coordinate systems. The annihilator consists of linear functionals that vanish on the subspace.

The product formula says the weighted absolute values of the common scalar multiply to one (our own).

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G50 (Heights), 14G40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

The good choice allows any sections with no common zero, which give a map to projective space that need not be an embedding.

**Problem.** Let f be a morphism of projective varieties over a number field, and L a line bundle on the target. The Weil height of f\*L equals the Weil height of L after f, up to a bounded function.

**How the definition helps.** If heights may come from any sections with no common zero, the claim is immediate for very ample L. The pulled back sections have no common zero and give the same coordinates as f followed by the embedding (our own). The very ample definition does not apply directly, because f\*L need not be very ample (our own). The work moves into the theorem that such sections give the same height as the very ample construction (our own). For general L, write L as a difference of very ample bundles and use additivity of heights (our own).

### Local weights give absolute heights

**Remember:** Weight each place by its degree before averaging over the field.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G50 (Heights), 14G40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A place of a number field is a choice of absolute value up to equivalence. At each place, extend the usual absolute value on ℚ there and take the logarithm of the largest projective coordinate size. Weight each logarithm by the degree of the completed field over the corresponding completion of ℚ. Sum and divide by the degree of the number field over ℚ.

**Problem.** The absolute logarithmic height of a projective point is independent of the number field containing its coordinates. For an algebraic number α, use the point with coordinates (1, α).

**How the definition helps.** The degree weights make each old contribution split into new contributions with the same total, in our own explanation. Above each place, the local extension degrees sum to the degree of the field extension. Division by the global degree cancels this factor, which an unnormalized sum would retain. The product formula also makes the sum unchanged when all coordinates are multiplied by one nonzero scalar.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G50 (Heights), 14K15. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

At 2ⁿP this error is still bounded, so it disappears after division by 4ⁿ (our own). Then f(2ⁿP) = 2ⁿf(P) gives the result (our own). *True by definition.* MSC 11G50 (Heights), 11G05. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**How the definition helps.** With Tate's limit, the claim is a shift of index, since ĥ(2P) = lim h(2ⁿ⁺¹P)/4ⁿ = 4ĥ(P). The real work is to show that the limit exists. For this one proves h(2P) = 4h(P) + O(1) with the duplication formula (our own). With Néron's definition the claim is not visible term by term, because the local heights are not quite quadratic. That the two definitions agree is a separate theorem (our own).

### Uniformly separated frequencies give metric equidistribution

**Remember:** For almost every multiplier, separated frequencies spread uniformly.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Call a real sequence uniformly separated if some g &gt; 0 satisfies \|aₙ − aₘ\| ≥ g whenever n ≠ m.

**Problem.** If a real sequence (aₙ) is uniformly separated, then for almost every real x the sequence aₙx is uniformly distributed modulo one. That is, the fraction of terms landing in each interval approaches its length.

**How the definition helps.** Separation limits how many frequencies can lie near any given frequency (our own). In increasing order, the jth neighbor on either side lies at distance at least jg (our own). Integrating the squared exponential average over a bounded interval then gives O(log N/N) at each nonzero integer frequency (our own). The metric convergence criterion of Davenport, Erdős and LeVeque turns this bound into uniform distribution almost everywhere (our own). Mere distinctness permits aₙ = 1/n, whose multiples converge to zero on the circle (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Metric uniform distribution on analytic curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06909v1). It says: “Then for almost every x ∈ ℝ the sequence (aₙx) is uniformly distributed modulo 1.”

### Powered intervals give approximation dimension

**Remember:** Keep the rational centers and shrink each interval by a power.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J83 (Metric theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write approximation as belonging to infinitely many intervals centered at reduced fractions p/q. Use intervals of diameter 2/q² to encode Dirichlet approximation. To make the test stricter, keep the centers and raise each diameter to a fixed power a greater than one.

**Problem.** Let a be greater than one. The real numbers approximable infinitely often within the inverse 2a-th power of the denominator have Hausdorff dimension 1/a. Hausdorff dimension measures size by covers at small scales.

**How the definition helps.** Powering the intervals lets one apply a theorem that converts full length measure into a dimension bound (our own). Dirichlet’s theorem gives full length measure for the original intervals, and the mass transference principle gives dimension at least 1/a for the powered ones (our own). For the upper bound, each bounded interval has at most a constant times q relevant fractions of denominator q (our own). Their covering costs sum to a finite number for every dimension above 1/a (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Diophantine approximation in metric space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.06776v1). It says: “Let a &gt; 1 and for a ball B, denote by Bᵃ a ball of the same centre as B and of diameter (diam B)ᵃ.”

### Independent bases prevent power cancellation

**Remember:** Independent bases make irrational algebraic powers survive multiplication.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J86 (Linear forms in logarithms; Baker's method), 11J81. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Positive numbers are multiplicatively independent if no product of their integer powers equals one except with all exponents zero. Use real logarithms to define powers of positive bases. Distinctness of the bases alone does not imply this independence.

**Problem.** Take multiplicatively independent positive algebraic bases and algebraic exponents. If at least one exponent is irrational, the product of those powers is transcendental.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplicative independence turns the logarithms of the bases into a rationally independent family (our own). Baker’s theorem says such logarithms of algebraic numbers remain linearly independent over the algebraic numbers. An algebraic product would give an algebraic dependence among its logarithm and theirs, and this forces every exponent to be rational (our own). Without independence, 2 raised to 2√2 times 4 raised to −√2 equals one (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Baker's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem). It says: “In particular this number is nonzero, so 1 and λᵢ are linearly independent over the algebraic numbers.”

**Sources:**

- [Alan Baker, Linear forms in the logarithms of algebraic numbers](https://doi.org/10.1112/s0025579300003971)

### Local ratios make approximation projective

**Remember:** Divide out the size of the coordinates at every place.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J87 (Schmidt Subspace Theorem and applications). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a number field K, a projective point represents a nonzero coordinate vector up to common scaling. At each place v, meaning a choice of absolute value, write Mᵥ for the largest absolute coordinate value. Normalize the absolute values so their product on each nonzero element of K equals one. The height H is the product of all Mᵥ.

**Problem.** Choose d independent K-linear forms in d variables at each of finitely many places. Multiply the ratios \|L(x)\|ᵥ/Mᵥ over every chosen form and place. For fixed ε &gt; 0, the points where this product is below 1/Hᵈ⁺ᵋ lie in finitely many proper projective linear subspaces.

**How the definition helps.** Each ratio removes the choice of coordinates, so the inequality applies directly to projective points (our own). Scaling multiplies the numerator and denominator by the same absolute value (our own). The height also stays fixed by the product formula (our own). The subspace theorem supplies the finite union, and its affine and projective versions are equivalent.

**Paper or page:** [Diophantine approximation and the subspace theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00731v1), [Diophantine approximation and the subspace theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00731v1). It says: “The projective subspace theorem is equivalent to the affine subspace theorem.”

### No zero subsums makes unit solutions finite

**Remember:** Remove cancelling groups before counting solutions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J87 (Schmidt Subspace Theorem and applications), 11D61. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An S-unit is a nonzero element of a number field whose principal fractional ideal has prime factors only in a fixed finite set S. A solution of a linear equation in S-units is nondegenerate if no nonempty group of terms on the left sums to zero.

**Problem.** Over a number field, a fixed linear equation in S-units with nonzero coefficients and right side one has finitely many nondegenerate solutions.

**How the definition helps.** The condition removes groups that can vary independently because their terms cancel (our own). Take ℚ with 2 in S (our own). The equation x + y + z = 1 then has solutions (2ᵏ, −2ᵏ, 1) for every positive k (our own). The S-unit theorem, proved using the subspace theorem, carries the finiteness work (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Sum of terms of recurrence sequences and S-units in the solution sets of norm form equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01688v1). It says: “has no vanishing subsums.”

### Fourier tests reveal polynomial equidistribution

**Remember:** Polynomial differences make Fourier averages easier to estimate.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K06 (General theory of distribution modulo \\(1\\)), 11K31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Uniform distribution modulo 1 means that the fraction of fractional parts in each interval tends to its length. In the equivalent Fourier test, average exp(2πihx) over the sequence for each nonzero integer h. Require each such average to tend to zero.

**Problem.** The values of a real polynomial at the positive integers are uniformly distributed modulo 1 if some nonconstant coefficient is irrational.

**How the definition helps.** The Fourier test replaces interval counts by averages whose phases have lower degree after differencing. In our own proof, split the indices into residue classes modulo a common denominator for the rational coefficients. On each class the rational terms are constant modulo 1, and the remaining polynomial has irrational leading coefficient. The van der Corput inequality reduces the degree by comparing terms a fixed distance apart. At degree one a geometric sum gives the limit. Weyl’s criterion justifies replacing the interval definition by these tests.

**Wikipedia:** [Equidistributed sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence). It says: “the sequence p(n) is uniformly distributed modulo 1.”

### Equidistribution makes normal numbers a consequence of ergodicity

**Remember:** A normal number visits intervals at the right frequencies under multiplication by its base.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K16 (Normal numbers, radix expansions, Pisot numbers, Salem numbers, good lattice points, etc.), 37A44. arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A real number x is normal in integer base b ≥ 2 if every length-k block of its digits has frequency 1/bᵏ. Equivalently, the fractional parts of bᵏx are equidistributed. This means their visits to each interval in \[0, 1) have frequency equal to the length of that interval.

**Problem.** For each integer base b ≥ 2, Lebesgue-almost every real number is normal in base b.

**How the definition helps.** The orbit definition makes normality an instance of the ergodic theorem for interval visits (our own). Multiplication by b modulo 1 preserves Lebesgue measure and is ergodic, meaning every invariant event has measure zero or one. Birkhoff’s theorem makes the frequency of visits to each interval with rational endpoints equal its length for almost every starting point. There are countably many such intervals, and they approximate arbitrary intervals. The digit definition instead asks for frequencies of overlapping digit blocks. The work goes into proving ergodicity and showing that each digit block corresponds to an interval with endpoints of the form j/bᵏ.

**Wikipedia:** [Normal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number). It says: “A number x is normal in base b if and only if the sequence {\\left( b<sup>k</sup> x \\right) }<sub>k=0</sub><sup>\\infty</sup> is equidistributed modulo 1”

**Sources:**

- [É. Borel, Les probabilités dénombrables et leurs applications arithmétiques, Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo 27 (1909) 247–271](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03019651)

### Block tests expose hidden dependence

**Remember:** Counting blocks catches dependencies that counting single points misses.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11K36 (Well-distributed sequences and other variations), 11K06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a fixed length k, form a point in the unit cube from each block of k consecutive fractional parts. Call the sequence completely uniformly distributed if, for every k, the fraction of these points in each box tends to its volume. Ordinary uniform distribution checks only k = 1.

**Problem.** For almost every α &gt; 1, the sequence of positive integer powers of α is completely uniformly distributed modulo 1. For irrational α, its positive integer multiples are uniformly distributed but fail the block test at length two.

**How the definition helps.** Testing adjacent terms together detects relations that disappear when each term is counted alone. For multiples of α, the second coordinate always equals the first plus α modulo 1. In our own argument, an open box away from this line receives no pairs, despite its positive area. The almost-everywhere theorem for powers requires separate estimates for the frequencies of blocks.

**Wikipedia:** [Equidistributed sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence). It says: “is completely uniformly distributed for almost all α &gt; 1”

### Continued fraction blocks bound rotation discrepancy

**Remember:** Use return-time blocks so each block contributes only constant count error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an irrational step α, write N in its Ostrowski expansion, the greedy sum of denominators of successive continued fraction approximations to α. Each denominator occurs at most as many times as the next continued fraction entry. Split the first N rotation steps into consecutive blocks of these lengths.

**Problem.** Suppose the continued fraction entries of α are bounded. For the points x+jα modulo one, the greatest absolute difference between arc frequency and arc length is O(log N/N), uniformly in x.

**How the definition helps.** The expansion selects block lengths for which the Denjoy–Koksma inequality bounds the absolute arc count error by two (our own). An arc indicator has total variation two because it jumps once at each endpoint (our own). The denominators at least double every two steps, and bounded entries bound each multiplicity (our own). Thus O(log N) blocks suffice, and adding their errors gives the result after division by N (our own).

### Fourier cutoffs bound arc discrepancy

**Remember:** Bound the sharp arc count from above and below with short Fourier sums.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an arc I of the unit circle, bound its indicator above and below by trigonometric polynomials using frequencies up to M ≥ 1. Selberg’s polynomials have constant terms \|I\| ± 1/(M+1), where \|I\| denotes arc length. At nonzero frequency k their coefficients are O(1/\|k\|).

**Problem.** For a circle probability μ, write μ̂(k) = ∫exp(−2πikx) dμ(x). Its arc discrepancy is the supremum of \|μ(I) − \|I\|\| over arcs I. It is at most C times 1/M + ∑ₖ₌₁ᴹ \|μ̂(k)\|/k, with an absolute constant C.

**How the definition helps.** Integrating the two polynomial bounds traps each arc mass using only finitely many Fourier coefficients (our own). The constant terms supply the length and its O(1/M) error (our own). Constructing bounds that hold at every point while controlling all coefficients is the substantive step (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Erdős–Turán inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Tur%C3%A1n_inequality). It says: “where the supremum is over all arcs A ⊂ ℝ/ℤ of the unit circle”

### Square-summed frequencies bound worst arc error

**Remember:** Square the weighted Fourier errors before choosing the cutoff.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a circle probability μ, its kth Fourier coefficient is μ̂(k) = ∫exp(−2πikx) dμ(x). Define A as the square root of ∑ₖ₌₁∞ \|μ̂(k)\|²/k².

**Problem.** For every arc I, the difference between μ(I) and its length has absolute value at most C times A raised to 2/3. The constant C is universal.

**How the definition helps.** The square sum controls every truncated Fourier sum by the same number A (our own). The Erdős–Turán inequality bounds arc error by an absolute constant times 1/M + ∑ₖ₌₁ᴹ \|μ̂(k)\|/k. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the sum by √M times A (our own). For 0 &lt; A ≤ 1, choosing M near A⁻²⁄³ balances the terms (our own). For A = 0 let M grow, and for A &gt; 1 use the trivial error bound one (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Erdős–Turán inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Tur%C3%A1n_inequality). It says: “This inequality holds for arbitrary natural numbers m,n”

### Gauss averages give denominator growth

**Remember:** The logarithm turns successive reciprocal tails into a sum.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K50 (Metric theory of continued fractions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Gauss map T sends irrational x between 0 and 1 to the fractional part of 1/x. It preserves the probability distribution with density 1/((1 + x) log 2). At each iterate record −log x, evaluated at the current point.

**Problem.** Truncate the continued fraction of x after n digits following the integer part, and let qₙ be the reduced denominator. For almost every x between 0 and 1, (log qₙ)/n tends to π²/(12 log 2).

**How the definition helps.** Recording logarithms turns denominator growth into a sum to which the ergodic theorem applies. In our own calculation, the reciprocal product of the first n iterates, starting at x, equals qₙ plus the previous denominator times the next iterate. This lies between qₙ and 2qₙ, so its logarithm differs from log qₙ by at most log 2. Ergodicity makes the average of the recorded values converge almost everywhere to their integral against the invariant density. That integral gives the stated constant.

**nLab:** [continued fraction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/continued+fraction). It says: “then τ is an ergodic transformation with respect to μ”

**Wikipedia:** [Lévy's constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9vy%27s_constant). It says: “The term “Lévy's constant” is sometimes used to refer to π²/(12 ln 2)”

### The Gauss map turns continued fraction digits into ergodic averages

**Remember:** Read each digit as the first digit of the next state.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K50 (Metric theory of continued fractions), 37A44. arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an irrational x in (0, 1), let a₁, a₂, … be its continued fraction digits, obtained by repeatedly taking reciprocals and removing integer parts. The Gauss map T takes x to the fractional part of 1/x. Thus aₙ is the integer part of the reciprocal after n − 1 applications of T.

**Problem.** Khinchin’s theorem says that for Lebesgue-almost every x in (0, 1), the geometric mean of its first n digits tends to the same constant. The constant is about 2.685.

**How the definition helps.** Defining the digits through the Gauss map makes their mean logarithm a time average of just one function, log a₁. The hard part is that T preserves the Gauss measure, with density 1/((1 + x) log 2), and is ergodic. Birkhoff’s ergodic theorem then makes the time average equal its integral almost everywhere, and this measure has the same null sets as Lebesgue measure. Exponentiating gives the limit of the geometric means.

**Wikipedia:** [Khinchin's constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khinchin%27s_constant). It says: “Moreover, it can be proved that T is an ergodic transformation of the measurable space I endowed with the probability measure μ (this is the hard part of the proof).”

### Completion transfers the Weil bound

**Remember:** Fourier modes turn a cut-off inverse phase into complete sums.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For prime p, nonzero b modulo p and unit x, let T(x)=exp(2πibx⁻¹/p), using the inverse modulo p. Set T(0)=0. Replace an interval indicator by its additive Fourier expansion on residues modulo p.

**Problem.** Take an integer a and an interval I containing at most p consecutive integers. The sum of T(x)exp(2πiax/p) over these integers has absolute value at most C√p log(2p) for an absolute constant C.

**How the definition helps.** The Fourier expansion replaces the interval restriction by complete sums over all residues. In our own derivation, each exponential in that expansion changes only the coefficient a. A geometric series bounds the sum of the absolute Fourier coefficients by C log(2p) when the coefficients include the factor 1/p. Weil bounds each complete sum by 2√p when its linear coefficient is nonzero. When that coefficient vanishes, the complete sum equals −1.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “Short Kloosterman sums are defined as trigonometric sums of the form”

### Grouping modulo pʳ isolates stationary residues

**Remember:** Group modulo the square root of the modulus to make the exponent linear.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Split the Kloosterman sum S(a, b; p²ʳ), the sum of exp(2πi(ax + bx⁻¹)/p²ʳ) over units x modulo p²ʳ, into classes of x with the same remainder u modulo pʳ.

**Problem.** For an odd prime p and a, b prime to p, the class of u contributes zero unless au² ≡ b modulo pʳ, and otherwise contributes pʳ times the term at any member.

**How the definition helps.** Grouping modulo pʳ makes the exponent linear in the index of the lift. In our own derivation, write x = u + pʳt with 0 ≤ t &lt; pʳ. Modulo p²ʳ its inverse equals u⁻¹ − pʳtu⁻². Summing over t gives zero unless a − bu⁻² vanishes modulo pʳ, and in that case every member has the same term.

**Paper or page:** [Subconvexity for GL₂ × GL₂ L-functions in the depth aspect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18727v1). It says: “Then, S(a,b;pⁿ) = 0 if ab ∉ (ℤₚˣ)².”

### Hyper-Kloosterman transforms are Gauss powers

**Remember:** A character splits the product constraint into one Gauss sum per variable.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a prime p and positive integer r, and write E(x)=exp(2πix/p). Define Kᵣ(a) by summing E(x₁)⋯E(xᵣ) over nonzero residues whose product equals a modulo p. A multiplicative character χ sends nonzero residues to complex numbers of absolute value one and satisfies χ(xy)=χ(x)χ(y). Write G(χ) for the sum of χ(x)E(x) over nonzero residues.

**Problem.** For every multiplicative character χ, summing χ(a)Kᵣ(a) over nonzero residues a gives G(χ)ʳ.

**How the definition helps.** The product constraint lets the character separate the variables. In our own generalization, keep all r variables instead of solving for the last one by division. Summing over a removes the constraint and leaves r independent copies of G(χ). This computes the transform directly. Bounding the original sum at each a requires further cancellation.

**Paper or page:** [The sixth moment of Dirichlet L-functions at the central point](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01457v1). It says: “where the hyper-Kloosterman sum”

### Joint primitivity prevents oversized sums

**Remember:** Exclude a common factor so the modulus measures the true oscillation.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For integers a,b and q ≥ 2, sum exp(2πi(ax+bx⁻¹)/q) over invertible residues x modulo q. Here x⁻¹ is the inverse modulo q. Write K(a,b;q) for this sum and call the pair jointly primitive when gcd(a,b,q) = 1.

**Problem.** On jointly primitive pairs, \|K(a,b;q)\| ≤ τ(q)√q, where τ counts positive divisors. Without the condition the bound fails, for example when q = 25 and a = b = 0.

**How the definition helps.** Joint primitivity makes the common-divisor factor in the general estimate equal to one. In our own example with q = 25 and a = b = 0, all 20 terms equal one. The proposed upper bound would be 3√25 = 15. The general estimate uses Weil’s prime-modulus bound and separate estimates for prime powers.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “\|K(a,b;m)\| ≤ τ(m) √gcd(a,b,m) √m.”

- [André Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Smooth weights suppress distant frequencies

**Remember:** Smooth weights let repeated integration by parts remove distant frequencies.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a prime p, an integer b coprime to p and a real N ≥ 1. Put K(n)=exp(2πibn⁻¹/p) for n invertible modulo p and K(n)=0 otherwise. Weight each integer n by W(n/N), where W is infinitely differentiable and vanishes outside a bounded interval. Define K̂(h)=∑ₓK(x)exp(2πihx/p) over residues and Ŵ(t)=∫ W(x)exp(−2πitx) dx over the real line.

**Problem.** Summing K(n)W(n/N) over all integers gives (N/p)∑ₕ K̂(h)Ŵ(Nh/p), with h over all integers. For H ≥ max(1,p/N), the terms with \|h\| &gt; H contribute at most C√p (p/(NH))ᴬ in absolute value. For each A &gt; 0 the constant depends only on A and W.

**How the definition helps.** Smoothness makes the transformed weight decrease faster than any fixed inverse power of frequency. Our own two-sided formula applies Poisson summation on each residue class. Repeated integration by parts bounds Ŵ, while Weil’s estimate gives \|K̂(h)\| ≤ 2√p. Summing those bounds gives the tail estimate.

**Paper or page:** [On a Finite Field Analogue of van der Corput Differencing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.02525v1). It says: “any even smooth function V compactly supported on ℝ”

### Exponent pairs interpolate

**Remember:** Interpolate two uniform bounds by taking their weighted geometric mean.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix s &gt; 0, N ≥ 1 and T ≥ Nˢ, and set Y = T/Nˢ. For 0 ≤ k ≤ ½ ≤ l ≤ 1, choose a positive derivative count R and relative tolerance δ ∈ (0,1). On \[N,2N\], require f′ and its derivatives through order R−1 to approximate their counterparts for T/xˢ within relative error δ. Call (k,l) an exponent pair if, for every s &gt; 0, such choices bound every sum of exp(2πif(n)) on integer subintervals by CYᵏNˡ. The bound must hold uniformly in N, T and f, and C may depend only on k, l and s.

**Problem.** Every convex combination of two exponent pairs is an exponent pair.

**How the definition helps.** Recording the two powers as coordinates turns interpolation between estimates into a line segment. In our own derivation, take the larger derivative order and the smaller error tolerance. Both estimates then apply, so their weighted geometric mean gives the claimed powers. Proving the initial estimates takes the analytic work.

**Wikipedia:** [Van der Corput's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Corput%27s_method). It says: “The set of exponents pairs is convex.”

### Monotone slopes prevent coherent repetition

**Remember:** Stay away from integer slopes and do not repeatedly retrace the same slopes.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be a continuously differentiable real function on a bounded interval I. Require f′ to be monotone and to stay at least λ &gt; 0 away from every integer throughout I.

**Problem.** The sum of exp(2πif(n)) over integers n in a bounded I is O(1/λ), with an absolute constant. Without monotonicity this bound can fail even with λ = 3/8.

**How the definition helps.** Monotonicity keeps successive phase increments in order, which controls the error in summation by parts. In our own proof, the increments stay inside one gap between integers, at least λ from either endpoint. The total variation of 1/(exp(2πit)−1) across that gap is bounded by a constant times 1/λ. Our own counterexample uses f(t)=t/2+cos(πt)/(8π). Its derivative stays in \[3/8,5/8\]. Each pair of consecutive integers starting at an even integer contributes 2i sin(1/4), so the sum grows with the interval.

**Paper or page:** [On Sárközy's theorem for shifted primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.08001v3). It says: “Let f : I → ℝ be continuously differentiable such that f′ is monotonic and ∥f′(t)∥ ≥ λ on I.”

### Separated phases factor major arcs

**Remember:** Residue classes handle the rational phase and the integral handles the drift.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix positive integers k, N and q, and integers a₁,…,aₖ with gcd(q,a₁,…,aₖ) = 1. Write the real polynomial phase as A(x)/q+B(x), where A(x)=∑ⱼaⱼxʲ and B(x)=∑ⱼβⱼxʲ for 1 ≤ j ≤ k. Let C be the mean of exp(2πiA(x)/q) over residues modulo q. Let I be the integral of exp(2πiB(x)) from 0 to N.

**Problem.** The sum of exp(2πi∑ (aⱼ/q+βⱼ)nʲ) over 1 ≤ n ≤ N equals CI plus an error. The error is O(q(1+∑ \|βⱼ\|Nʲ)), with a constant depending only on k.

**How the definition helps.** The two factors separate the periodic part from the slowly varying part. In our own proof, group integers by their residues modulo q. On each group the periodic part is constant. Comparing the remaining sum with its integral costs at most a constant times one plus the integral of the absolute derivative. Summing these errors gives the stated bound.

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ maximal estimates for Weyl sums with k ≥ 3 on 𝕋](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15527v1). It says: “S<sub>k</sub>(\\bm {u},N) = q<sup>-1</sup>S<sub>k</sub>(q<sup>-1</sup>\\bm {r};q)I(\\bm {\\xi }) + \\Delta .”

### Vinogradov moments count power sums

**Remember:** Each integral keeps just the tuples with equal sums of powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix positive integers k, N and s. For α in the unit k-dimensional cube, let F(α) sum exp(2πi∑ⱼαⱼnʲ) over integers 1 ≤ n ≤ N. The inner sum runs from j = 1 to k. Define the mean value as the integral of \|F(α)\|²ˢ over the cube.

**Problem.** The mean value counts ordered pairs of lists, each containing s integers from 1 through N. The lists must have equal sums of jth powers for every j from 1 through k.

**How the definition helps.** Integrating one coefficient per power tests all the equations at once. Our own specialization of the lemma uses the points (n,n²,…,nᵏ). Expand the integrand to get one term per pair of lists. Each coordinate integral gives zero for unequal power sums and one for equal sums. Estimating the resulting integral supplies the difficult counting bound.

**Paper or page:** [Decoupling estimates in Fourier analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00652v1). It says: “For any finite set A ⊂ ℤᵈ, ∫<sub>\[0,1\]<sup>d</sub></sup> \|f<sub>A</sub>(x)\|<sup>2s</sup> dx = E<sub>s</sub>(A).”
