### In upper numbering, abelian ramification jumps are integers

**Remember:** Abelian extensions only jump at whole numbers in upper numbering.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A jump of the upper ramification filtration is an index t where the group Gᵗ changes. The lower index s is turned into the upper index η(s), the integral from 0 to s of 1/\|G₀ : Gₓ\|. Here G₀ is the inertia group.

**Problem.** For a finite abelian extension of local fields, every jump of the upper ramification filtration is an integer.

**How the definition helps.** The upper numbering matches the unit groups 1 + mⁿ under the Artin map, and those come in integer steps, so the theorem has a natural form there. In the lower numbering the claim would be empty, because lower jumps are always integers. Hasse proved the case of finite residue fields, and Arf proved the general case. For non-abelian extensions, upper jumps can be fractions, and Serre gives an example with a jump at 3/2.

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse–Arf theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse%E2%80%93Arf_theorem), [Ramification group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_group), [Conductor (class field theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_%28class_field_theory%29). It says: “With the above set up of an abelian extension L/K, the theorem states that the jumps of the filtration {Gᵗ(L/K) : t ≥ −1} are all rational integers.”

**Sources:**

- [Cahit Arf, Untersuchungen über reinverzweigte Erweiterungen diskret bewerteter perfekter Körper, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 181 (1940)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1940.181.1)

### Reduced poles give ramification breaks

**Remember:** Remove p-divisible poles before reading the ramification break.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write a cyclic extension of degree p of K = k((t)), with k a finite field of characteristic p, as yᵖ − y = a. Replacing y by y + b changes a by bᵖ − b. Call a reduced when every negative power of t in a has exponent prime to p.

**Problem.** If a reduced parameter a has a pole of order m, then m is the unique positive ramification break, in both the lower and the upper numbering.

**How the definition helps.** Reduction removes spurious poles, so the largest pole order measures how long automorphisms act trivially modulo powers of the maximal ideal (our own). In the extension, t has valuation p and y has valuation −m. Since m is prime to p, some product of powers of t and y is a uniformizer (our own). Translating y by a nonzero constant of the prime field moves that uniformizer by an element of valuation m + 1 (our own). Hence the only lower break is m, and the upper numbering agrees up to the first break (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin–Schreier theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Schreier_theory). It says: “is the splitting field of an Artin–Schreier polynomial”

**Paper or page:** [Newton Polygons of Sums on Curves II: Variation in p-adic Families](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08657v1). It says: “p<sup>j-1</sup>\\max \\{  k p<sup>-v<sub>p</sub>(c<sub>k</sub>)</sup>: v<sub>p</sub>(c<sub>k</sub>) &lt; j \\}  &amp;  \\text{if } v<sub>p</sub>(c<sub>k</sub>) &lt; j \\text{ for some } k”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Swan conductors ignore tame twists

**Remember:** Tame characters act trivially on every group the Swan conductor sees.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Swan conductor of a complex representation V of a finite local Galois group is a sum over the lower ramification groups Gᵢ with i ≥ 1. The term for Gᵢ is \|Gᵢ\|/\|G₀\| times the codimension in V of the vectors fixed by Gᵢ. A tame character is a character that is trivial on G₁.

**Problem.** Twisting a complex representation of a finite local Galois group by a tame character leaves its Swan conductor unchanged.

**How the definition helps.** The sum leaves out the inertia group G₀, so it sees only groups on which a tame character is trivial (our own). Twisting multiplies each matrix by the character value, which is 1 on these groups, so every fixed space in the sum stays the same (our own). The Artin conductor also counts the G₀ term, which can change, even for a twist of the trivial representation (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin conductor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_conductor). It says: “f(χ) − (χ(1) − χ(G₀))”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Tame ramification is exactly what a projective ring of integers needs

**Remember:** No wild ramification, and the integers form a projective Galois module.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11R33. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L be a Galois extension of ℚ. Its ring of integers factors each prime p into distinct primes, each to the same power e. The number e is the ramification index of p. The prime p is tamely ramified when p does not divide e, and L is tamely ramified when every prime is.

**Problem.** For a finite Galois extension L of ℚ with group G, the ring of integers is a projective ℤ\[G\]-module exactly when L is tamely ramified. A projective module is a direct summand of a free module.

**How the definition helps.** Tame ramification is the condition that makes the local trace map onto, and that gives a local normal basis at each prime (our own). The page gives the Gaussian field ℚ(i) as a field with no normal integral basis. There 2 is not tamely ramified, since its ramification index is 2 (our own). The page says that the gap between free and projective has its own large theory.

**Wikipedia:** [Galois representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_representation). It says: “Then Noether's theorem states that tame ramification is necessary and sufficient for OL to be a projective module over Z\[G\].”

**Sources:**

- [Emmy Noether, Normalbasis bei Körpern ohne höhere Verzweigung, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 167 (1932)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1932.167.147)

### Tame ramification makes trace surjective

**Remember:** The trace of one is a unit across a tame totally ramified extension.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite extension of p-adic fields, tame means the ramification index is prime to the residue characteristic p. The ramification index is the valuation of a generator of the base maximal ideal, measured in the extension.

**Problem.** The trace on the rings of integers of a finite extension of p-adic fields is onto exactly when the extension is tame.

**How the definition helps.** Tameness makes the ramification index e a unit, and this is what the trace needs (our own argument). Split the extension into an unramified stage, where the trace reduces to the onto trace of finite fields, and a totally ramified stage of degree e. In the totally ramified stage, the trace sends each residue a to ea modulo the maximal ideal, so it is onto when p does not divide e. If p divides e, every trace from that stage lies in the maximal ideal, so the full trace is not onto (our own argument).

**Wikipedia:** [Ramification (mathematics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_%28mathematics%29). It says: “A finite generically étale extension B/A of Dedekind domains is tame if and only if the trace Tr: B → A is surjective.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Tameness gives the different exponent

**Remember:** A tame different has exponent one less than the ramification index.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite separable extension of non-Archimedean local fields with ramification index e is tame when the residue characteristic does not divide e. The different is the inverse of the trace dual of the ring of integers.

**Problem.** For a tame finite Galois extension of non-Archimedean local fields, the different has exponent e − 1.

**How the definition helps.** Tameness makes every higher ramification group trivial, so Hilbert’s formula ∑ (\|Gᵢ\| − 1) keeps only the inertia term e − 1 (our own). In the wild extension ℚ₂(√2), the derivative 2√2 of X² − 2 generates the different (our own). Its valuation is three, although e − 1 is one (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “is equal to e − 1 if P is tamely ramified”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Trace duality makes differents multiply

**Remember:** Trace in stages to multiply the different ideals.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite separable extension L/K of local fields, define the inverse different as the trace dual of the integers. It consists of x in L whose trace after multiplication by any integer of L is integral in K. The different is the inverse fractional ideal.

**Problem.** In a tower M/L/K of finite separable extensions of local fields, the different of M/K is the different of M/L times the different of L/K extended to M.

**How the definition helps.** The trace-dual definition turns the tower rule into two integrality tests, because traces compose (our own proof). By transitivity, x lies in the inverse different of M/K exactly when Tr₍M/L₎(xy) lies in the inverse different of L/K for every integer y of M. If d generates that ideal, this says that x/d lies in the inverse different of M/L. Computing the different from a polynomial derivative would instead need a single generator of the integer ring (our own comparison).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “In a tower of fields L/K/F the relative differents are related by δ₍L/F₎ = δ₍L/K₎ δ₍K/F₎.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Trace duals make differents multiply

**Remember:** Trace duals compose because traces compose.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite separable extension of local fields, an integer is a field element of nonnegative valuation. The inverse different contains exactly those x for which the trace of xy is a base-field integer for every extension-field integer y. The different is its inverse as a fractional ideal, an ideal allowing denominators.

**Problem.** Consider a tower L/K/F of finite separable extensions of non-Archimedean local fields. The different of L/F equals the product of the different of L/K and the extended different of K/F.

**How the definition helps.** The trace definition replaces a calculation with derivatives of defining polynomials by composition of traces (our own). Choose integral bases at both steps and their dual bases for the trace pairing (our own). Trace transitivity shows that products of dual basis elements form the dual basis to the product basis (our own). Thus the inverse differents multiply after extending the lower ideal to the top field (our own). Inverting the ideals gives the formula for differents (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “In a tower of fields L/K/F the relative differents are related by δ(L/F) = δ(L/K)δ(K/F).”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Upper numbering makes ramification groups pass to quotients

**Remember:** Lower numbering suits subgroups; upper numbering suits quotients.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11S20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take a Galois extension of local fields with group G, and let w be the valuation of the larger field. The lower group Gᵤ is the set of σ with w(σ(a) − a) ≥ u + 1 for every integer a of the larger field. The Herbrand function φ is an increasing piecewise linear rescaling of u. The upper groups are Gᵗ = Gᵤ with t = φ(u).

**Problem.** For a normal subgroup H of G, the image of Gᵗ in G/H is (G/H)ᵗ. This is Herbrand's theorem in upper numbering.

**How the definition helps.** The page says that the upper numbering is defined so that quotients behave well. The work moves into Herbrand's theorem for the lower numbering, which needs the Herbrand function. The lower numbering is compatible only with subgroups. Compatibility with quotients lets one define upper groups for infinite extensions, such as the absolute Galois group of a local field (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ramification group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramification_group). It says: “The upper numbering is defined so as to be compatible with passage to quotients:”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 67, Springer (1979)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Upper ramification indices rescale for subgroups

**Remember:** Restrict upper groups by changing their indices, not their elements.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Herbrand’s function φ turns lower ramification indices into upper ones. It is φ(u) = u for −1 ≤ u ≤ 0, and φ(u) = ∫₀ᵘ dt/\[G₀ : G<sub>t</sub>\] for u ≥ 0. The upper group at v is the lower group at ψ(v), where ψ is the inverse of φ.

**Problem.** Let M/K be a finite Galois extension of local fields and L/K a Galois subextension. Write ψ for the inverse change of index for L/K. For u ≥ −1, intersecting the upper group at u with Gal(M/L) gives the upper group for M/L at ψ(u).

**How the definition helps.** Lower indices pass to subgroups unchanged, so the rule follows by turning lower indices into upper ones in M/K and in M/L (our own). This translation uses ψ₍M/K₎ = ψ₍M/L₎ ∘ ψ₍L/K₎, which rests on Herbrand’s quotient theorem (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Ramification groups of some finite Galois extensions of maximal nilpotency class over local fields of positive characteristic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07928v4). It says: “Then we have $G<sup>i\\cap</sup> H=H<sup>\\psi (i)</sup>$ for all $i\\geq -1$.”

### De Rham representations admit tensor products

**Remember:** Tensor invariant bases to get another invariant basis.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S20 (Galois theory), 14F30. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a finite extension of ℚₚ and V a finite-dimensional ℚₚ-vector space with continuous action of its absolute Galois group. Fontaine’s de Rham period field B carries a compatible action with fixed field K. Call V de Rham if extending its scalars to B gives a basis of Galois-fixed vectors.

**Problem.** Tensor products of de Rham representations are de Rham. Their spaces of fixed vectors after extension to B tensor over K.

**How the definition helps.** Tensoring two fixed bases gives a fixed basis for the tensor product (our own proof). In a fixed basis, a vector is fixed exactly when each coefficient belongs to K. This also identifies the space of periods, meaning the fixed vectors after extending scalars. The usual dimension test agrees because fixed vectors independent over K remain independent over B (our own explanation).

**nLab:** [p-adic Hodge theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/p-adic+Hodge+theory). It says: “If the dimension of V is equal to the dimension of V₍dR₎, we say that V is de Rham.”

### Cartier duals detect missing roots

**Remember:** Keep the Galois action on the roots when taking the dual.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Cartier dual of a finite Galois module M is Hom(M, K̄ˣ), with Galois acting on both the input and the output. For the constant module ℤ/nℤ, the Cartier dual is the group μₙ of nth roots of unity with its Galois action.

**Problem.** Let K be a p-adic field and n a positive integer. The order of H²(K, ℤ/nℤ) is the number of nth roots of unity in K.

**How the definition helps.** Tate local duality makes H²(K, ℤ/nℤ) dual to the Galois-fixed part of the Cartier dual, which is the group of nth roots of unity in K. Dual finite groups have the same size (our own). For n = 3 over ℚ₂, only one cube root of unity is fixed, while a trivial action would wrongly predict three (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Duality for the condensed Weil-étale realisation of 1-motives over p-adic fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19910v2). It says: “Then we have a perfect cup-product pairing\\\[  \\H^ q(G<sub>F</sub>,N)\\otimes \\H^ {2-q}(G<sub>F</sub>,\\operatorname{Hom}(N,\\overline{F}<sup>\\times </sup>))\\rightarrow \\H^ 2(G<sub>F</sub>,\\overline{F}<sup>\\times </sup>)=\\mathbbm {Q}/\\mathbbm {Z}.  \\\]”

### Norm-one tori count local norms

**Remember:** The first cohomology of the norm-one torus counts missing norms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite separable extension L/K, view the multiplicative group of L as an algebraic group over K. The norm-one torus T is the kernel of the norm map from this group to the multiplicative group of K.

**Problem.** For a finite abelian extension L/K of non-Archimedean local fields, H¹(K, T) has order \[L:K\].

**How the definition helps.** The kernel definition turns first Galois cohomology into the group of elements that fail to be norms (our own). The cohomology sequence of the norm map identifies H¹(K, T) with Kˣ/N(Lˣ), by Hilbert’s theorem 90 and Shapiro’s lemma (our own). Local reciprocity identifies this quotient with the Galois group, whose order is \[L:K\] (our own).

**nLab:** [Galois cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Galois+cohomology). It says: “Galois cohomology refers to the group cohomology of G with coefficients in a G-module naturally associated to L.”

**Wikipedia:** [Local class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_class_field_theory). It says: “the reciprocity map induces an isomorphism of the quotient group K×/N(L×)”

### Twisted duals make local Tate duality perfect

**Remember:** Dual into roots of unity, not into ℚ/ℤ, and the pairing becomes perfect.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A be a finite Galois module over a p-adic field K. Its twisted dual A′ is the group of homomorphisms from A to the roots of unity. Galois acts on both A and the roots of unity.

**Problem.** Cup product gives a perfect pairing between Hⁱ(K, A) and H²⁻ⁱ(K, A′) with values in the Brauer group ℚ/ℤ, for i = 0, 1, 2.

**How the definition helps.** Pairing into the roots of unity matches the Galois action, since H²(K, μₙ) is the n-torsion of the Brauer group (our own). The plain dual fails, for example for A = ℤ/ℓ over ℚₚ with p not 1 modulo ℓ and ℓ ≠ p. There H⁰(A) is ℤ/ℓ, but H² of the plain dual is 0, since it is dual to H⁰ of the roots of unity (our own). The work went into local class field theory, which computes the Brauer group.

**Wikipedia:** [Local Tate duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_Tate_duality). It says: “It shows that the dual of such a Galois module is the Tate twist of usual linear dual.”

**Sources:**

- [Jürgen Neukirch, Alexander Schmidt and Kay Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, Springer (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-37889-1)

### Unramified classes are Frobenius quotients

**Remember:** Remove inertia, then one Frobenius operator computes the group.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S25 (Galois cohomology), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let M be a finite abelian group with continuous action of the Galois group of a local field with finite residue field. Inertia is the subgroup acting trivially on the residue field. Call a first cohomology class unramified if it comes from the residue field’s Galois group acting on the inertia-fixed elements of M.

**Problem.** Write A for the inertia-fixed subgroup and F for Frobenius, the map raising residues to the residue field size. The unramified first cohomology group is A modulo the image of F − 1.

**How the definition helps.** The Galois group of the residue field is generated topologically by Frobenius, so a cocycle is fixed by its value at F (our own). Every value in A occurs, because A is finite and F acts on it through a finite cyclic quotient (our own). Changing a cocycle by a coboundary changes its value at F by an element of (F − 1)A (our own).

**nLab:** [Selmer group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Selmer+group). It says: “the unramified local condition is defined as follows:”

### Cup products invert swapped symbols

**Remember:** Swapping two degree-one classes inverts their Hilbert symbol.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a non-Archimedean local field that contains the nth roots of unity, with n prime to the characteristic. The Hilbert symbol (a, b) is the cup product of the Kummer classes of a and b, read as an nth root of unity through the local invariant.

**Problem.** For all nonzero a and b in K, the Hilbert symbols (a, b) and (b, a) multiply to one.

**How the definition helps.** Cup products of degree-one classes are anticommutative, so swapping a and b negates the class (our own). The swap also exchanges the two coefficient factors, but this exchange acts trivially when the roots of unity lie in K (our own). In the group of nth roots of unity, negation is inversion (our own). The substantive step is that this symbol agrees with the one defined by local reciprocity (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_symbol). It says: “skew symmetric: (a,b) = (b,a)⁻¹”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Fundamental classes make norms commute

**Remember:** Compatible fundamental classes turn norm compatibility into the projection formula.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois extension E/K of non-Archimedean local fields, the fundamental class is the Brauer class with local invariant 1/\[E:K\] modulo integers. Inverse reciprocity is cup product with this class.

**Problem.** Let L be intermediate between K and E. Inclusion of the two Galois groups induces a map after quotienting each group by its commutators. Under inverse reciprocity this is the norm map from L×/N(E×) to K×/N(E×), using norms from E to each base field.

**How the definition helps.** Defining inverse reciprocity by cup product makes norm compatibility an instance of the projection formula (our own). Restricting the fundamental class to the smaller Galois group gives its fundamental class. The projection formula lets the map back to the larger group pass through cup product with that class (our own). On the two sides this map gives inclusion after abelianization and the field norm (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Class formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_formation). It says: “the restriction (of cohomology classes) of a fundamental class is another fundamental class.”

**Sources:**

- [John Tate, The Higher Dimensional Cohomology Groups of Class Field Theory](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969801)
- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Lubin–Tate torsion extends cyclotomy

**Remember:** Formal group torsion supplies the unit directions that cyclotomy misses.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a finite extension of ℚₚ and choose a generator π of its maximal ideal. A Lubin–Tate formal group describes addition and scalar multiplication by power series. Multiplication by π has linear coefficient π and reduces to raising to the residue field size. Its division tower adjoins all points killed by repeated multiplication by π.

**Problem.** The division tower and the maximal unramified extension together generate the maximal abelian extension of K. If \[K:ℚₚ\] exceeds one, adjoining all roots of unity of p-power order to the maximal unramified extension gives a smaller field.

**How the definition helps.** Choosing division by π supplies an action by the full unit group of K (our own). Lubin–Tate reciprocity identifies that group with the Galois group of the division tower (our own). Together with the maximal unramified extension, this gives every abelian extension. Up to finite index, the units have \[K:ℚₚ\] independent p-adic directions (our own). Roots of unity of p-power order yield at most one such direction, even over the maximal unramified extension (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Théorie locale du corps de classes et (φ,Γ)-modules Lubin-Tate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13986v1). It says: “L'extension Fⁿʳ · F∞ est l'extension abélienne maximale de F”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Lubin–Tate torsion gives abelian extensions

**Remember:** Torsion carries scalar multiplication, so Galois acts through units.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a complete discretely valued field with finite residue field of size q. A uniformizer π generates the maximal ideal of its integer ring O. A Lubin–Tate formal group uses power series over O for addition and scalar multiplication. Multiplication by π has linear term πx and reduces to the qth power modulo π.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, adjoining all points killed by πⁿ gives a totally ramified extension, meaning its ramification index equals its degree. Its Galois group is the unit group of O modulo πⁿ, that is, (O/πⁿO)ˣ.

**How the definition helps.** Scalar multiplication puts the torsion points in a module whose automorphisms commute (our own explanation). The substantive steps prove this module is free of rank one over O/πⁿO and every unit occurs as a Galois action. A polynomial for a generating point gives the degree and total ramification (our own account).

**Wikipedia:** [Lubin–Tate formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law). It says: “The compositum of all fields formed by adjoining such modules to the original field gives the ramified part.”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields (1965)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Openness rules out false norm groups

**Remember:** A finite quotient must also be continuous to describe a class field.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In local class field theory use open subgroups of finite index in the multiplicative group. Openness requires the subgroup to contain all units sufficiently close to one. Finite index alone does not impose this condition in positive characteristic.

**Problem.** Open subgroups of finite index in Kˣ are exactly the norm subgroups of finite abelian extensions. In positive characteristic, some subgroups of finite index are not open, so they are not norm subgroups.

**How the definition helps.** Openness excludes dense proper subgroups that pass a finite-index test (our own). Over K = 𝔽ₚ((t)), the quotient of Kˣ by pth powers is a vector space over 𝔽ₚ. It is uncountable, because products of the factors 1 + tⁿ with n prime to p give distinct classes (our own). A nonzero linear functional can vanish on the countable image of the dense subgroup 𝔽ₚ(t)ˣ (our own). Its kernel pulls back to a dense subgroup of index p, which is not open (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Local class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_class_field_theory). It says: “between open subgroups of finite index in the multiplicative group”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Primitive torsion polynomials are Eisenstein

**Remember:** Removing the earlier torsion leaves an Eisenstein polynomial.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let π generate the maximal ideal of a non-Archimedean local field and let q be the residue field size. Choose f(X) = πX + Xᑫ as the power series for multiplication by π in a Lubin–Tate formal group. Primitive points of level n are the new roots of the nth iterate, for n ≥ 1.

**Problem.** A primitive point of level n generates a totally ramified extension of degree (q − 1)qⁿ⁻¹.

**How the definition helps.** Choosing this polynomial makes the equation for the new roots Eisenstein without computing their conjugates (our own). Dividing successive iterates gives π plus the preceding iterate raised to the power q − 1 (our own). This monic polynomial reduces to a pure power of X and its constant term is π (our own). Eisenstein’s criterion gives irreducibility, and adjoining a root gives total ramification, with unchanged residue field (our own). The degree follows by multiplying degrees under composition (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lubin–Tate formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law). It says: “If g is an Eisenstein polynomial, f(t) = tg(t) and F the Lubin–Tate formal group”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Strict isomorphisms preserve division fields

**Remember:** Changing coordinates changes torsion points but not their fields.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a generator π of the maximal ideal of a non-Archimedean local field. A Lubin–Tate formal module describes addition and multiplication by integers of the field through power series. A strict isomorphism is an invertible change of coordinate over those integers with linear coefficient one that respects both operations.

**Problem.** For fixed π, every Lubin–Tate formal module generates the same field at each division level.

**How the definition helps.** A coordinate change respecting multiplication by π identifies the division points without comparing their defining polynomials (our own). At level n these are the points killed by n successive multiplications by π (our own). Their positive valuations ensure the change of coordinate and its inverse converge in the fields generated by the points (our own). The two inclusions give equality of fields (our own). The substantial input is the existence of a strict isomorphism for a fixed π (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lubin–Tate formal group law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lubin%E2%80%93Tate_formal_group_law). It says: “All such group laws, for different choices of e satisfying these conditions, are strictly isomorphic.”

**Sources:**

- [Jonathan Lubin and John Tate, Formal Complex Multiplication in Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970622)

### Unit levels detect wild ramification

**Remember:** Level one detects wild ramification, while level zero detects inertia.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite abelian extension of non-Archimedean local fields, the conductor exponent is the first unit level consisting entirely of norms. Level zero contains all units of the base field. For positive n, level n contains the units congruent to one modulo the nth power of the maximal ideal.

**Problem.** The conductor exponent is zero for unramified extensions and one for ramified tame extensions. It is at least two for wild extensions.

**How the definition helps.** Testing the first two unit levels distinguishes all three cases (our own). Local reciprocity maps the units onto inertia, the group acting trivially on the residue field (our own). It maps level one onto wild inertia, the subgroup of inertia whose order is a power of the residue characteristic (our own). The extension is unramified when inertia is trivial, and tame when wild inertia is trivial (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Conductor (class field theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_%28class_field_theory%29). It says: “Equivalently, n is the smallest integer such that the local Artin map is trivial”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Unramified norms have divisible valuations

**Remember:** An unramified norm has valuation divisible by the extension degree.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an unramified extension of non-Archimedean local fields, define the Artin map by sending a to Frobᵛ⁽ᵃ⁾. Here v is the normalized valuation, and Frob is arithmetic Frobenius, which raises residues to the size of the base residue field.

**Problem.** In the unramified extension of degree n of a non-Archimedean local field, the norms are exactly the elements with valuation divisible by n.

**How the definition helps.** Writing the Artin image as a Frobenius power replaces a product of conjugates with a divisibility test (our own). Frobenius has order n, so its power is trivial exactly when n divides the valuation (our own). Local reciprocity identifies this kernel with the norm group (our own).

### The Weil group makes the reciprocity map an isomorphism

**Remember:** Allow only integer powers of Frobenius, and K× matches exactly.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S37 (Langlands-Weil conjectures, nonabelian class field theory), 11S31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a p-adic field, the Weil group is part of the absolute Galois group. Its elements act on the residue field by an integer power of Frobenius. It is a dense subgroup with its own topology.

**Problem.** For a non-archimedean local field K, the reciprocity map gives an isomorphism from K× to the abelianized Weil group.

**How the definition helps.** K× contains ℤ as the powers of a uniformizer, a generator of the maximal ideal of the integers. The Weil group contains ℤ as the powers of Frobenius, so the two match. The Galois group has the profinite integers in that place. So the map from K× into the abelianized Galois group is injective with dense image, but not onto (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weil group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weil_group). It says: “The reciprocity map of the class formation (G,A) induces an isomorphism from Aᴳ to the abelianization of the Weil group.”

- [André Weil, Sur la théorie du corps de classes, Journal of the Mathematical Society of Japan 3 (1951)](https://doi.org/10.2969/jmsj/00310001)

### Weil characters need not be periodic

**Remember:** Discrete Frobenius powers allow arbitrary nonzero complex eigenvalues.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S37 (Langlands-Weil conjectures, nonabelian class field theory), 11S20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let K be a local field with residue field of size q. Its Weil group consists of absolute Galois automorphisms acting on the algebraic residue field by integer powers of Frobenius, the qth power map. Inertia is the kernel of this action. Give inertia its usual topology and make it an open subgroup.

**Problem.** A complex character of the Weil group that is trivial on inertia can assign any nonzero complex number to Frobenius. It extends continuously to the absolute Galois group exactly when that number is a root of unity.

**How the definition helps.** Making inertia open gives the discrete quotient ℤ, so its generator can take any nonzero complex value (our own argument). The absolute Galois quotient is instead the profinite completion of ℤ, which is compact. A small arc around 1 in the unit circle contains no nontrivial subgroup, so a continuous character of this compact group has finite image. Every root of unity gives a character through a finite cyclic quotient (our own argument).

**nLab:** [Weil group](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Weil+group). It says: “defined as the inverse image of Frobenius automorphisms”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Brauer invariants equate period and index

**Remember:** The reduced denominator gives both the period and the index.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S45 (Algebras and orders, and their zeta functions), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A central simple algebra is a finite-dimensional algebra with center the base field and no nontrivial two-sided ideals. Its Brauer class identifies matrix algebras over the same division algebra. The index is the square root of that division algebra’s dimension over its center. The period is the order of the class under tensor product.

**Problem.** For a central simple algebra over a non-Archimedean local field, its period equals its index.

**How the definition helps.** The local invariant turns both quantities into the denominator n of one reduced fraction (our own). The invariant identifies the Brauer group with the rationals modulo the integers, so n is the period (our own). Extending scalars to the unramified extension of degree n multiplies the invariant by n, so that extension splits the algebra (our own). The index divides every splitting degree and the period divides the index, so both equal n (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer_group). It says: “the index of A is equal to the period of A.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Scalar extension multiplies Brauer invariants

**Remember:** Extending scalars multiplies the invariant by the extension degree.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S45 (Algebras and orders, and their zeta functions), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a non-Archimedean local field, identify two central simple algebras if matrix algebras over them are isomorphic. The resulting equivalence classes are Brauer classes. Represent a class by an unramified cyclic extension of degree n and an element u acting on that field by Frobenius conjugation. The invariant is the normalized valuation of uⁿ divided by n, taken modulo the integers.

**Problem.** For any finite extension E/K of non-Archimedean local fields, the invariant of the restricted Brauer class is \[E:K\] times the original invariant.

**How the definition helps.** The invariant replaces matrix calculations with multiplication by two field degrees (our own). Extending scalars multiplies normalized valuations by the ramification index e (our own). The new Frobenius is the old one raised to the residue degree f, which multiplies the character value by f (our own). Since ef = \[E:K\], the invariant is multiplied by the extension degree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse invariant of an algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_invariant_of_an_algebra). It says: “The invariant map attaches the element k/n mod 1 to the class.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Finite differences extract Mahler coefficients

**Remember:** One difference lowers the binomial degree by one.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, \\(p\\)-adic integration, etc.)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be a continuous function from the p-adic integers ℤₚ to the p-adic numbers ℚₚ. Expand f in the binomial polynomials binom(x, n). The forward difference is Δf(x) = f(x + 1) − f(x).

**Problem.** In the Mahler expansion of f, the coefficient of binom(x, n) is the nth forward difference of f at zero.

**How the definition helps.** The binomial basis makes Δ lower the index by one, by Pascal’s identity (our own calculation). At zero, every positive-index basis polynomial vanishes. Applying Δ repeatedly therefore picks out one coefficient at a time (our own calculation). With ordinary powers, each difference mixes several degrees. Mahler’s theorem supplies the uniformly convergent expansion.

**Wikipedia:** [Mahler's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_theorem). It says: “the coefficients aₙ = (Δⁿf)(0) → 0 in ℚₚ as n → ∞.”

**Sources:**

- [Kurt Mahler, An Interpolation Series for Continuous Functions of a p-adic Variable (1958)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1958.199.23)

### Kummer congruences determine measures

**Remember:** Congruences on a dense set are continuity tests for the integral.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, \\(p\\)-adic integration, etc.)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ℂₚ be the completed algebraic closure of the p-adic numbers. Write O for its elements of absolute value at most one. An integral measure on the p-adic units is a continuous ℂₚ-linear functional on continuous ℂₚ-valued functions that sends O-valued functions into O.

**Problem.** Take continuous O-valued functions on the p-adic units whose ℂₚ-linear span is dense, and assign each function a value in O. These values come from a unique integral measure exactly when the following test holds for every finite ℂₚ-linear combination and every integer m. If the combination takes values in pᵐO, then the same combination of the assigned values lies in pᵐO.

**How the definition helps.** The functional definition turns the existence question into a bound on finite linear combinations (our own explanation). The test sends zero relations to zero and gives continuity on the span. Density and completeness then give a unique extension (our own argument).

**Paper or page:** [On p-adic Measures for Quaternionic Modular Forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11822v3). It says: “is equivalent to the following Kummer congruences”

**Sources:**

- [On p-adic Measures for Quaternionic Modular Forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11822v3)

### Trace duals locate character conductors

**Remember:** The inverse different is the largest ideal the trace character kills.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, \\(p\\)-adic integration, etc.)), 11S15. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite separable extension L/K of non-Archimedean local fields, the inverse different is the set of x in L with Tr(xy) integral for every integer y of L. Fix an additive character ψ of K whose largest fractional ideal of triviality is the integer ring of K. Pull it back to L as ψ ∘ Tr.

**Problem.** The pulled-back additive character is trivial on a fractional ideal of L precisely when that ideal is contained in the inverse different.

**How the definition helps.** The trace definition identifies the conductor directly, without computing a generator of the different (our own). The trace of a nonzero fractional ideal is a fractional ideal of K by linearity and separability (our own). The character kills this image exactly when it lies in the base integer ring (our own). Multiplying by any extension integer preserves the original ideal, so this integrality tests every pairing defining the inverse different (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “It plays a basic role in Pontryagin duality for p-adic fields.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Pierre Serre, Local Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5673-9)

### Limits of powers make the Teichmüller lift multiplicative

**Remember:** Limits preserve products, and one more power shifts the sequence.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S85 (Other nonanalytic theory), 12J25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let p be prime and let a be a p-adic integer with residue x modulo p. Define the Teichmüller lift ω(x) as the p-adic limit of a raised to pⁿ as n grows. Another definition takes the unique root of Tᵖ = T with residue x, which Hensel’s lemma provides.

**Problem.** For residues x and y modulo p, ω(xy) = ω(x)ω(y). Also, ω(x) has residue x and satisfies ω(x)ᵖ = ω(x).

**How the definition helps.** With the limit definition, multiplicativity follows by taking limits of products of the powers. Taking the pth power shifts the sequence by one term, which proves the root equation (our own). The work moves into proving that congruence modulo pᵏ implies congruence of pth powers modulo pᵏ⁺¹ for k ≥ 1 (our own). Successive powers agree modulo increasing powers of p, so they converge, and the same estimate proves independence from a (our own). The root definition instead uses uniqueness to compare the lift of xy with the product of the lifts (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Teichmüller character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teichm%C3%BCller_character). It says: “If x is an integer mod p, then ω(x) is the unique solution of ω(x)ᵖ = ω(x) that is congruent to x mod p.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Principal units have unique prime-to-p roots

**Remember:** A principal unit has just one prime-to-p root with residue one.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S85 (Other nonanalytic theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a finite extension of the p-adic numbers, reduce each integer modulo the maximal ideal to obtain its residue. The principal units are the integers with residue one.

**Problem.** For each positive integer m prime to p, raising to the mth power is an automorphism of the principal units of a p-adic field.

**How the definition helps.** Restricting to principal units fixes the residue of the root in advance (our own proof). For a principal unit u, the equation xᵐ = u has the simple root 1 modulo the maximal ideal. Its derivative there is m, which is nonzero in the residue field. Hensel’s lemma lifts that root uniquely with the same residue. Among all units the assertion fails because −1 has no square root modulo 3 (our own example).

**Paper or page:** [Duality for condensed cohomology of the Weil group of a p-adic field](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05565v1). It says: “For m coprime to p, the continuous homomorphism (−)ᵐ: 𝒰ₖⁿ → 𝒰ₖⁿ is an isomorphism of topological groups.”

**Sources:**

- [Duality for condensed cohomology of the Weil group of a p-adic field](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05565v1)

### Artin–Schreier sheaves encode lifted characters

**Remember:** A single additive cover encodes every lifted character.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a nontrivial additive character ψ of the prime field 𝔽ₚ, so ψ turns addition into multiplication. Above each x, take all solutions of yᵖ − y = x. Translation by 𝔽ₚ permutes these solutions. Use the one-dimensional space of functions h satisfying h(y + a) = ψ(a)h(y).

**Problem.** For x in any finite extension k, geometric Frobenius has trace ψ(Tr(x)) on this space. Here Tr is the field trace from k to 𝔽ₚ.

**How the definition helps.** Our own construction replaces a separate lifted character over each field with one space of functions above each point. Write q = \|k\|. Adding the successive pth powers of the defining equation shows that the qth power of y equals y + Tr(x). Geometric Frobenius acts on functions by precomposition with the qth-power map on solutions. The translation rule therefore gives the claimed scalar.

**nLab:** [Artin-Schreier sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Artin-Schreier+sequence). It says: “F − id ≔ (−)ᵖ − (−) : (𝔾ₐ)ₓ → (𝔾ₐ)ₓ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced phases expose the true degree

**Remember:** Remove pth-power differences before measuring a phase.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over a finite field k of characteristic p, call two polynomial phases equivalent if their difference is gᵖ − g for some polynomial g. Replace a term a x raised to pm by b x raised to m, where bᵖ = a and m ≥ 1. Repeat after collecting terms until no positive exponent is divisible by p.

**Problem.** Let ψ be a nontrivial additive character of 𝔽ₚ, and let S(f) be the sum of ψ(Tr(f(x))) over x in k, with Tr the field trace to 𝔽ₚ. Equivalent phases give the same sum. If the reduced phase has degree d ≥ 1, then \|S(f)\| ≤ (d − 1)√\|k\|.

**How the definition helps.** Reduction measures the degree only after discarding differences invisible to the field trace. Our own calculation uses Tr(gᵖ) = Tr(g) at every input. The Weil bound applies because the remaining degree is prime to p. For example, xᵖ − x reduces to zero and its sum equals \|k\|.

**nLab:** [Artin-Schreier sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Artin-Schreier+sequence). It says: “There is a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves over the étale site”

**Sources:**

- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 11](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/ik-ant-exp-sums.pdf)

### Smooth top forms give Deligne cancellation

**Remember:** Test the highest-degree terms on projective space.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Take a polynomial f of degree d ≥ 2 in m ≥ 2 variables over 𝔽𝓆. Assume the characteristic does not divide d. Call f smooth at infinity if its degree-d part and all its first partial derivatives have no common nonzero zero over the algebraic closure.

**Problem.** Let ψ be a nontrivial additive character and let f be smooth at infinity. Then the sum of ψ(f(x)) over all x in 𝔽𝓆ᵐ has modulus at most (d − 1)ᵐ√(qᵐ).

**How the definition helps.** Testing only the top form excludes flat directions that can make a multivariable sum too large. Our own example in odd characteristic is f(x) = x₁². Each of the other variables multiplies the quadratic Gauss sum by q, giving modulus qᵐ/√q. Deligne’s theorem supplies the bound under the smoothness condition.

**Wikipedia:** [Exponential sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_sum). It says: “The Weil conjectures had major applications to complete sums with domain restricted by polynomial conditions”

**Sources:**

- [Deligne, La conjecture de Weil I](https://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1974__43__273_0/)
- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 11](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/ik-ant-exp-sums.pdf)

### Unique shifts force Burgess cancellation

**Remember:** A shift used once gives a zero or pole of order one.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 11L40. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a nonprincipal multiplicative character χ modulo a prime p and set χ(0) = 0. Consider an ordered list of 2r shifts modulo p, with r ≥ 1. Call it exceptional if every shift appearing in the list occurs at least twice.

**Problem.** For each x modulo p, multiply χ(x + b) over the first r shifts b and its complex conjugate over the last r. For a nonexceptional list, the sum of these products over x has modulus at most 2r√p.

**How the definition helps.** A shift that appears once gives a simple zero or pole of the quotient of the two products of linear factors. So the quotient is not a power of degree equal to the order of χ (our own explanation). The character bound in Corollary 11.24 of Iwaniec and Kowalski then applies, including at the excluded zeros. Repeating the first half as the second gives p minus the number of distinct shifts.

**Paper or page:** [On the correlations between character sums of division polynomials under shifts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09271). It says: “Assume that Ψ is not a non-trivial power of a function in”

**Sources:**

- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 11](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/ik-ant-exp-sums.pdf)

### Negative Gauss sums lift multiplicatively

**Remember:** Negating each Gauss sum absorbs the sign in the lifting formula.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11T24 (Other character sums and Gauss sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A multiplicative character χ sends products to products, and an additive character ψ sends sums to products of complex numbers of absolute value one. Define the signed Gauss sum as the negative of the sum of χ(x)ψ(x) over nonzero field elements. Over an extension, evaluate χ on the norm, the product of conjugates, and ψ on the trace, their sum.

**Problem.** For nontrivial characters over a finite field, the signed sum over an extension of degree n equals the nth power of the signed base sum.

**How the definition helps.** In our own normalization, taking the negative absorbs the alternating sign in the Davenport–Hasse lifting theorem. That theorem supplies the relation between fields for the ordinary Gauss sums. Multiplying its formula by −1 gives precisely the nth power of the signed base sum.

**Paper or page:** [Davenport and Hasse's theorems and lifts of multiplication matrices of Gaussian periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14872). It says: “Then, for any integer n ≥ 1, we have Gₙᵣ(ψ′) = (−1)ⁿ⁻¹Gᵣ(ψ)ⁿ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Nonpowers give Kummer cancellation

**Remember:** A perfect power makes the character constant away from its zeros and poles.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11T24 (Other character sums and Gauss sums), 11T23, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let χ be a multiplicative character of order d &gt; 1 on the nonzero elements of a field with q elements. Take a nonzero rational function f over that field. Test whether f is a dth power after extending its coefficients to the algebraic closure.

**Problem.** If f fails the power test, the sum of χ(f(x)) over field elements outside the zeros and poles of f has modulus at most (s − 2)√q. Here s counts infinity and all distinct finite zeros and poles over the algebraic closure.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation uses the orders of zeros and poles to test whether the character can stay constant. On the projective line, f is a geometric dth power exactly when d divides every such order. For f(x) = xᵈ, every nonzero input contributes one. The Weil bound for multiplicative character sums supplies the estimate in the other case.

**nLab:** [Kummer sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Kummer+sequence). It says: “the group of nth roots of unity.”

**Sources:**

- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 11](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/ik-ant-exp-sums.pdf)

### Diophantine sets with parameters let Hilbert's tenth problem meet computability

**Remember:** Parameters in, solvability out: that is a computably enumerable set.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11U05 (Decidability (number-theoretic aspects)), 03D25. arXiv math.NT, math.LO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A set S of tuples of natural numbers is Diophantine if one polynomial p(a, x) with integer coefficients describes it. Namely, a is in S exactly when p(a, x) = 0 has a solution x in natural numbers.

**Problem.** Every computably enumerable set is Diophantine (the MRDP theorem). Hence no algorithm decides whether a polynomial equation with integer coefficients has a solution, which answers Hilbert's tenth problem.

**How the definition helps.** A single equation has a yes-or-no answer, but a family indexed by parameters defines a set, which can be compared with computably enumerable sets. A noncomputable computably enumerable set then gives a family of equations with no decision method. The hard part is the MRDP theorem itself, in particular Matiyasevich's proof that exponentiation is Diophantine.

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert's tenth problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert%27s_tenth_problem). It says: “In a Diophantine equation, there are two kinds of variables: the parameters and the unknowns. The Diophantine set consists of the parameter assignments for which the Diophantine equation is solvable.”

**Sources:**

- [Davis, M. (1973). Hilbert's tenth problem is unsolvable. American Mathematical Monthly 80, 233–269.](https://doi.org/10.1080/00029890.1973.11993265)

### Continued fractions with minus signs make the half-line a terminal coalgebra

**Remember:** Always round strictly up, so every number has only one expansion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions), 18C40. arXiv math.NT, math.CT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write a real number x ≥ 1 as a continued fraction with minus signs: x = a₀ − 1/(a₁ − 1/(a₂ − ⋯)). At each step, let β(x) be the smallest integer strictly greater than x. Take β(x) as the next digit, and continue with the number −1/(x − β(x)). This gives a map ξ : ℝ≥1 → ℕ≥2 × ℝ≥1, which sends a number to its first digit and the rest.

**Problem.** With the lexicographic order, (ℝ≥1, ξ) is the terminal coalgebra of the functor X ↦ ℕ≥2 × X on linear orders. So a real number x ≥ 1 is the same thing as its infinite stream of digits.

**How the definition helps.** Rounding strictly up removes the double expansions that stop ordinary continued fractions from working. With ordinary continued fractions, rational numbers have two expansions. The standard expansion of 2 is just 2, never 1 + 1/1, so no element maps to (1, 1, ∞). That is why ordinary continued fractions make only the irrationals a terminal coalgebra.

**nLab:** [continued fraction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/continued+fraction). It says: “It may be tempting to believe that this F-coalgebra structure makes 𝐑 the terminal coalgebra. That is unfortunately not correct because the coalgebra structure ξ: 𝐑 → F(𝐑) is not an isomorphism”

**Sources:**

- [Dusko Pavlović, Vaughan Pratt, On coalgebra of real numbers, Electron. Notes Theor. Comput. Sci. 19 (1999) 103–117](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1571-0661(05)80272-5)

### Hindman's shift theorem holds for upper Banach density but not upper density

**Remember:** Move the measuring window to see density that an initial interval misses.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B05 (Density, gaps, topology), 37A44. arXiv math.DS, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Upper Banach density measures the largest fraction a set occupies in intervals of increasing length. The intervals can start anywhere. Ordinary upper density uses only intervals starting at 1.

**Problem.** Let E be a set of positive integers with positive upper Banach density, and let ε &gt; 0. For some k, the union E ∪ (E − 1) ∪ ⋯ ∪ (E − k) has upper Banach density greater than 1 − ε.

**How the definition helps.** Upper Banach density lets the theorem measure coverage in long intervals without fixing their starting point. In our own example, take intervals from N to 2N with each N much larger than the last. Any fixed number of shifts leaves ordinary upper density at one half. Upper Banach density is already one in that example. The hard part is proving the result for every set of positive upper Banach density.

**Paper or page:** [An ergodic correspondence principle, invariant means and applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03029v2). It says: “Curiously, this result does not hold if one replaces the upper Banach density d∗ with the upper density d̄.”

**Sources:**

- [Vitaly Bergelson, Andreu Ferré Moragues, An ergodic correspondence principle, invariant means and applications, arXiv:2003.03029 (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03029v2)

### Intersective polynomials remove modular obstructions

**Remember:** If a polynomial misses zero modulo q, multiples of q avoid its differences.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B05 (Density, gaps, topology), 11B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An integer polynomial is intersective if it has a root modulo every positive integer.

**Problem.** Suppose a set occupies a fixed positive fraction of {1, …, N} for arbitrarily large N. For every nonconstant intersective polynomial h, two distinct members have difference h(n) for some positive integer n.

**How the definition helps.** Intersectivity excludes an obstruction from the multiples of any integer q. In our own argument, their differences are multiples of q, so they miss every value of a polynomial without a root modulo q. For example, no two even integers differ by 2n + 1. The cited density bound proves that removing all such obstructions suffices.

**Paper or page:** [A maximal extension of the Bloom-Maynard bound for sets with no square differences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.03345v1). It says: “for any intersective polynomial h ∈ ℤ\[x\] of degree k”

**Sources:**

- [A maximal extension of the Bloom–Maynard bound for sets with no square differences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.03345v1)

### Additive energy finds structured subsets

**Remember:** Many repeated sums can reveal a structured subset inside a noisy set.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The additive energy E(A) counts ordered quadruples (a,b,c,d) from A satisfying a+b=c+d. Each possible sum contributes the square of its number of representations.

**Problem.** Let A be a finite nonempty subset of an abelian group with E(A) ≥ \|A\|³/K for K ≥ 1. Some subset B has \|B\| ≥ c\|A\|/K and \|B−B\| ≤ CK⁴\|B\| for absolute constants c,C &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** Energy lets the hypothesis count repeated sums without requiring a bound on the total number of sums (our own explanation). Scattered points can add many new sums while a structured subset still contributes many quadruples. The Balog–Szemerédi–Gowers theorem extracts a large subset B with few distinct differences b−b′.

**Paper or page:** [Note on the Theorem of Balog, Szemerédi, and Gowers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10245). It says: “Given a real K ≥ 1 every additive set A with energy E(A) ≥ \|A\|³/K has a subset A′ ⊆ A”

**Sources:**

- [Christian Reiher and Tomasz Schoen, Note on the Theorem of Balog, Szemerédi, and Gowers, arXiv:2308.10245v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10245)

### Circle values extend cubic phases

**Remember:** Cube differences see polynomial phases whose values are not signs.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a binary vector space, let P take values modulo 1. A difference in direction h replaces P(x) by P(x + h) − P(x). Say P has degree at most d if every sequence of d + 1 differences gives zero. Its phase is exp(2πiP), whereas a polynomial taking binary values gives a phase taking only signs.

**Problem.** On the group with two elements, the function P with P(0) = 0 and P(1) = 1/8 is a polynomial of degree at most 3 with values modulo 1. Its phase exp(2πiP) is not a constant times a sign-valued phase.

**How the definition helps.** Circle-valued polynomials capture phases that pass the difference test even when sign-valued polynomials miss them. In our own calculation, successive unit differences at zero are 1/8, −1/4, 1/2 and 0 modulo 1. At one these differences have opposite signs, and any zero step gives zero. The ratio of the two phase values is exp(πi/4), which cannot occur between two signs. The cited theorem classifies these polynomials in every degree.

**Paper or page:** [Non-classical polynomials and the inverse theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07495v1). It says: “Then P : V → ℝ/ℤ is a non-classical polynomial of degree at most d if and only if it can be expressed in the form”

### Cut tests give sparse weights bounded models

**Remember:** Intersect the sets in two cut tests to get another cut test.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For fixed r≥2, test f on ℤ/Nℤ by averaging f(x₁+⋯+xᵣ) times a product of r indicators over independent uniform inputs. The i-th indicator tests an arbitrary subset of all coordinates except xᵢ. The arithmetic cut norm is the supremum of the absolute values of these averages.

**Problem.** For every ε &gt; 0 there is an η &gt; 0, independent of N, with this property. Suppose ν ≥ 0, the cut norm of ν − 1 is at most η, and 0 ≤ f ≤ ν. Then some function g with values in \[0,1\] makes the cut norm of f − g at most ε.

**How the definition helps.** The product of two cut tests is another cut test because their indicators multiply by intersecting sets (our own explanation). The dense model theorem uses convex separation to test whether a bounded approximation exists. Polynomial approximation reduces the separating test to products that the cut norm already controls.

**Wikipedia:** [Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem). It says: “A more general relative Szemerédi theorem has since been given by David Conlon, Jacob Fox, and Yufei Zhao.”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, The Green–Tao theorem: an exposition, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 1 (2014), 249–282](https://doi.org/10.4171/emss/6)

### Entropic doubling contracts under homomorphisms

**Remember:** Measure doubling with entropy, and homomorphisms can only shrink it.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity), 11B13, 94A17. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Entropic doubling replaces the doubling constant \|A + A\|/\|A\| of a finite set by a quantity for a random variable X. In our own gloss, it is exp(H(X₁ + X₂) − H(X)), where X₁ and X₂ are independent copies of X and H is Shannon entropy. A related entropic distance between two random variables plays the role of a sumset comparison.

**Problem.** Entropic doubling does not grow under a group homomorphism π. More precisely, Proposition 1.4 bounds the entropic distance of X₁ and X₂ from below. The bound is the distance of their images under π plus an average distance on the fibres of π.

**How the definition helps.** Entropy splits along a homomorphism into an image part and a fibre part, while sets have no such clean rule (our own reading). Proposition 1.4 states this split as an inequality, and the contraction follows from it. So an argument can pass to a quotient group and to its fibres without losing control (our own reading). Results with entropy must still be turned back into results about sets, and that is the remaining work (our own note).

**Paper or page:** [Sumsets and entropy revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403), [Sumsets and entropy revisited](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403). It says: “it enjoys somewhat better properties; for instance, it contracts upon applying a homomorphism.”

**Sources:**

- [Ben Green, Freddie Manners, Terence Tao, Sumsets and entropy revisited, Random Struct. Alg. (2024) 1-33, arXiv:2306.13403](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13403)

### Finite complexity separates binary prime problems

**Remember:** A parallel pair cannot be separated into any allowed classes.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take fixed nonconstant affine forms with integer coefficients, and write vᵢ for the coefficient vector of the linear part of form i. For each i, partition the remaining vectors into at most s+1 classes whose rational spans all exclude vᵢ. The complexity is the least nonnegative s that works for every i, or infinity if none works.

**Problem.** Take t affine forms of finite complexity, and a convex region K in \[−N,N\]ᵈ on which all forms are positive. The sum over integer points n of K of ∏ Λ(ψᵢ(n)) is vol(K)∏ₚβₚ + o(Nᵈ). Here Λ gives log p to each prime power pᵃ and zero elsewhere. The factor βₚ is the fraction of n modulo p at which no form vanishes, divided by (1 − 1/p)ᵗ.

**How the definition helps.** The partition condition identifies systems covered by the counting theorem and excludes pairs with proportional slopes (our own explanation). If no slopes are proportional, singleton classes suffice. The forms n and n+2 share a slope, so the theorem makes no claim about twin primes. The asymptotic requires Green and Tao’s prime counting theorem and the later results that establish its hypotheses.

**Paper or page:** [Improved quadratic Gowers uniformity for the Möbius function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09635). It says: “Let Ψ be affine forms such that no two ψᵢ differ by a constant.”

**Sources:**

- [Green and Tao, Linear equations in primes, Annals of Mathematics 171 (2010), 1753–1850](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2010.171.1753)

### Linear forms tests transfer Szemerédi's theorem

**Remember:** Test the doubled patterns that appear in the counting proof.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix k ≥ 3 and sample two independent uniform residues for each of k coordinates modulo a prime N, all choices independent. For each j from 1 to k, form every sum Σᵢ≠ⱼ(j−i)zᵢ using either residue at each coordinate i ≠ j. Evaluate the nonnegative weight ν on each indexed sum. The k-linear forms condition requires the mean of every subproduct to approach one as N grows.

**Problem.** Suppose ν satisfies this condition, 0 ≤ f ≤ ν, and the mean of f is at least δ &gt; 0. The mean of f(x)⋯f(x+(k−1)d) over uniform x,d is at least c(k,δ)−o(1), with c(k,δ)&gt;0.

**How the definition helps.** The tests control the extra products created when Cauchy–Schwarz duplicates an input (our own explanation). Conlon, Fox and Zhao compare the progression count with that of a bounded function with similar mean. The dense form of Szemerédi’s theorem supplies a positive lower bound for that function.

**Wikipedia:** [Szemerédi's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szemer%C3%A9di%27s_theorem). It says: “It is not implied by Szemerédi's theorem because the primes have density 0 in the natural numbers.”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, A relative Szemerédi theorem, Geometric and Functional Analysis 25 (2015), 733–762](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-015-0324-9)

### Local factors count prime progressions

**Remember:** Separate real volume from each prime’s divisibility correction.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity), 11N13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix k ≥ 3 and count pairs (x,d) modulo p for which none of x,x+d,…,x+(k−1)d vanishes. Divide their fraction by (1−1/p)ᵏ to obtain βₚ. The singular series is the product of βₚ over primes p.

**Problem.** For fixed k≥3, the count of strictly increasing k-term prime progressions at most N is asymptotic to N²∏ₚβₚ divided by 2(k−1)(log N)ᵏ.

**How the definition helps.** The singular series collects each prime’s correction to the count predicted by independent divisibility (our own explanation). For p≤k only d=0 works, giving p−1 pairs. For p&gt;k each nonzero difference forbids k starts, giving (p−1)(p−k+1) pairs in total. The region of increasing progressions contributes the leading area N²/(2(k−1)). Green and Tao’s counting theorem and its later supporting results supply the asymptotic.

**Wikipedia:** [Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem). It says: “for the number of k tuples of primes p₁ &lt; p₂ &lt; ⋯ &lt; pₖ ≤ N in arithmetic progression.”

**Sources:**

- [Green and Tao, Linear equations in primes, Annals of Mathematics 171 (2010), 1753–1850](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2010.171.1753)
