### Minimum quadratic rank gives uniform fibers

**Remember:** Check every combination, because two high-rank quadratics can cancel.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let Q comprise d quadratic polynomials on a finite vector space H over a field of odd prime order p. For a quadratic part q, its rank is the matrix rank of the bilinear form q(x+y)−q(x)−q(y). The tuple rank is the minimum rank among combinations whose coefficients are not all zero.

**Problem.** If Q has rank at least R, each equation Q(x)=b has \|H\|p⁻ᵈ solutions up to an error of at most \|H\|/√(pᴿ).

**How the definition helps.** Testing all combinations controls every oscillating term in the Fourier expansion of the solution count (our own explanation). For example, the pair (q,q) never takes a value with unequal coordinates, however large the rank of q. The quadratic exponential sum estimate bounds each nonconstant term by the reciprocal of √(pᴿ) after averaging over H. Subtracting b reduces any target to the quoted zero count.

**Paper or page:** [An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³-norm relative to quadratic level sets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07962). It says: “be a d-tuple of quadratic polynomials on H of rank at least R.”

**Sources:**

- [Sean Prendiville, An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³-norm relative to quadratic level sets, arXiv:2409.07962v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.07962)

### Normal form exposes the counting bound

**Remember:** Each rival form misses a coordinate that the chosen form uses.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix s ≥ 1 and linear forms over a field of prime order p. For each form, select at most s+1 coordinates with nonzero coefficients. Require each other form to omit at least one selected coordinate. Such a system is in s-normal form.

**Problem.** Give the forms independent uniform inputs from a finite vector space over this field. For functions fᵢ with values in \[0,1\], let Λ(f₁, …, fₜ) be the average of the product of fᵢ applied to form i. Then replacing each fᵢ by gᵢ with values in \[0,1\] changes Λ by at most the sum of the order-(s+1) Gowers norms of fᵢ − gᵢ.

**How the definition helps.** The selected coordinates specify which variables to duplicate in Cauchy–Schwarz (our own explanation). Each competing factor disappears at a step involving a coordinate it omits. What remains is a Gowers norm, which measures an alternating product over the vertices of an additive cube. The counting lemma gives the bound for one replacement, and adding the bounds covers all replacements.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “Let Φ : Gᵏ → Gᵐ be a system of linear forms in s-normal form, and suppose that Φ is coprime.”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)

### Power dependence defeats lower-order counting

**Remember:** A relation among powers makes the phases cancel in the product.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let ψ₁,…,ψₜ be linear forms over the field of prime order p&gt;d≥2. Test their d-th powers for linear dependence as homogeneous polynomials. Apply each form coordinate by coordinate to vectors of length n over the field.

**Problem.** If the dth powers of the forms are linearly dependent, there are functions fᵢ of modulus one whose product along the forms equals one at every input. Yet at least one fᵢ has order-d Gowers norm tending to zero as n grows.

**How the definition helps.** A relation Σᵢaᵢψᵢᵈ = 0 supplies phases whose product is identically one (our own finite-field example). Put ζ = exp(2πi/p) and let fᵢ(x) be ζ raised to aᵢ times the sum of the dth powers of the coordinates of x. For aᵢ ≠ 0, differencing d times gives the exponent aᵢ·d!·h₁⋯h<sub>d</sub> per coordinate, up to sign, and this phase has mean of modulus below one. Independence across coordinates raises that modulus to the nth power, so the Gowers norm tends to zero.

**Paper or page:** [On a conjecture of Gowers and Wolf](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15437). It says: “the polynomials ψ₁ˢ⁺¹, …, ψₜˢ⁺¹ are linearly independent.”

**Sources:**

- [Daniel Altman, On a conjecture of Gowers and Wolf, arXiv:2106.15437v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15437)

### Relative density reaches sparse prime subsets

**Remember:** Compare a set of primes with the primes themselves.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let π(N) count primes at most N. For a set A of primes, use the upper relative density limsup as N → ∞ of \|A ∩ \[1,N\]\|/π(N). This uses the primes as the reference set instead of all integers.

**Problem.** Every set of primes with positive upper relative density contains infinitely many nonconstant arithmetic progressions of each fixed length k ≥ 2.

**How the definition helps.** Relative density gives a prime subset a positive share even when its density among integers is zero (our own explanation). Green and Tao prove that Szemerédi’s progression theorem extends to sets bounded by suitable weights. A sieve supplies such a weight for the primes.

**Wikipedia:** [Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem). It says: “the set A contains infinitely many arithmetic progressions of length k.”

**Sources:**

- [Green and Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Annals of Mathematics 167 (2008), 481–547](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2008.167.481)

### Rough weights make prime uniformity measurable

**Remember:** Compare primes with integers that avoid the same small prime divisors.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let P be the product of primes below w, and let φ(P) count residues coprime to P. The Cramér model M assigns P/φ(P) to integers coprime to P and zero elsewhere. Its mean over a period equals one.

**Problem.** Take w=exp((log N)¹ᐟ¹⁰) and fixed k ≥ 2. On \[1,N\], the order-k Gowers norm of Λ−M is O((log log N)⁻ᶜ) for some c=c(k)&gt;0. This norm averages products over additive cubes, and Λ gives weight log p to positive powers of p and zero elsewhere.

**How the definition helps.** The model preserves the small-prime biases that prevent the constant function from approximating Λ (our own explanation). For example, the mean of (Λ(n)−1)exp(2πin/3) tends to −1/2 by the prime number theorem in residue classes. Tao and Teräväinen’s quantitative uniformity theorem bounds the remaining cube averages.

**Paper or page:** [Improved quadratic Gowers uniformity for the Möbius function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09635). It says: “\\\|\\Lambda - \\Lambda <sub>Q</sub>\\\| <sub>U<sup>s</sup>(\[N\])</sub> \\ll (\\log \\log (N))<sup>-c</sup>”

**Sources:**

- [Tao and Teräväinen, Quantitative bounds for Gowers uniformity of the Möbius and von Mangoldt functions, JEMS 27 (2025), 1321–1384](https://doi.org/10.4171/jems/1404)

### Squared sieve weights dominate primes

**Remember:** Beyond the divisor cutoff, a prime contributes only its divisor one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity), 11N13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Choose smooth χ supported on \[−1,1\], with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1 and χ(0)=1. Define S(m) by summing μ(d)χ(log d/log R) over divisors d of m, using the Möbius function μ. Let W be the product of primes up to w and c the integral of \|χ′\|² over \[0,1\]. On residues N/2 ≤ n &lt; N use ν(n)=φ(W)log(R)S(Wn+1)²/(Wc), and use one elsewhere.

**Problem.** Fix k ≥ 3, take R=Nᵃ with a=1/(8k·2ᵏ), and let w grow sufficiently slowly with N. The weight passes the k-linear forms test for counting progressions, which requires mean 1+o(1) for every subproduct of the doubled progression forms. At primes Wn+1 in the specified half, ν(n) is at least (a/2c)(φ(W)/W)log(Wn+1).

**How the definition helps.** Squaring the divisor sum makes the weight nonnegative while preserving its size at large primes (our own explanation). At primes above R only the divisor one contributes, so S equals one. Since log(Wn+1) ≤ 2 log N for large N, this gives the stated lower bound. Proposition 8.3 of the cited exposition estimates products of divisor sums to prove the linear forms condition.

**Wikipedia:** [Green–Tao theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green%E2%80%93Tao_theorem). It says: “To construct this set, Green and Tao used ideas from Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım's work on prime gaps.”

**Sources:**

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, The Green–Tao theorem: an exposition, EMS Surveys in Mathematical Sciences 1 (2014), 249–282](https://doi.org/10.4171/emss/6)
- [Green and Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Annals of Mathematics 167 (2008), 481–547](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2008.167.481)

### Unique square completion turns a 1-step nilspace into an abelian group

**Remember:** Fix an origin, then the fourth corner of a square is the sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.CO, math.DS. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A nilspace is a set X with chosen maps from the vertices of each cube {0,1}ⁿ into X, called cubes. Cubes stay cubes under the maps between discrete cubes, and every pair of points is a 1-cube. Every corner, a cube with one vertex missing, extends to a full cube. A nilspace is 1-step when every corner of a square, three of its vertices, has exactly one completion.

**Problem.** Every 1-step nilspace X has an abelian group A that acts on X freely and transitively. The cubes of X are exactly the maps ω ↦ x + ω₁h₁ + … + ωₙhₙ, for x in X and h₁, …, hₙ in A.

**How the definition helps.** Unique completion lets one define addition directly. In our own explanation, fix an origin o, complete the square with corners o, x and y, and call the fourth corner x + y. The hard part, done in the paper, is proving the group laws and showing that this one group describes the cubes of every dimension.

**Paper or page:** [Notes on nilspaces: algebraic aspects](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03693v3). It says: “Then there is an abelian group A such that 𝒩 is a principal homogeneous space of A and the cubes on 𝒩 are the projections of the degree-1 cubes on A.”

**Sources:**

- [Pablo Candela, Notes on nilspaces: algebraic aspects, arXiv:1601.03693 (2017). Discrete Analysis, 2017:15, 59pp](https://arxiv.org/abs/1601.03693v3)

### Weighted deletion extends arithmetic removal

**Remember:** Delete little weight, even when the support has tiny density.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a nonnegative weight f modulo a prime N, deleting B costs the sum of f on B divided by N. The progression count averages f₁(x)f₂(x+d)⋯fₖ(x+(k−1)d) over uniform residues x,d. For each j from 1 to k, form every sum Σᵢ≠ⱼ(j−i)zᵢ using two independent uniform choices per coordinate, shared across sums. The k-linear forms test requires the mean of every subproduct of ν on these indexed sums to approach one.

**Problem.** Fix k ≥ 3 and ε &gt; 0, let N be a large prime, let ν pass the k-linear forms test, and let 0 ≤ fᵢ ≤ ν. If the weighted progression count is below a constant c(k,ε) &gt; 0, then each fᵢ admits a deletion costing at most ε. After the deletions, no progression has its jth term in the remaining support of f<sub>j</sub> for every j.

**How the definition helps.** Weighted deletion measures the mass that actually contributes to the count, even when the support occupies few residues (our own explanation). Conlon, Fox and Zhao’s relative arithmetic removal lemma gives the deletions. Its proof represents progressions by overlapping coordinate sets and applies the weighted removal theorem to those sets.

**Paper or page:** [The Green-Tao theorem for affine curves over 𝔽(q)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00839). It says: “Then there is a family of subsets”

- [Conlon, Fox and Zhao, A relative Szemerédi theorem, Geometric and Functional Analysis 25 (2015), 733–762](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-015-0324-9)

### Sidon sets give error-correcting codes

**Remember:** Repeated pair sums are exactly the short column relations that spoil the code.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B75 (Other combinatorial number theory), 94B05. arXiv math.CO, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a binary vector space, call a set Sidon if its unordered pairs of distinct elements have distinct sums. Translate such a set to contain zero. Use its nonzero elements as the columns of a matrix over the field with two elements. A binary linear code is a subspace of such binary vectors.

**Problem.** Let n &gt; t ≥ 2. A Sidon set of size n + 1 exists in the t-dimensional binary vector space exactly when a certain binary linear code exists. The code has length n, dimension n − t, and no nonzero word with fewer than five nonzero coordinates.

**How the definition helps.** Using the set as matrix columns turns each short codeword into an equality of pair sums. Distinct nonzero columns rule out codewords of weight one or two (our own proof). Because the set contains zero, a codeword of weight three or four would repeat a pair sum. So the kernel of the matrix contains a code of dimension n − t with the required minimum weight. Conversely, the columns of a parity-check matrix with t rows, together with zero, form the required Sidon set.

**Paper or page:** [Sidon sets, sum-free sets and linear codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07906v3). It says: “There is no Sidon set M ⊆ 𝔽₂ᵗ of size n + 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Sidon sets, sum-free sets and linear codes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.07906v3)

### Oriented quadratic algebras let twisted binary forms describe Picard groups

**Remember:** Orient the algebra first, then the form classes give its ideal classes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms), 11R65, 14F06. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A quadratic algebra over a scheme S is an algebra that is locally free of rank two. A line bundle on S is a module that is locally free of rank one. The Picard group is the group of invertible modules under tensor product. For a line bundle N, an N-orientation is an isomorphism from the quotient of the algebra by the scalars to the dual of N.

**Problem.** Let S be a scheme on which 2 is not a zero divisor, and fix a line bundle N, a discriminant and a parity. Classes of primitive N-twisted binary quadratic forms with these invariants match the Picard group of the N-oriented algebra with them.

**How the definition helps.** The orientation keeps track of the algebra when the quotient by scalars has no global basis. The paper shows that the discriminant and the parity classify the oriented algebras. The paper says that Wood's earlier bijection needs this refinement to give Picard groups.

**Paper or page:** [Recovering the Picard group of quadratic algebras from Wood's binary quadratic forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13422v5). It says: “Extending the notion of orientation of quadratic algebras to the non-free case is another key step, eventually leading us to the desired parametrization.”

**Sources:**

- [William Dallaporta, Recovering the Picard group of quadratic algebras from Wood's binary quadratic forms, arXiv:2111.13422v5 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.13422v5)

### Primitive values distinguish binary forms

**Remember:** Use coprime inputs to tell primitive forms apart.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11E16 (General binary quadratic forms). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A binary quadratic form is a polynomial ax² + bxy + cy². An integral form is primitive if its coefficients have greatest common divisor one. Its primitive values come from integer pairs with coprime coordinates. Its discriminant is b² − 4ac.

**Problem.** Primitive integral binary quadratic forms with nonsquare discriminants are equivalent if they have the same primitive values. Equivalence means an invertible integer change of variables.

**How the definition helps.** Coprime inputs distinguish two inequivalent forms that represent the same integers when all inputs count (our own). The forms x² + xy + y² and x² + 3y² have the same ordinary values but different discriminants. The first represents 4 only when both coordinates are even, while the second gives 4 at (1,1) (our own). Fouvry and Koymans prove that equal primitive value sets force equivalence.

**Paper or page:** [Binary quadratic forms with the same value set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09575v2), [Binary quadratic forms with the same value set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09575v2). It says: “Let F and G be two primitive quadratic forms, with non square discriminants and with F(ℤ²ₚᵣᵢₘ) = G(ℤ²ₚᵣᵢₘ).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Forms with integer matrix need only 1 to 15 to be universal

**Remember:** Integer matrix means even cross terms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11E12. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A quadratic form has integer matrix if its symmetric matrix has integer entries. Then every cross term 2aᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ has an even coefficient. A form is integral, or integer-valued, if it takes only integer values. For example, x² + xy + y² is integer-valued but does not have integer matrix.

**Problem.** A positive definite quadratic form with integer matrix is universal, meaning that it represents every positive integer, if it represents each of 1, 2, …, 15.

**How the definition helps.** The narrower definition gives a smaller constant and a much easier proof. Conway and Schneeberger proved the 15 theorem, and Bhargava later found a short proof. For the larger class of integer-valued forms the bound becomes 290, and the Bhargava–Hanke proof needs large computations. Our own view is that the narrower definition does not remove the hard case, it only sets it aside.

**Wikipedia:** [15 and 290 theorems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15_and_290_theorems). It says: “The 15 theorem says that a quadratic form with integer matrix is universal if it takes the numbers from 1 to 15 as values.”

**Sources:**

- [M. Bhargava, On the Conway–Schneeberger fifteen theorem, in Quadratic Forms and Their Applications (Dublin, 1999), Contemporary Mathematics (2000)](http://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~aar/books/dublin.pdf)

### Weighting forms with extra symmetry gives Hurwitz class numbers modular behaviour

**Remember:** Count the square and hexagonal forms fractionally, and generating functions become modular.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11E41 (Class numbers of quadratic and Hermitian forms), 11F37. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Hurwitz class number H(N) counts classes of positive definite binary quadratic forms of discriminant −N. A class is weighted by 2/g, where g is the order of its group of automorphisms. So the class of x² + y² counts 1/2, and the class of x² + xy + y² counts 1/3. One also sets H(0) = −1/12.

**Problem.** With these weights, the generating function Σ H(N) qᴺ is a mock modular form of weight 3/2. That is, Zagier showed that adding a simple correction term makes it transform like a modular form of weight 3/2.

**How the definition helps.** The weights count each form as a point with its symmetry taken into account, which is how modular objects count (our own). The forms x² + y² and x² + xy + y² have extra symmetries of orders 4 and 6, and counting them as 1 breaks the identities (our own). An example is the Kronecker–Hurwitz relation Σ H(4n − t²) = 2σ(n) − Σ min(d, n/d) (our own). For n = 1 it gives H(4) + 2H(3) + 2H(0) = 1/2 + 2/3 − 1/6 = 1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hurwitz class number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz_class_number). It says: “forms are weighted by 2/g for g the order of their automorphism group, and where H(0) = –1/12.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Weighting lattices by one over their symmetries gives the mass formula

**Remember:** Count each lattice as one over its symmetries, and the total is computable.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E41 (Class numbers of quadratic and Hermitian forms), 11E08. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Two positive definite integral quadratic forms are in the same genus when they are equivalent over the p-adic integers for every prime p (our own). The mass of a genus is Σ 1/\|Aut(Λ)\| over its classes Λ. Here Aut(Λ) is the finite group of symmetries of the lattice.

**Problem.** For dimension n ≥ 2, the mass of a genus equals an explicit product of local factors, one for each prime.

**How the definition helps.** The weight 1/\|Aut\| makes the count a volume, and volumes split into pieces at each prime (our own). The plain number of classes in a genus has no such product formula (our own). For example, the E₈ lattice is alone in its genus, so its mass is 1/696729600, one over the order of its symmetry group (our own). The page warns that the factors at the prime 2 are hard to get right.

**Wikipedia:** [Smith–Minkowski–Siegel mass formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith%E2%80%93Minkowski%E2%80%93Siegel_mass_formula). It says: “a formula for the sum of the weights of the lattices (quadratic forms) in a genus, weighted by the reciprocals of the orders of their automorphism groups.”

**Sources:**

- [H. J. S. Smith, On the orders and genera of quadratic forms containing more than three indeterminates. Second notice, Proc. Roy. Soc. London 16 (1867) 197–208](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspl.1867.0036)
- [C. L. Siegel, Über die analytische Theorie der quadratischen Formen, Ann. of Math. 36 (1935) 527–606](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968644)
- [J. H. Conway and N. J. A. Sloane, Low-dimensional lattices. IV. The mass formula, Proc. Roy. Soc. London A 419 (1988)](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1988.0107)

### Relative completion retains modular monodromy

**Remember:** Keep the reductive quotient before completing.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F06 (Structure of modular groups and generalizations; arithmetic groups), 20G30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A unipotent matrix has all eigenvalues one. Ordinary rational unipotent completion collects all homomorphisms to unipotent algebraic groups over ℚ in one universal group. Relative completion starts with a homomorphism whose image is dense for polynomial equations in a reductive group R. It collects lifts to extensions of R by unipotent groups, taking their inverse limit.

**Problem.** The ordinary rational unipotent completion of the modular group SL₂(ℤ) is trivial. Its completion relative to the standard inclusion surjects onto the algebraic group SL₂ over ℚ.

**How the definition helps.** Fixing the target SL₂ keeps a quotient that ordinary unipotent completion loses (our own). The upper and lower triangular elementary integer matrices are dense in the two one-parameter subgroups they belong to (our own). These subgroups generate SL₂, so relative completion has the required dense starting map (our own). The modular group has finite abelianization and hence no nonzero rational additive character (our own). Any nontrivial unipotent image would yield such a character from the smallest algebraic group containing it (our own).

**nLab:** [Malcev completion](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Malcev+completion). It says: “Mal'cev completion is a left adjoint functor to the embedding of the category of uniquely divisible nilpotent groups into the category of nilpotent groups.”

**Sources:**

- [Richard Hain, The Hodge-de Rham Theory of Modular Groups](https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9781316387887.019)

### Big theta quotients detect pairs

**Remember:** Take the largest quotient with the desired first action.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F27 (Theta series; Weil representation; theta correspondences), 11F70. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over a p-adic field of odd residue characteristic, take an orthogonal group and a symplectic group acting together in the Weil representation. Use their covering groups when the action requires them. For an irreducible smooth complex representation π of the first group, take the largest quotient on which that group acts by copies of π. Write this quotient as π tensored with Θ(π), called the big theta lift.

**Problem.** Take an irreducible smooth complex representation σ of the second group. The Weil representation surjects onto π tensored with σ exactly when Θ(π) surjects onto σ. Such a σ is unique up to isomorphism and is called the small theta lift.

**How the definition helps.** The largest quotient collects all maps onto pairs with first factor π in a single representation (our own). Its defining property reduces testing each pair separately to testing quotients of Θ(π) (our own). Howe duality proves the further assertion that a nonzero big lift has a unique irreducible quotient.

**Paper or page:** [Equal rank local theta correspondence as a strong Morita equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.13484v3). It says: “Θ(π) is either zero or has a unique irreducible quotient, so that θ(π) is irreducible.”

**Sources:**

- [Wee Teck Gan and Shuichiro Takeda, A proof of the Howe duality conjecture](https://doi.org/10.1090/jams/839)

### Transposition gives Hecke duality

**Remember:** Duality swaps the two maps and replaces each isogeny by its dual.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F60 (Hecke-Petersson operators, differential operators (several variables)), 11F41. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a Hilbert modular variety for a totally real field in which p splits completely, use the full integral matrix group at p. Define the normalized Hecke operator at a prime 𝔭 above p by a correspondence. Pull sections back along one projection from the space of 𝔭-isogenies, apply a normalized map between coefficient lines, and sum along the other projection.

**Problem.** Serre duality pairs the cohomology of weight (k,w) on the compactified variety with the cohomology of weight (2 − k, −w) in the complementary degree. The second group uses sections vanishing on the boundary, and 2 − k subtracts each component of k from two. The adjoint of the normalized Hecke operator in weight (k,w) acts in weight (2 − k, −w).

**How the definition helps.** Defining the operator through a correspondence lets duality interchange its pullback and trace (our own). The dual isogeny identifies the exchanged correspondence with the original one. The work is checking the normalized map on coefficient lines and identifying the dual line using Kodaira–Spencer (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Higher Hida theory for Hilbert modular varieties in the totally split case](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05666v3). It says: “Since the correspondence X₀(𝔭) is isomorphic to its transpose, by sending the isogeny π to the isogeny πᴰ”

**Sources:**

- [Giada Grossi, Higher Hida theory for Hilbert modular varieties in the totally split case, Proposition 3.1.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05666v3)

### A three-block product excludes exceptional zeros

**Remember:** Four copies of a real zero overwhelm three poles.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let π be a unitary cuspidal representation distinct from its dual π̃, with central character trivial on positive real scalars. Form the list Π = (1,π,π̃), where 1 is the trivial character. Define D(s) by multiplying the nine Rankin–Selberg functions pairing this list with its dual list.

**Problem.** For fixed rank and number field, some effective c &gt; 0 excludes real zeros of L(s,π) in \[1−c/log(3+C),1). The analytic conductor C combines the finite conductor and the sizes of the gamma factors at height zero.

**How the definition helps.** In our own proof, the list forces four copies of any real zero but gives only three poles at 1. Two factors equal L(s,π), and two equal its complex conjugate on the real line. Only the three matched dual pairs contribute poles. Positivity of the coefficients of −D′/D bounds the number of nearby zeros by three, counting multiplicities. Conductor estimates for the nine factors give the stated interval.

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2). It says: “is not self-dual, then L(s,π) has no exceptional zero.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Abelian quotient isolates zero-free factors

**Remember:** Remove the scalar line before bounding the other factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a full-level holomorphic cuspidal Hecke eigenform and write π for its normalized representation. Its mth symmetric power, written Symᵐπ, uses the action on homogeneous polynomials of degree m in two variables. For m ≥ 1 set R(s) = L(s,Symᵐπ×Symᵐπ)/ζ(s). Let C denote the analytic conductor of π, which measures its finite and gamma factors.

**Problem.** There is an absolute, effectively computable c &gt; 0 such that R(s) has no real zeros for s ≥ 1−c/(m² log(3mC²)).

**How the definition helps.** The quotient removes the scalar part before stating nonvanishing for all the remaining factors together. The paper divides by this one-dimensional factor, which here is ζ(s), when the two symmetric powers coincide. In our own specialization, full level gives trivial central character and finite conductor one, and such forms have no complex multiplication, as the theorem requires. The zero-free estimate itself requires the paper’s theorem.

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2). It says: “There exists an absolute, effectively computable constant”

**Sources:**

- [Jesse Thorner, Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2)

### Additive twists encode modular transformations

**Remember:** A rational additive twist records the cusp used in a transformation.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Start with an absolutely convergent series ∑ a(n)/nˢ on Re s &gt; 1 and set e(x) = exp(2πix). Define its completed additive twist T(s,x) = γ(s)∑ a(n)e(nx)/nˢ for rational x. Take γ(s) = Qˢ∏Γ(λs+μ), with Q,λ positive, ∑λ = 1 and Re μ &gt; −λ/2 for each factor. Fix a positive level N, a multiplicative character χ modulo N and a nonzero constant ω.

**Problem.** Let q &gt; 0 be divisible by N, and let ab ≡ 1 modulo q. Suppose that for all such q, a and b, the twists T(s, a/q) and T(s, −b/q) extend to entire functions of finite order. Suppose also that T(s, a/q) = ωχ(b) q¹⁻²ˢ T(1 − s, −b/q). Then for some positive integer k, the numbers a(n)n⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾ᐟ² are the coefficients of a modular Fourier series of weight k, level N and character χ.

**How the definition helps.** The additive phase identifies the two rational shifts that a modular transformation relates. In our own explanation, the factor e(nx) translates the nth Fourier term by x. The converse theorem recovers modular symmetry from the paired functional equations. Identifying the gamma factor and inverting the Mellin transform supply the analytic work.

**Paper or page:** [An extension of Venkatesh's converse theorem to the Selberg class](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00451v1). It says: “Given any α ∈ ℚ, define the complete twisted L-function”

**Sources:**

- [Andrew R. Booker, Michael Farmer, Min Lee, An extension of Venkatesh's converse theorem to the Selberg class](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00451v1)

### Analytic conductor measures sum length

**Remember:** The square root of the conductor sets the central sum length.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f and g be level-one Maass cusp forms that are Hecke eigenforms, with normalized Hecke eigenvalues λf(n) and λg(n). The analytic conductor C of L(s, f×g) at the center is its finite conductor times the product of 3 + \|κ\| over its gamma factors Γℝ(s+κ).

**Problem.** Let Q &gt; 1 and ε &gt; 0. There is a smooth weight W, depending only on Q and ε and vanishing beyond Q raised to ½+ε, with this property. Let S(t) be the sum of λf(n)λg(n)W(n) divided by n raised to ½ + it. For every such pair with C ≤ Q, \|L(½,f×g)\|² is at most a constant times Qᵋ∫\|S(t)\|²dt + Q⁻¹⁰⁰, over \|t\| ≤ log Q.

**How the definition helps.** The conductor gives one cutoff for every pair with C ≤ Q, so the cited lemma can choose W using only Q and ε. In our own explanation, estimates for the gamma factors in the functional equation give the square-root scale.

**Paper or page:** [Uniform subconvexity bounds for GL(2) × GL(2) L-functions in the spectral aspect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05968v1). It says: “Then there exists a function W(x) depending on Q and ε only”

**Sources:**

- [Zhao Xu, Uniform subconvexity bounds for GL(2) × GL(2) L-functions in the spectral aspect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.05968v1)

### Dual tensor products give squares

**Remember:** The trace of a tensor with its conjugate is an absolute square.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a unitary cuspidal representation, let p be unramified, meaning its local L-factor has the full list of eigenvalues. Put these eigenvalues on the diagonal of A. For the product with the dual, define the prime factor as 1/det(I−(A⊗Ā)/pˢ). Here Ā conjugates each entry, and the tensor product pairs all eigenvalues.

**Problem.** In −L′(s)/L(s) for this product, the term at pʳ has coefficient (log p)\|tr(Aʳ)\|² for every integer r ≥ 1. Every such coefficient is nonnegative.

**How the definition helps.** In our own derivation, the tensor definition turns the coefficient into a trace times its complex conjugate. Taking the logarithmic derivative of the determinant gives (log p)tr((A⊗Ā)ʳ). Multiplying the two separate local L-factors would add their traces instead. The identification uses the description of unramified parameters for a unitary representation and its dual. The cited positivity theorem also covers ramified primes.

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional zeros of Rankin-Selberg L-functions and joint Sato-Tate distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06482v2). It says: “If Π ∈ 𝔄ₙ, then −L′/L(s, Π × Π̃) has non-negative Dirichlet coefficients.”

### Gamma poles delimit the critical integers

**Remember:** A critical integer avoids gamma poles on both sides.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For two full-level holomorphic Hecke cusp forms of even weights k &gt; ℓ, use the normalization reflecting s to k+ℓ−1−s. Call an integer critical when the completing gamma factors are finite there and the dual gamma factors are finite at its reflection.

**Problem.** The critical integers for the Rankin–Selberg function of these two forms are exactly ℓ, ℓ+1, …, k−1.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, checking the definition amounts to imposing one lower bound on each side of reflection. The gamma factors have arguments s and s−ℓ+1, and their poles occur at nonpositive integers. Finiteness therefore requires s ≥ ℓ and k+ℓ−1−s ≥ ℓ. Computing the gamma factors is the separate representation-theoretic step.

**Paper or page:** [An Euler system for the adjoint of a modular form](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.04665v2). It says: “The critical values (in the sense of Deligne)”

**Sources:**

- [Deligne, Valeurs de fonctions L et périodes d’intégrales](https://doi.org/10.1090/pspum/033.2/546622)

### Isobaric sums count repeated poles

**Remember:** Each copy pairs with every dual copy of its block.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An isobaric sum Π groups cuspidal representations into a list of blocks, allowing repetitions. Its dual Π̃ replaces each block by its dual. Define L(s,Π×Π̃) by multiplying the Rankin–Selberg factors for all ordered pairs from the two lists. Use unitary blocks whose central characters equal one on positive real scalars.

**Problem.** If each distinct block occurs m times, with m allowed to depend on the block, the pole order at 1 equals ∑ m².

**How the definition helps.** In our own count, the ordered product pairs each copy with every dual copy of the same block. The pole theorem gives a simple pole at 1 precisely for a block paired with its dual. Nonvanishing at 1 for the remaining pairs prevents cancellation.

**Paper or page:** [A new zero-free region for Rankin-Selberg L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16889v6). It says: “If Π is an isobaric sum, then the Rankin–Selberg L-function”

### Pole correction makes convexity uniform

**Remember:** Cancel the pole without changing growth far from it.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take two unitary cuspidal representations π and π′ over a number field, normalized so their central characters equal one on positive real scalars. Write L(s) for their Rankin–Selberg function, formed by pairing their local parameters. Set R(s) = L(s) unless π′ is dual to π. In that case set R(s) = L(s)(s−1)/(s+1).

**Problem.** R is holomorphic for Re s &gt; −1. For σ ≥ 0 and integers j ≥ 0, its jth derivative at σ+it is O(C(t) raised to max(1−σ,0)/2+ε). Here C(t) combines finite and gamma factors at height t, with the constant depending only on ranks, field degree, j and ε &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** The correction cancels the possible pole at 1 and stays bounded on the right half-plane. This gives one estimate even for dual pairs near the pole. In our own explanation, the simple-pole theorem justifies cancellation, strip estimates control size, and Cauchy’s formula bounds derivatives.

**Paper or page:** [Oscillations and first-ever negative Fourier coefficients of symmetric square L-functions over sparse set](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18994v1), [A new zero-free region for Rankin-Selberg L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16889v6). It says: “consider the holomorphic function”

**Sources:**

- [Gergely Harcos, Jesse Thorner, A new zero-free region for Rankin-Selberg L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16889v6)

### Smooth additive twists have dual length

**Remember:** A smooth twist at length X returns at length q²/X.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F66 (Langlands \\(L\\)-functions; one variable Dirichlet series and functional equations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let λ(n) denote the normalized Fourier coefficients of a level-one holomorphic Hecke cusp form of weight k. Choose a smooth function v supported in \[1,2\]. Define H(u) = ∫v(y)Jₖ₋₁(4π√(uy))dy over positive y, where Jₖ₋₁ is the Bessel function of the first kind. Put e(x) = exp(2πix).

**Problem.** For coprime integers a,q with q &gt; 0 and X &gt; 0, consider S = ∑ λ(n)e(an/q)v(n/X). If ab ≡ 1 modulo q, then S = (2πiᵏX/q)∑ λ(n)e(−bn/q)H(nX/q²). For fixed k and v, H(u) decays faster than every inverse power as u grows.

**How the definition helps.** The transform H makes the original and reflected sums use reciprocal length scales X and q²/X. The cited summation formula replaces the original weight by an integral transform. In our own calculation, changing variables gives its argument nX/q² and its prefactor X. Smoothness removes boundary terms under repeated integration by parts and gives rapid decay. The underlying Voronoi summation theorem supplies the equality.

**Paper or page:** [Subconvexity for GL(1) twists of Rankin-Selberg L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.09646v5). It says: “v be a compactly supported smooth function on (0,∞).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Monodromy distinguishes Steinberg

**Remember:** The Weil action can agree while monodromy differs.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11F70 (Representation-theoretic methods; automorphic representations over local and global fields), 11F85. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The local Langlands correspondence assigns parameters to representations of GL₂ over a finite extension of the p-adic numbers. A parameter records a Weil group action, which encodes field symmetries, and a compatible operator N. This operator is nilpotent, meaning some power is zero.

**Problem.** The trivial representation and the Steinberg representation have the same Weil action after decomposition into simple factors. Here Steinberg means locally constant complex functions on the projective line modulo constants. Their full parameters differ.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping the operator separates two representations that otherwise have the same data (our own). The operator is zero for the trivial representation and has rank one for Steinberg (our own). The work lies in the local Langlands calculation of these two parameters (our own).

**nLab:** [local Langlands conjecture](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/local+Langlands+conjecture). It says: “A Weil-Deligne representation is a pair (ρ₀,N)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Noninvariant characters induce cusp forms

**Remember:** A character must move under conjugation to give a cusp form.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F70 (Representation-theoretic methods; automorphic representations over local and global fields), 11F41. arXiv math.NT, math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a quadratic extension L of a number field F, a Hecke character is a continuous character of the idele class group of L. This group combines local multiplicative groups and identifies tuples differing by a global scalar. Call a character regular if the nonidentity automorphism of L over F changes it.

**Problem.** Automorphic induction transfers the character to a representation of GL₂ over F. This representation is cuspidal, meaning its constant terms vanish, exactly when the character is regular.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity removes exactly the characters whose induction splits as a sum of two characters (our own). For example, the trivial character induces the sum formed from the trivial character and the quadratic character attached to L over F (our own). The quadratic automorphic induction theorem proves the cuspidality criterion.

**Paper or page:** [Vignéras orbifolds: isospectrality, regulators, and torsion homology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07240v1). It says: “is cuspidal if and only if Ψ<sup>σ</sup> ≠ Ψ.”

**Sources:**

- [James Arthur and Laurent Clozel, Simple Algebras, Base Change, and the Advanced Theory of the Trace Formula (1989)](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400882403)

### Crystalline periods detect good reduction

**Remember:** At the residue prime, test for a full set of crystalline periods.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11G07. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K be a finite extension of ℚₚ. A p-adic representation describes a continuous Galois action on a finite-dimensional ℚₚ-vector space. Call it crystalline if it has a Galois-fixed basis after extending scalars to Fontaine’s crystalline period ring. This ring supplies coefficients with their own Galois action.

**Problem.** An elliptic curve over K has good reduction if it has a smooth elliptic model over the integers of K. This happens exactly when its rational Tate module, formed from compatible points of p-power order by extending scalars to ℚₚ, is crystalline.

**How the definition helps.** The crystalline test allows the ramification that good elliptic curves can have at p (our own). The curve y² = x³ − x stays smooth modulo five (our own). Its determinant records the action on roots of unity of five-power order, which requires ramified extensions of ℚ₅ (our own). The crystalline comparison theorem proves necessity, and Coleman and Iovita prove sufficiency (our own).

**nLab:** [p-adic Hodge theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/p-adic+Hodge+theory). It says: “We can also apply this construction with Bcrys instead of BdR; if the dimension stays the same we say that V is crystalline.”

**Sources:**

- [Coleman and Iovita, The Frobenius and monodromy operators for curves and abelian varieties](https://doi.org/10.1215/s0012-7094-99-09708-9)

### Determinants retain small-characteristic information

**Remember:** A trace keeps one coefficient, while a determinant law keeps them all.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A dimension-d determinant assigns a scalar to each element of the group algebra. It preserves products and the identity, and acts polynomially with degree d, homogeneously and compatibly after every extension of scalars. Its trace is the coefficient of t in the determinant of 1 + tx, viewed as a function of x. A trace pseudocharacter satisfies the trace identities for d-dimensional matrices.

**Problem.** Over a commutative coefficient ring where d! is invertible, taking traces gives a bijection between dimension-d determinants and trace pseudocharacters. In small characteristic the trace can lose information.

**How the definition helps.** The determinant retains coefficients that the trace alone can lose (our own). A cyclic cubic Galois group has a nontrivial character χ into the multiplicative group of the field of four elements (our own). Two copies of χ have zero trace, as do two trivial characters (our own). Their determinants differ because χ² is nontrivial (our own). The cited theorem supplies the reconstruction when d! is invertible.

**Paper or page:** [On the relation between pseudocharacters and Chenevier's determinants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18034v1). It says: “a bijection between A-valued d-dimensional determinants on R and A-valued d-dimensional pseudocharacters on R.”

**Sources:**

- [On the relation between pseudocharacters and Chenevier's determinants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18034v1)

### Fontaine's (φ,Γ)-modules are Laurent F-crystals evaluated on one prism

**Remember:** Γ is the symmetry group of one prism, not extra data.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K be a finite extension of ℚₚ with integers 𝒪, and Γ = Gal(K(μ)/K), where μ is all p-power roots of unity. An étale φ-module is a finite free module with a Frobenius-semilinear map whose linearization is an isomorphism. A (φ,Γ)-module is an étale φ-module over Fontaine's ring 𝐀(K) with a commuting semilinear Γ-action. A Laurent F-crystal over 𝒪 is a compatible family of étale φ-modules over the p-completed A\[1/I\], for all prisms (A, I) over 𝒪.

**Problem.** (φ,Γ)-modules over 𝐀(K) are equivalent to Laurent F-crystals over 𝒪. Wu also shows that Laurent F-crystals are equivalent to ℤₚ-representations of Gal(K̄/K), which gives a new proof of Fontaine's theorem.

**How the definition helps.** Wu's prism is Fontaine's ring 𝐀(K)⁺ with the ideal generated by a Frobenius power of 1 + q + ⋯ + qᵖ⁻¹. Its automorphism group among prisms over 𝒪 is Γ, so a (φ,Γ)-module is the crystal's value there with its symmetries. The work went into Wu's proof that this prism covers the final object among prisms over 𝒪.

**Paper or page:** [Galois representations, (φ, Γ)-modules and prismatic F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12105), [Galois representations, (φ, Γ)-modules and prismatic F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12105), [Galois representations, (φ, Γ)-modules and prismatic F-crystals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12105). It says: “Then (φ,Γ)-modules over 𝐀<sub>K</sub> are equivalent to prismatic F-crystals in 𝒪\_Δ\[1/I\]<sup>∧<sub>p</sub>-modules</sup> over (𝒪<sub>K</sub>)\_Δ.”

**Sources:**

- [Z. Wu, Galois representations, (φ,Γ)-modules and prismatic F-crystals, Documenta Mathematica 26 (2021) 1771–1798](https://doi.org/10.4171/dm/855)
- [J.-M. Fontaine, Représentations p-adiques des corps locaux (1ère partie), Modern Birkhäuser Classics (2007 reprint)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-8176-4575-5_6)

### Frames make Galois lifts glue

**Remember:** Fixed matrices glue entry by entry.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let G be an inverse limit of finite groups, acting continuously by matrices over a finite field k of characteristic p. A framed lift gives matrices over a complete local ring that reduce to the original matrices over k. An unframed lift identifies matrices related by a basis change that reduces to the identity.

**Problem.** Suppose every open subgroup of G has only finitely many continuous homomorphisms to the group of order p. Then one universal ring parametrizes the framed lifts to all complete Noetherian local algebras over the Witt vectors of k with residue field k.

**How the definition helps.** Keeping the basis lets two compatible lifts glue entry by entry (our own). The resulting matrices still satisfy the group law (our own). Without a frame, gluing also requires a choice of compatible basis changes (our own). Schlessinger’s criterion converts gluing and a finite number of first-order parameters into a universal ring (our own).

Multiplying the map by a scalar multiplies its exponent by that scalar squared (our own). Compatibility of the Weil pairing with the dual isogeny gives the multiplier n (our own). This compatibility supplies the geometric input (our own).

**Remember:** The group law gives cocycles, and changes of basis give coboundaries.

*True by definition.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14D15. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let ρ̄ be a representation over a finite field k of a profinite group G, a limit of finite groups such as a Galois group. A first-order deformation is a lift of ρ̄ to k\[ε\], where ε² = 0. Two lifts count as the same if a matrix that reduces to the identity conjugates one into the other. Framed lifts keep the basis and do not divide out this conjugation.

**Problem.** The tangent space of the deformation functor of ρ̄ is H¹(G, ad ρ̄). Here ad ρ̄ is the matrix algebra over k, with G acting by conjugation through ρ̄.

**How the definition helps.** The definition makes the tangent space a quotient of cocycles by coboundaries, which is H¹ by definition. A lift g ↦ (1 + εc(g))ρ̄(g) is a homomorphism exactly when c(gh) = c(g) + g·c(h), the cocycle rule (our own). Conjugating by 1 + εX changes c by a coboundary (our own). To read this as the tangent space of a ring needs Mazur's representability theorem, under its hypotheses (our own).

**nLab:** [Galois deformation ring](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Galois+deformation+ring). It says: “where two lifts are considered equivalent if they are conjugate by an element of the kernel of the reduction map.”

### Log prisms extend the crystalline correspondence to semistable lattices

**Remember:** Add a log structure, and crystalline becomes semistable.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

### Oddness excludes nonmodular real representations

**Remember:** Complex conjugation must have opposite signs in the two directions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 11F11. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The absolute Galois group of ℚ consists of the automorphisms of its algebraic closure fixing ℚ. A two-dimensional representation of this group is odd if complex conjugation has determinant −1. In odd characteristic its eigenvalues are then 1 and −1.

**Problem.** Take a continuous odd representation over a finite field of odd characteristic that stays irreducible over the algebraic closure. Serre’s modularity theorem says it arises from a cuspidal modular eigenform, a modular form vanishing at the cusps and diagonalizing the Hecke operators.

**How the definition helps.** Oddness imposes the determinant sign that modular forms require (our own). The cubic x³ − 4x + 1 has no rational root, and its discriminant 229 is positive and not a square. So it has three real roots and Galois group S₃ (our own). Over the field of five elements, permuting three coordinates on the plane with coordinate sum zero gives an absolutely irreducible representation (our own). Complex conjugation fixes every root, so it acts trivially and this representation is not odd (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Serre's modularity conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serre%27s_modularity_conjecture). It says: “Additionally, assume ρ is odd, meaning the image of complex conjugation has determinant -1.”

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11F80 (Galois representations), 14F30, 11S20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

Its Frobenius map from φ\*M(A) to M(A) becomes an isomorphism once I is inverted.

An isogeny identifies the rational Tate modules and carries one Frobenius action to the other. Conversely, Frobenius acts semisimply, so its polynomial determines the rational representation. The Tate isogeny theorem turns this linear comparison into an isogeny.

**Paper or page:** [Traces of Hecke operators on Drinfeld modular forms for 𝔽q\[T\]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04555). It says: “Then cφ(X) = cψ(X) if and only if φ is isogenous to ψ.”

### Ideal classes classify rank one Drinfeld modules

**Remember:** At rank one, period lattices become fractional ideals up to scaling.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.), 11R58. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a place called infinity on a smooth projective curve over a finite field. Let A consist of rational functions regular away from infinity. Work over the completed algebraic closure of the function field completed at infinity. Represent a rank-one Drinfeld module, an action of A by additive polynomials, by the kernel of its exponential, called its period lattice.

**Problem.** The ideal class group acts freely and transitively on the rank one Drinfeld modules up to isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, choosing a basis of the lattice’s one-dimensional span makes the lattice a fractional ideal of A. A fractional ideal becomes an ordinary ideal after multiplication by a nonzero element of A. Changing the basis scales the ideal, leaving precisely its ideal class. Multiplication of ideal classes now acts freely and transitively. Drinfeld’s uniformization theorem identifies lattices up to scaling with polynomial actions up to isomorphism.

**Paper or page:** [Drinfeld Module and Weil pairing over Dedekind domain of class number two](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.16919). It says: “The set of isomorphism classes of A-Drinfeld modules is the principle homogeneous space of the class group of A”

### Lattice enlargement composes ideal isogenies

**Remember:** Ideal isogenies enlarge the period lattice by inverse ideals.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G09 (Drinfel'd modules; higher-dimensional motives, etc.). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a Drinfeld module, an action of a curve’s coefficient ring A by additive polynomials. Here A consists of functions regular away from a chosen place at infinity. Over the completed algebraic closure at infinity, let Λ denote the kernel of the module’s exponential. For a nonzero ideal I of A, define the quotient using the larger lattice I⁻¹Λ.

**Problem.** Taking the quotient for I and then for J gives the quotient for IJ up to isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, enlarging the lattice twice gives J⁻¹I⁻¹Λ, exactly the lattice for IJ. Uniformization identifies the inclusion with an isogeny, a map of modules with finite kernel. Its kernel consists of the points killed by I. Normalizing the polynomial for this map can scale the target lattice, as the cited formula shows.

**Paper or page:** [Drinfeld Module and Weil pairing over Dedekind domain of class number two](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.16919). It says: “Then we have Λψ = Λφ · ∂(λ) I⁻¹.”

### Forgetting signs lets twists share j

**Remember:** A modular curve sees torsion bases only up to curve automorphisms.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G18 (Arithmetic aspects of modular and Shimura varieties), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An elliptic curve’s j-invariant determines it up to isomorphism over an algebraic closure. Let H be an open subgroup of the invertible two-by-two matrices over the profinite integers, which encode compatible residues modulo all positive integers. The modular curve X(H) records compatible torsion bases up to H and curve automorphisms. For j different from 0 and 1728, those automorphisms are identity and negation.

**How the definition helps.** Identifying opposite bases allows a basis class to be fixed even when Galois changes its sign (our own). A rational point requires some fixed class, which accounts for the choice of conjugate (our own). A quadratic twist changes the torsion action by signs, so it gives the same test (our own). Identifying the geometric points above j with basis classes supplies the geometric input (our own).

### Component graphs count torus rank

**Remember:** Each independent loop supplies one multiplicative direction in the Jacobian.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A split semistable model extends a smooth curve to a family whose special fiber has only ordinary crossings. Its components, crossings and branches are all defined over the residue field. Its dual graph has one vertex per component and one edge per crossing, including loops.

**Problem.** Take a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of positive genus over ℚ with split semistable reduction at a prime. Its Jacobian, which parametrizes divisor classes of degree zero, has torus rank equal to the number of independent loops in this graph. This rank counts multiplicative group factors in the connected part of its reduced group model.

**How the definition helps.** The dual graph records exactly where line bundles must be glued across crossings, in our own explanation. Each crossing contributes one nonzero gluing scalar. Rescaling on each component changes these scalars, while a common rescaling does nothing. The remaining number of parameters is edges minus vertices plus one, the loop count for a connected graph. The geometric input identifies this gluing group with the torus in the special fiber of the Jacobian’s Néron model.

### Ramification scales node thickness

**Remember:** An edge length is a valuation, so ramification multiplies it.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14G20. arXiv math.AG, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A split semistable curve model has a reduced special fiber whose only singularities are crossings with two branches over the residue field. Draw a vertex for each component and an edge for each crossing. In completed local coordinates, write a crossing as xy = a. Give its edge length v(a), where the valuation v counts powers of a generator of the maximal ideal.

**Problem.** Start with such a model over a complete discrete valuation ring. After a finite totally ramified extension of index e, the pulled-back model has the same graph with every length multiplied by e.

**How the definition helps.** Measuring edges by valuations gives the new length directly from the old local equation, in our own explanation. The pulled-back equation is still xy = a. The new normalized valuation takes the value e times the old one on elements of the original field. The residue field stays the same, so the special fiber retains its crossings and components. The geometric input is the local equation for a node, which lets us compute lengths without resolving the new model.

**Paper or page:** [Models of Bihyperelliptic Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.09730v1). It says: “with the same dual graph as 𝒞, but with the lengths of all edges multiplied by e.”

### Under semistability, invariant valuations determine the reduction graph of hyperelliptic curves

**Remember:** Require semistability before reading a reduction graph from invariants.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G20 (Curves over finite and local fields), 14H45. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A hyperelliptic curve has a degree-two map to the projective line. It is semistable if it has a proper flat model over the ring of integers whose special fibre is reduced, with only ordinary double points. The dual graph of the special fibre has a vertex for each component and an edge for each double point.

**Problem.** Let C be a hyperelliptic curve of genus g ≥ 2 over a local field K of odd residue characteristic. The paper gives a finite list of invariants that depends only on g. If C is semistable, their valuations determine the dual graph of its minimal regular model over the maximal unramified extension of K.

**How the definition helps.** Semistability removes the curves whose graph the invariants cannot see, so the valuations then determine the graph. The paper shows by a counterexample that, for genus at least two, no list of invariants works for curves that are not semistable. The result is the analog of Tate’s algorithm, where ord(j) gives the graph of a semistable elliptic curve. The work is the explicit method that reads the graph from the valuations.

### Serre–Frobenius groups separate ordinary and supersingular curves

**Remember:** An elliptic curve's Serre–Frobenius group is a circle or a small cyclic group.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G25 (Varieties over finite and local fields), 11G10, 11G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let A be an abelian variety over a finite field with q elements. Divide each eigenvalue of its Frobenius map by √q, so that it has absolute value 1. The Serre–Frobenius group is a compact group built from these numbers, and it records which products of them equal 1.

**Problem.** The normalized traces of the powers of Frobenius are equidistributed for the Haar measure on the Serre–Frobenius group. An elliptic curve is ordinary exactly when this group is the circle U(1). It is supersingular exactly when the group is one of the cyclic groups C₁, C₂, C₃, C₄, C₆, C₈ or C₁₂.

**How the definition helps.** Our own reason: the group turns eigenvalue relations into one compact group, so the distribution law has a single form. For a supersingular curve the normalized eigenvalues are roots of unity, so the group is finite (our own note). For an ordinary curve they are not, so the group is the whole circle (our own). The work in higher dimension lies in finding the relations among the eigenvalues (our own note).

**Paper or page:** [Frobenius distributions of low dimensional abelian varieties over finite fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02237), [Frobenius distributions of low dimensional abelian varieties over finite fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.02237). **Remember:** A regular cover can move any chosen sheet to any other.

**Definition.** A dessin is a connected cover of the sphere branched only over 0, 1 and ∞. Call it regular if its symmetries over the sphere act transitively on each unbranched fiber. Its field of moduli consists of the algebraic numbers fixed by every Galois automorphism preserving its isomorphism class.

**Problem.** Every regular dessin admits defining equations over its field of moduli.

**How the definition helps.** Regularity lets a marked sheet select exactly one isomorphism from each conjugate cover. In our own argument, mark a point above the rational value 2. A symmetry fixing that point fixes every sheet by continuation, so the adjustment is unique. Uniqueness makes the chosen isomorphisms compatible with composition. Galois descent then gives equations over the field of moduli.

### Zero-cycles with modulus give class field theory

**Remember:** The modulus D bounds ramification along the boundary, as a conductor does.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G45 (Geometric class field theory), 19F05, 14C25. arXiv math.AG, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Problem.** Let U be smooth and quasi-projective over a finite field, inside a normal proper X whose boundary supports an effective Cartier divisor C. Then the reciprocity maps give an isomorphism from the inverse limit over D ⊂ C and m of CH₀(X\|D) ⊗ ℤ/m onto π₁ᵃᵇ(U).

Here π₁ᵃᵇ(U) is the abelian étale fundamental group, the Galois group of all finite abelian covers of U. The paper also proves the degree-zero form, that the reciprocity map from C(U)⁰ to π₁ᵃᵇ(U)⁰ is an isomorphism. The work went into Bloch's formula, which links zero-cycles with modulus to Milnor K-sheaves.

**Remember:** An invariant metric turns pullback into exact multiplication of heights.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G50 (Heights), 14G40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let f map a projective variety over a number field to itself. Let L be an ample line bundle with a fixed isomorphism from the pullback f\*L to the qth tensor power of L, for an integer q &gt; 1. Call norms on L at all places invariant when this isomorphism preserves them.

**Problem.** For such a map, invariant norms exist, and the height h that they define satisfies h(f(P)) = qh(P).

**How the definition helps.** The invariant norms make pullback multiply the height exactly, in our own explanation. Arbitrary norms on the same bundle generally give this relation only up to bounded error. Heights pull back with maps and add when bundles are tensored. The existence theorem constructs the compatible norms by repeated pullback and normalization, starting with norms from an integral model outside finitely many places.

**Remember:** Alternating the relative product makes the Kummer tensors symmetric.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

The Kummer motive K records degree-one cohomology of the multiplicative line relative to the points 1 and 1/z. Take degree-n relative cohomology of its n-fold product, marking every face where a coordinate equals either point. Select the part where exchanging two coordinates acts by minus one.

**Problem.** This part of the relative cohomology motive is the symmetric tensor power Symⁿ(K).

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, selecting the sign cancels the sign already contributed by exchanging two degree-one cohomology factors. The relative product theorem identifies the whole group with a tensor power and explains this extra sign. The selected part therefore corresponds to symmetric tensors. This realizes the abstract symmetric power by an explicit product of marked lines.

### Clean polylogarithms erase product terms

**Remember:** Project away products before taking a single-valued period.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

Take its de Rham image, which retains its algebraic differential data. Apply the Dynkin projection, a linear operator whose kernel in positive weight consists of sums of products of positive-weight elements. Evaluate the single-valued period and take its real part in odd weight or its imaginary part in even weight.

**Problem.** Suppose a rational linear combination of formal integrals of the same positive weight equals a sum of products of positive-weight elements. The corresponding clean functions then sum to zero with the same coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** The projection kills the entire sum before numerical evaluation. Our own comparison is with ordinary single-valued evaluation, which preserves multiplication and can retain nonzero products. The substantive step identifies the kernel of the Dynkin projection.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344), [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344). It says: “The kernel of Π is generated by all non-trivial products”

### Clean polylogarithms reverse interior letters

**Remember:** After products vanish, reversal preserves odd lengths and negates even lengths.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write a multiple polylogarithm as an iterated integral, specified by two endpoints and an ordered list of interior letters. Its clean version projects its algebraic differential data onto representatives modulo products of positive weights. Evaluate the resulting single-valued period, taking its real part for odd length and its imaginary part for even length.

**Problem.** In a clean iterated integral of length n &gt; 0, reversing the interior letters multiplies it by (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ without exchanging endpoints.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the clean projection kills the product terms that occur when reversing an ordinary integral’s letters. The shuffle identity interleaves lists to express products of integrals. Its reversal formula pairs the original word with its signed reversal and adds products from all nonempty proper cuts. Only the two uncut words survive. The proof uses the shuffle identity and the kernel theorem for the projection.

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344). It says: “Iᶜˢᵛ(x₀; xₙ, …, x₁; xₙ₊₁) = (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ Iᶜˢᵛ(x₀; x₁, …, xₙ; xₙ₊₁).”

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

For a weight-four symbol, split after its second position and subtract the result with the two halves exchanged. Take both halves modulo products to obtain the weight-(2,2) cobracket.

**Problem.** The weight-(2,2) cobracket vanishes on every rational sum of classical tetralogarithm symbols modulo products. Thus a nonzero value rules out any such expression.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, this test selects the split where the classical tetralogarithm has a repeated logarithm in its second half. That two-letter tensor is half the shuffle square of the logarithm, so it vanishes modulo products. Linearity gives the same result for any rational sum. Applying this obstruction to a particular function requires computing its cobracket.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19F27. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

The elliptic dilogarithm changes sign under negation, so it respects the imposed relation. The formula supplies the link with integration.

**Remember:** The five-term identity lets the dilogarithm act on classes of symbols.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a subfield F of ℂ, start with formal integer sums of symbols \[x\], where x belongs to F and differs from 0 and 1. For distinct such x and y impose \[x\]−\[y\]+\[y/x\]−\[(1−x⁻¹)/(1−y⁻¹)\]+\[(1−x)/(1−y)\]=0. The resulting quotient is the pre-Bloch group.

**Problem.** The Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm D gives a homomorphism \[x\] ↦ D(x) from the pre-Bloch group to ℝ.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation uses the quotient to replace checking every change of representative with checking one family of relations. The analytic five-term identity says exactly that D sends each defining relation to zero.

### Integrable symbols exclude path dependence

**Remember:** Adjacent wedge tests remove the local obstruction to path independence.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a smooth complex variety, remove the zeros and poles of the rational functions under consideration. Represent each function f by the differential form df/f, and represent ordered lists of these forms by tensors. For each adjacent pair, replace its two forms by their exterior product, leaving the other positions intact. A sum of tensors is integrable when every such replacement gives zero after summing.

**Problem.** An integrable tensor gives a homotopy-invariant linear combination of logarithmic iterated integrals. Homotopies fix both endpoints and stay in the open variety.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, integrability kills the adjacent exterior products in Chen’s formula for changing the path of integration. Each form df/f is closed, so the formula has no terms from differentiating individual forms. Our own example uses the form dx/x followed by dy/y on pairs of nonzero complex numbers. From (1,1) to (2,2), moving first in x gives (log 2)². Moving first in y gives zero, although the two paths are homotopic with endpoints fixed.

**nLab:** [iterated integral](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/iterated+integral), [polylogarithm](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/polylogarithm). It says: “Iterated integrals include nested integration of differential forms”

**Remember:** The antipode inverts the whole variation matrix.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Arrange the formal coefficients of multiple polylogarithms in their triangular variation matrix V, with ones on the diagonal. Write W for its transpose. The coproduct splits Wᵢⱼ into the sum of Wᵢₖ ⊗ Wₖⱼ over intermediate indices k.

**Problem.** The antipode, the operation undoing a coproduct under multiplication, sends V entry by entry to V⁻¹.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the matrix definition turns the antipode identity into ordinary matrix multiplication. For W the identity reads S(W)W = I, where I is the identity matrix. Transposing gives the formula for V because the coefficients commute. **Remember:** Multiplication sends torsion to zero and rescales each graded piece invertibly.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let π be the fundamental group of a complex elliptic curve at zero. In its rational group ring, let I be the ideal of sums whose coefficients add to zero. Keep terms through degree n by taking the quotient by Iⁿ⁺¹. The pointed logarithm system transports this vector space along loops by group multiplication and marks the element 1 at zero.

**Problem.** For N ≥ 1, multiplication by N identifies this system with its pullback, whose fiber at P is the original fiber at NP. Thus every point killed by N has a canonical identification of its fiber with the fiber at zero.

**How the definition helps.** In our own argument, the group-ring model turns comparison of two systems of differential equations into a substitution on loops. The substitution sends each group element to its Nth power, which preserves the marked element and respects transport. Modulo terms of higher degree, it multiplies degree k by the kth power of N. These scalars are invertible over ℚ, so the map on each truncated ring is invertible. Sprang’s comparison with logarithm bundles connects this description to differential equations.

The second multiplies the integrals between successive selected positions, counting both endpoints as boundaries.

**Problem.** Splitting the first factor again gives the same three-factor sum as splitting the second factor again.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, both expansions list exactly the same pairs of nested subsequences. One expansion chooses the larger subsequence first. The other chooses the smaller subsequence first, then selects additional letters in each gap. The comparison with the coproduct defined by periods still requires the theorem identifying it with the cut formula.

**How the definition helps.** In our own example, the boundary test removes a symbol that cannot be the image of an indecomposable K₃ class. For \[t\] over ℚ(t), take orders of vanishing at 0 and 1. They send t and 1 − t to the two standard basis vectors, so their wedge is nonzero. Combinations with cancelling boundaries still qualify. Suslin’s exact sequence proves that every qualifying class comes from K₃ and that the kernel there is torsion.

**How the definition helps.** Our own explanation sums over all representatives because the ordinary dilogarithm D(x) can depend on the choice of x. Multiplying x by q only shifts the summation index. Replacing k by −k and using D(1/z)=−D(z) gives the sign under inversion. **Remember:** Once the residue is fixed, there is no class left to add.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with \\(K\\)-theory), 14F40. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.
