### Exact symbols give boundary integrals

**Remember:** Each term supplies a primitive, so only the boundary remains to integrate.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a polynomial P(x,y,z), work where its zero surface is smooth and all functions below have neither zeros nor poles. Form alternating products of nonzero rational functions, writing their multiplication as addition and allowing rational coefficients. Require x ∧ y ∧ z to be a finite sum of terms f ∧ (1−f) ∧ g with rational coefficients.

**Problem.** Over \|x\| = \|y\| = 1, collect the roots with \|z\| ≥ 1, counting multiplicities and orienting by the angles θ, φ of x,y. Assume they form a piecewise smooth chain Γ in this open set, including its boundary. Then the logarithmic Mahler measure minus that of the leading coefficient in z equals a boundary integral.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the decomposition gives a primitive for each term, so their sum replaces an integral over Γ with one over its boundary. Here a primitive is a one-form β whose differential on Γ equals log\|z\| dθ ∧ dφ. Jensen’s formula identifies the integral of this differential, divided by (2π)², with the stated difference of logarithmic circle averages. Stokes’ theorem now gives the integral of β along the oriented boundary, with the same factor. Trieu’s regulator identities supply the primitives, and finding the decomposition still takes work.

**Paper or page:** [The Mahler measure of exact polynomials and special L-values of K3 surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00893). It says: “\\mathrm{m}(P) - \\mathrm{m}(\\tilde P) = \\dfrac {(-1)<sup>n-1</sup>}{(2\\pi i)<sup>n-1</sup>} \\int <sub>\\partial \\Gamma </sub> \\rho (\\xi ).”

**Sources:**

### Exterior roots give regulator integrals

**Remember:** Jensen keeps the exterior roots, and the regulator form reads their logarithms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let P(x,y) = 0 define an elliptic curve, and let P\* be the leading coefficient in y. As x travels counterclockwise around the unit circle, follow the roots y outside that circle, counting multiplicities. Together these oriented paths form γ.

**Problem.** Assume γ consists of finitely many smooth paths on the curve. Write m(P) for the average of log\|P\| with both variables uniform on the unit circle. Then m(P) − m(P\*) equals −1/(2π) times the integral along γ of η = log\|x\| d arg y − log\|y\| d arg x.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, the path selects exactly the root terms in Jensen’s formula for the circle average in y. On γ, log\|x\| vanishes, leaving only −log\|y\| times the angular change of x. Integrating this expression gives the stated sign and factor.

### Short relation bounds imply equidistribution

**Remember:** Every fixed nonconstant character disappears from the average once the height is large enough.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Problem.** Fix the target and let the Boyd heights tend to infinity. Then the source averages of each continuous target function composed with these maps approach its uniform target average. The same conclusion holds for log\|P\| for each fixed nonzero Laurent polynomial P, giving convergence of logarithmic Mahler measures.

**How the definition helps.** In our own argument, the height bound ensures that every fixed nonconstant monomial eventually stays nonconstant. Its uniform average is then zero. Finite sums of monomials approximate every continuous function on the target uniformly. For log\|P\| the Boyd–Lawton theorem also controls the contribution near zeros, where uniform approximation fails.

### Tempered faces prevent tame obstructions

**Remember:** Cyclotomic edge roots make every boundary tame symbol torsion.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 19D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a polynomial allowing negative exponents in two variables, take the convex hull of its exponent vectors. Along each edge, list its coefficients in successive lattice positions, including zeros at missing positions. Use that list as coefficients of a one-variable polynomial. Call the original polynomial tempered if every nonzero root of every edge polynomial is a root of unity.

**Problem.** Take an irreducible tempered polynomial over ℚ whose exponent polygon has positive area. On its smooth complete curve, every tame symbol of the coordinate functions x and y is a root of unity. Thus their symbol has no boundary obstruction after allowing rational coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, an edge root gives the leading boundary value needed to compute the tame symbol. At a curve point write x = tᵐa and y = tⁿb, using a local coordinate t and nonvanishing factors a,b; the tame symbol there is (−1)ᵐⁿaⁿ/bᵐ evaluated at the point. If either order is nonzero, the terms of least order in the polynomial lie on one edge, and their cancellation makes the tame symbol a signed integer power of an edge root. Our own example x + y + 2 has tame symbol −1/2 at x = 0.

**Paper or page:** [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974). It says: “Qₖ(x,y) and Qₖ(x−1,y) are tempered polynomials.”

### Euclidean ideal classes force cyclic class groups

**Remember:** Let the Euclidean algorithm run on ideals, and the class group becomes cyclic.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 13F07, 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The class group of a number field K measures how far its ring of integers is from having unique factorization. Lenstra defined when an ideal class is Euclidean, by a division-with-remainder condition that uses ideals in place of numbers. Our own note: the ring of integers is a Euclidean domain in the usual sense only if the trivial class is Euclidean in this sense.

**Problem.** A Euclidean ideal class forces a cyclic class group. Murty and Graves prove a converse: if K is Galois over ℚ, its Hilbert class field is abelian over ℚ, and its unit rank is at least 4, then a class is Euclidean exactly when it generates the class group.

**How the definition helps.** A Euclidean domain has class number 1, so the old notion says nothing about other class groups (our own). Lenstra’s notion, which the abstract calls a generalization of the Euclidean domain, puts the division condition on ideal classes, and Lenstra proved that a Euclidean class forces a cyclic class group. Our own note: what stays hard is to show that a given class is Euclidean. The paper does this for a family of biquadratic fields with class number 2.

**Paper or page:** [On the existence of a non-principal Euclidean ideal class in biquadratic fields with class number two](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.06464), [Low degree extensions with Cyclic class group](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00225). It says: “Lenstra introduced the notion of a Euclidean ideal class, which is a generalization of the Euclidean domain. Lenstra also proved that the Euclidean ideal in a number field K implies that the class group of K is cyclic.”

### Pólya groups equal strongly ambiguous classes, giving short proofs

**Remember:** Galois-fixed ideals are products over whole fibres, so the groups agree.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R32, 11R34. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let L/K be a Galois extension of number fields with group G. The class group of L is its group of ideals modulo principal ideals. The relative Pólya group Po(L/K) is the subgroup generated by the classes of the products of all primes of L above one prime of K. A strongly ambiguous class is an ideal class that contains an ideal fixed by G.

**Problem.** The relative Pólya group Po(L/K) is the group of strongly ambiguous classes. Its order is h(K) times the product of the ramification indices, divided by the order of H¹(G, U(L)), where h(K) is the class number of K and U(L) is the unit group of L (Corollary 2.3).

**How the definition helps.** Our own argument: G permutes the primes of L above one prime of K among themselves, so an ideal fixed by G is a product of the generators of the Pólya group, and the equality with strongly ambiguous classes is close to the definition. The work then moves into a known exact sequence of Brumer–Rosen and Zantema, which the abstract says gives short proofs of classical results, such as the order formula. Our own note: Pólya groups matter because a trivial Pólya group of K over ℚ means the integer-valued polynomials on K have a regular basis.

**Paper or page:** [Ostrowski quotients for finite extensions of number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00442). It says: “For L/K a finite Galois extension of number fields, the relative Pólya group Po(L/K) coincides with the group of strongly ambiguous ideal classes in L/K.”

**Sources:**

- [Ehsan Shahoseini, Ali Rajaei, Abbas Maarefparvar, Ostrowski quotients for finite extensions of number fields, Pacific J. Math. 321 (2022) 415-429, arXiv:2111.00442](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00442)

### Galois sets identify completions

**Remember:** Restrict the Galois action to read the local field factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let L be a finite Galois extension of ℚ with group G. For an intermediate field K fixed by H, the cosets H∖G represent the embeddings of K into L. For a prime of L above p, its decomposition group D consists of the automorphisms preserving that prime.

**Problem.** For two intermediate fields, form the products of their completions above p. These products are isomorphic as ℚₚ-algebras exactly when their coset sets are isomorphic with the action of D.

**How the definition helps.** Restricting the coset action to D records the local fields and their multiplicities together (our own). Each orbit supplies one completion, the field fixed by a point stabilizer inside the chosen completion of L (our own). The converse uses the correspondence between finite separable algebras and finite sets with Galois action (our own). The cited proposition applies this argument to fields whose coset actions have equal fixed-point counts for every element of G (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Stronger arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4). It says: “if and only if \[H₁∖G\] and \[H₂∖G\] are isomorphic as D𝔭-sets.”

**Sources:**

- [Andrew V. Sutherland, Stronger arithmetic equivalence (Proposition 2.19)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4)

### Locally integrally equivalent number fields have isomorphic class groups

**Remember:** Keep integer information at every prime, and the class group survives.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R33 (Integral representations related to algebraic numbers; Galois module structure of rings of integers), 11R29, 11R42. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K₁ and K₂ be number fields with a common Galois closure L, and let Hᵢ = Gal(L∕Kᵢ) in G = Gal(L∕ℚ). The group G permutes the cosets of H₁ and of H₂, and this gives two permutation modules. The fields are locally integrally equivalent if these modules are isomorphic over the ℓ-adic integers for every prime ℓ.

**Problem.** Locally integrally equivalent number fields have isomorphic ideal class groups. They also have the same zeta function and the same regulator.

**How the definition helps.** The definition keeps integer information at each prime ℓ, and this controls the ℓ-part of the class group. Equality of zeta functions only keeps rational information. In our own remark, fields with the same zeta function can have different class numbers, so the weaker definition does not give the theorem.

**Paper or page:** [Stronger arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4). It says: “In addition to having the same Dedekind zeta function (the usual notion of arithmetic equivalence), number fields that are equivalent in any of these stronger senses must have the same class number”

**Sources:**

- [Andrew V. Sutherland, Stronger arithmetic equivalence, arXiv:2104.01956v4 (2021). Discrete Anal. 2021, Paper No. 23, 23 pp](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4)

### Cartesian conditions preserve Selmer torsion

**Remember:** Pull back the local tests to get the same test on torsion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Selmer group consists of global Galois cohomology classes whose restrictions satisfy chosen tests at each prime. Let T be a free module over a discrete valuation ring modulo πᵐ, where π generates the maximal ideal. Cartesian tests on the points killed by πⁱ are inverse images of the tests on T. On T modulo πⁱ, transport those tests by multiplication by π to the power m − i.

**Problem.** Suppose the Galois group of the number field fixes no nonzero element of T modulo π. For 1 ≤ i ≤ m, both smaller Selmer groups identify with the subgroup killed by πⁱ in the Selmer group on T.

**How the definition helps.** Pulling the tests back makes membership on the smaller module exactly membership of its image on T (our own). The absence of fixed vectors gives the needed injections through the exact sequences of Galois cohomology (our own). These sequences identify the image with the classes killed by πⁱ (our own). The cited theorem verifies the Cartesian property for a particular family of tests.

**Paper or page:** [Bipartite Euler Systems for certain Galois Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05181v1). It says: “The Selmer structure ℱ(𝔫) is cartesian for any 𝔫 ∈ 𝒩.”

**Sources:**

- [Bipartite Euler Systems for certain Galois Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05181v1)

### Ext into units extends Artin–Verdier duality

**Remember:** Pair against the units, and every constructible sheaf gets a dual.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11R37, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let X be the spectrum of the ring of integers of a totally imaginary number field. Artin–Verdier duality pairs étale cohomology on X with Ext groups into the sheaf 𝔾ₘ of units. A constructible sheaf is locally constant and finitely generated on the pieces of a finite partition of X.

**Problem.** For a constructible sheaf F on X, Deninger's theorem identifies the dual of Hʳ(X, F) with Ext³⁻ʳ(F, 𝔾ₘ) for r = 0, 1. For r = 2, 3 it identifies Hʳ(X, F) with the dual of that Ext group.

**How the definition helps.** Ext into 𝔾ₘ makes sense for every sheaf, so the duality needs no torsion hypothesis. For F = ℤ and r = 2, H²(X, ℤ) is the dual of the Galois group of the Hilbert class field (our own). The group Ext¹(ℤ, 𝔾ₘ) is the class group, so this case says that this Galois group is the class group (our own). That is unramified class field theory.

**Wikipedia:** [Artin–Verdier duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Verdier_duality). It says: “proved Artin–Verdier duality for constructible, but not necessarily torsion sheaves. For such a sheaf F, the above pairing induces isomorphisms”

**Sources:**

- [Christopher Deninger, An extension of Artin–Verdier duality to non-torsion sheaves, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 366 (1986)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1986.366.18)

### Tate-modified compact supports make Artin–Verdier duality hold

**Remember:** Tate cohomology at real places removes the 2-torsion that never stops.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let U be an open subscheme of the spectrum of a ring of integers. Compactly supported cohomology of a sheaf on U is defined from a cone, a complex that subtracts the local cohomology at the places outside U. At real places, the definition uses Tate cohomology of the group of order 2 in place of ordinary group cohomology.

**Problem.** Let F be a constructible sheaf on U, one that is locally constant with finite stalks on the pieces of a finite partition. Then the Tate-modified compactly supported cohomology Ĥⁱc(U, F) is finite, is dual to Ext³⁻ⁱ(F, 𝔾ₘ) for every i, and vanishes for i ≥ 4.

**How the definition helps.** Tate cohomology at the real places cancels the 2-torsion that real places add in all high degrees (our own). Without it, the cohomology of the spectrum of ℤ with coefficients ℤ/2 is nonzero in all large degrees, which breaks a duality of dimension 3 (our own). The usual statement avoids this by assuming the number field is totally imaginary. With the modified definition, the theorem holds for every number field and every open U.

**Wikipedia:** [Artin–Verdier duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Verdier_duality). It says: “The sum is taken over all places of K, which are not in U, including the archimedean ones.”

**Paper or page:** [Special values of L-functions on regular arithmetic schemes of dimension 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00811). It says: “If F is constructible, all groups are finite and the Artin-Verdier arrow is an isomorphism.”

**Sources:**

- [Barry Mazur, Notes on étale cohomology of number fields, Annales scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure 6 (1973)](https://doi.org/10.24033/asens.1257)
- [Adrien Morin, Special values of L-functions on regular arithmetic schemes of dimension 1, arXiv:2108.00811](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00811)

### Unit cohomology detects capitulation

**Remember:** A generator upstairs records the lost class through its conjugates.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois extension K/F, choose a finite set S containing all infinite places and all ramified finite primes of F. Form ideal classes using only prime factors outside S and identifying ideals differing by a principal ideal outside S. An S-unit is a nonzero element with prime exponent zero outside S. Upstairs, use the primes above S.

**Problem.** The kernel of extension on S-ideal classes is the first cohomology of the Galois group acting on the S-units of K.

**How the definition helps.** Ratios of conjugates encode a class that becomes principal upstairs, without its choice of generator (our own). If a generates the extended ideal outside S, the ratios c(g) = g(a)/a are S-units with c(gh) = c(g)g(c(h)), and changing a by an S-unit changes the family by a coboundary (our own). Hilbert’s Theorem 90 supplies a field element a for every such family (our own). Its ideal outside S descends because no prime there ramifies (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The S-relative Pólya groups and S-Ostrowski quotients of number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.09362v1). It says: “0 → Ker(ε<sub>K/F,S</sub>) → H¹(G,U<sub>K,S</sub>)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A torus detects common scales

**Remember:** One cohomology class records whether all norms share a scale.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take finite separable extensions of a number field K. Map a tuple of nonzero extension elements and one nonzero base scalar to their field norms multiplied by that common scalar. Let T be the kernel as an algebraic group over K. It is a torus, meaning it becomes a product of multiplicative groups over a separable closure.

**Problem.** Suppose a tuple of nonzero base elements becomes a tuple of norms after common rescaling at each completion of K. The projective Hasse norm principle asks whether one scalar in K suffices. It holds exactly when the map from first Galois cohomology of T to the product of its local counterparts is injective.

**How the definition helps.** The kernel torus assigns one obstruction class to the entire tuple, retaining the requirement of a common scalar (our own). The connecting map in Galois cohomology assigns this class, which vanishes exactly when the tuple has a preimage (our own). Hilbert’s theorem 90 shows that every class arises this way, both globally and locally (our own). Thus injectivity says that vanishing at every completion forces global vanishing (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Projective Twist on the Hasse Norm Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11159v1). It says: “{PHNP} \_K(L<sub>1</sub>, L<sub>2</sub>, \\ldots , L<sub>n</sub>) is true if and only if H<sup>1</sup>(L/K, \\mathbf {T}(L)) \\to \\prod <sub>w\\mid v</sub> H<sup>1</sup>(L<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>v</sub>, \\mathbf {T}(L<sub>w</sub>)) is injective.”

**Sources:**

- [Thomas Rüd, Alan Bu, A Projective Twist on the Hasse Norm Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11159v1)

### Local unit intersections join ring class fields

**Remember:** Intersect the subgroups to join the fields.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K be an imaginary quadratic field with ring of integers O and units ±1. For a positive integer f, the order of conductor f is the subring ℤ + fO. Finite ideles are tuples of nonzero local elements that are units almost everywhere. Class field theory assigns the ring class field to the subgroup generated by diagonal elements of K× and the completed order’s local units.

**Problem.** The smallest field containing the ring class fields of conductors f and g is the ring class field of their least common multiple.

**How the definition helps.** The subgroup description turns the field calculation into an intersection (our own). Class field theory assigns the smallest field containing both to the intersection of their defining subgroups, and for an idele in both subgroups the two diagonal factors differ by a unit of O, which belongs to every order (our own). At each rational prime the intersection takes the smaller unit group, which corresponds to the larger prime exponent in the conductor (our own). This computes the conductor without constructing generators for either field (our own).

**Paper or page:** [CM Elliptic Curves: Volcanoes, Reality and Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13316v1). It says: “The compositum of finitely many ring class fields of K is a ring class field of K.”

**Sources:**

- [CM Elliptic Curves: Volcanoes, Reality and Applications (Corollary 4.4)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13316v1)

### Degree-one counts determine zeta functions

**Remember:** Degree-one counts give the whole permutation character.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Embed both number fields in one finite Galois extension L of ℚ. For each field K, the Galois group of L over ℚ permutes the embeddings of K into L. Its permutation character counts how many embeddings each automorphism fixes.

**Problem.** Suppose that, outside finitely many rational primes p, both fields have the same number of prime ideals of norm p. Then their Dedekind zeta functions, which sum over nonzero integral ideals by norm, are equal.

**How the definition helps.** Counting fixed embeddings turns degree-one prime counts into values of a single group character, which replaces a comparison of all coefficients in the two zeta functions. At an unramified prime, the embeddings fixed by Frobenius count the primes of norm p. In our own deduction, Chebotarev supplies each conjugacy class infinitely often, so the characters agree everywhere. Artin’s induction formula identifies their L-functions with the two zeta functions, including factors at ramified primes.

**Paper or page:** [Density questions on arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1), [Stronger arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4). It says: “{\\rm Trace}(\\rho <sub>K</sub>({\\rm Frob}<sub>\\ell </sub>)) =a<sub>\\ell </sub>(K).”

**Sources:**

- [Guillermo Mantilla-Soler, Density questions on arithmetic equivalence (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1)
- [Andrew V. Sutherland, Stronger arithmetic equivalence (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4)

### Degree-zero divisors read Stark ranks

**Remember:** Taking degree zero subtracts one trivial character.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let H/F be a finite abelian extension of number fields with group G. Let S be a finite set of places of F containing all infinite places and all ramified primes. Take one complex basis vector for each place of H above S, with G permuting those vectors. Let X consist of the vectors whose coefficients sum to zero.

**Problem.** For a complex character χ of G, omit the finite prime factors at S from its Artin L-function. Its order of vanishing at zero equals the number of copies of χ in X.

**How the definition helps.** The zero-sum condition supplies the single correction needed for the trivial character, in our own count. Each place in S contributes one orbit of basis vectors, which contributes χ exactly when χ is trivial on the subgroup fixing one place above it, and passing to X removes one copy of the trivial character. The functional equation and nonvanishing at one give the infinite-place contributions. Removing the finite factors adds the remaining contributions.

**Paper or page:** [Borel's rank theorem for Artin L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10044). It says: “Consider the Artin L-function L(s,ρ) attached to a Galois representation”

**Sources:**

- [Karl Rubin, A Stark conjecture over ℤ for abelian L-functions with multiple zeros (1996)](https://aif.centre-mersenne.org/articles/10.5802/aif.1505/)

### Mixed parities exclude critical integers

**Remember:** Opposite signs rule out every integer on one side.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Hecke L-function has one gamma factor for each real embedding of a totally real field, a field whose embeddings all land in ℝ. For a finite-order character the factor is Γ((s+ε)/2) times a nonvanishing factor. Here ε is zero for the trivial local character and one for the sign character. Call m critical when m is an integer and all gamma factors at m and all dual factors at 1−m are finite.

**Problem.** A finite-order Hecke character of a totally real field has no critical integers if both real signs occur.

**How the definition helps.** Testing both ends of the functional equation forces a pole for every integer when both signs occur. Our own calculation uses the nonpositive integer poles of Γ. For m ≤ 0, choose ε so that m+ε is even and nonpositive. For m ≥ 1, apply the same test to 1−m, since the dual character has the same signs.

**Paper or page:** [Notes on the arithmetic of Hecke L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.03399v1). It says: “If there exists $v<sub>1</sub>, v<sub>2</sub> \\in S<sub>r</sub>$, such that $\\epsilon <sub>v<sub>1</sub></sub> \\neq \\epsilon <sub>v<sub>2</sub></sub>$ then ${\\rm Crit}(L(s,\\chi )) = \\emptyset .$”

**Sources:**

- [A. Raghuram, Notes on the arithmetic of Hecke L-functions (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.03399v1)

### Prime norms extend Brauer–Siegel

**Remember:** Count places per log discriminant to keep the missing corrections.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For each number field in the tower let g = log√D, where D is its absolute discriminant. For each prime power q, let φ(q) be the limiting number of prime ideals of residue field size q divided by g. Define φ(ℝ) and φ(ℂ) likewise using real embeddings and conjugate pairs of nonreal embeddings.

**Problem.** Consider a strictly increasing tower of finite Galois extensions of ℚ with these limits. Then log(hR)/g tends to 1 + ∑ φ(q)log(q/(q−1)) − φ(ℝ)log 2 − φ(ℂ)log(2π), summing over prime powers. Here h counts ideal classes and the regulator R measures the volume of a cell in the logarithmic unit lattice.

**How the definition helps.** In our own comparison, dividing each prime count by g gives a limiting coefficient for every term in the logarithm of the zeta product. Tsfasman and Vlăduţ prove the required limit for the zeta residues. The class number formula supplies the terms for real and complex embeddings. All correction terms vanish when the degree divided by g tends to zero.

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer–Siegel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer%E2%80%93Siegel_theorem). It says: “\[Kᵢ : ℚ\]/log\|Dᵢ\| → 0 as i → ∞.”

**Sources:**

- [M. A. Tsfasman and S. G. Vlăduţ, Infinite global fields and the generalized Brauer–Siegel theorem (2002)](https://doi.org/10.17323/1609-4514-2002-2-2-329-402)
- [A. I. Zykin, Asymptotic properties of the Dedekind zeta-function in families of number fields (2009), Theorem 1](https://doi.org/10.1070/RM2009v064n06ABEH004657)

### Primitive characters isolate a zeta quotient

**Remember:** Exclude each prime-order subgroup from the character kernel.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let E/F be a cyclic extension of number fields of degree m. Call a complex character of its Galois group primitive if its kernel is trivial. For each divisor d of m, write E(d) for the field fixed by the subgroup of order d.

**Problem.** The product of the Artin L-functions of all primitive characters equals the product over d dividing m of the Dedekind zeta function of E(d) raised to μ(d), where μ is the Möbius function.

**How the definition helps.** The kernel condition selects the desired factors by inclusion-exclusion, in our own explanation. A nontrivial kernel contains a subgroup of prime order. Characters trivial on the subgroup of order d give exactly the characters of its quotient. Their L-functions multiply to the zeta function of E(d) by Artin’s factorization theorem.

**Paper or page:** [Equivariant algebraic K-theory and Artin L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03578). It says: “Let χ : Gal(F′/F) ↪︎ ℂ× be a primitive (injective) character.”

**Sources:**

- [Elden Elmanto and Ningchuan Zhang, Equivariant algebraic K-theory and Artin L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03578)

### Reflection bounds fields by zeta values

**Remember:** Reflect past zero to expose a positive discriminant power.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Complete the Dedekind zeta function ζₖ(s) by multiplying by exp((s/2)log D) and the gamma factors attached to the field embeddings. Here D is the absolute discriminant of the number field K. The completed function takes equal values at s and 1−s.

**Problem.** Fix a positive integer n, a negative real noninteger s, and B &gt; 0. Only finitely many degree-n number fields up to isomorphism satisfy \|ζₖ(s)\| ≤ B. For real s &gt; 1, infinitely many quadratic fields satisfy this inequality for some common B.

**How the definition helps.** Completion lets us compare the unknown value at s with a positive series at 1−s. In our own fixed-degree argument, reflection contributes the factor exp((½−s)log D), and the remaining gamma ratio takes finitely many nonzero values because only finitely many embedding counts occur. The series at 1−s starts with one and has positive terms, so B bounds D, and Hermite’s theorem gives finiteness. For s &gt; 1 the quadratic Euler products are all bounded by the square of the Riemann zeta function.

**Paper or page:** [On the Northcott property of Dedekind zeta functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13854v1), [On the Northcott property of Dedekind zeta functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13854v1). It says: “The Northcott property does not hold”

**Sources:**

- [Xavier Généreux, Matilde Lalín, On the Northcott property of Dedekind zeta functions (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13854v1)

### Smoothing clears Stickelberger denominators

**Remember:** Smoothing multiplies by factors that clear denominators.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let H/F be a finite abelian extension with F totally real and H a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field, and let S be a finite set of places containing all infinite and ramified ones. The Stickelberger element has value L(S,χ⁻¹,0) at each character χ, omitting Euler factors at S. Smooth it at a disjoint finite set T of primes by multiplying by 1−Nv·σᵥ⁻¹ for each v in T, where Nv is the residue field size and σᵥ is the automorphism inducing the Nv-th power map on residues.

**Problem.** Suppose only the identity root of unity in H reduces to one at every prime above T. Then the smoothed Stickelberger element has integer coefficients in the basis of Galois automorphisms.

**How the definition helps.** Smoothing excludes fractional coefficients that already occur for the Gaussian rationals, in our own example. For ℚ(i)/ℚ take S to consist of infinity and 2. The trivial character value is zero and the nontrivial value is one half. The unsmoothed element is therefore (1−c)/4, where c is complex conjugation. Integrality after smoothing uses the theorem of Deligne and Ribet and of Cassou-Noguès.

**Paper or page:** [Two encounters with the p-adic Stark conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.03299). It says: “The Brumer–Stark conjecture holds over ℤ\[1/2\].”

**Sources:**

- [Samit Dasgupta and Mahesh Kakde, On the Brumer–Stark conjecture (2023)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2023/197-1/p05)
- [Karl Rubin, A Stark conjecture over ℤ for abelian L-functions with multiple zeros (1996)](https://aif.centre-mersenne.org/articles/10.5802/aif.1505/)

### Conductor norms sharpen Chebotarev

**Remember:** Measure the Hecke factors over the fixed field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a finite Galois extension L/F with group G, choose an abelian subgroup H meeting a conjugacy class C, and let K be its fixed field, with absolute discriminant D and degree n over ℚ. Let Q be the largest norm of the conductor of a character of H, the smallest finite modulus needed for its Hecke character. The conductor scale is B = DQ exp(n log n).

**Problem.** Let π(x) count unramified primes of F of norm at most x with Frobenius in C. Let M(x) = \|C\|Li(x)/\|G\|, minus \|C\|χ(c)Li(exp(β log x))/\|G\| for c in C ∩ H if a Hecke character χ for L/K has an exceptional real zero β near one. For L ≠ ℚ and x ≥ Bᵃ, \|π(x)/M(x)−1\| ≤ A(exp(−b log x/log B)+exp(−b√(log x/n))) for positive, absolute, effective constants A, a and b.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the largest conductor gives one scale controlling every character needed to count primes in C. Thorner and Zaman prove the bound by estimating the zeros of these L-functions.

**Paper or page:** [A new bound on the relative error in the Chebotarev density theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01802v2). It says: “and K = Lᴴ is the subfield of L fixed by H, then”

**Sources:**

- [Jesse Thorner and Zhuo Zhang, A new bound on the relative error in the Chebotarev density theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01802v2)

### Cyclic induction reduces Chebotarev

**Remember:** Induce one cyclic point to its whole conjugacy class.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let G be the Galois group of a finite extension of number fields, and let C be the conjugacy class of c. Its cyclic subgroup H consists of the powers of c. Induce the point indicator at c by counting elements x of G satisfying x⁻¹gx = c and dividing by \|H\|.

**Problem.** The induced function equals \|G\|/(\|C\|·\|H\|) on C and zero elsewhere. Consequently, prime counts weighted by the class indicator can be studied through abelian L-functions.

**How the definition helps.** Induction expresses the whole class indicator using one point of a cyclic group. Our own calculation counts \|G\|/\|C\| conjugators for each element of C. On H, the point indicator expands in homomorphisms to the unit circle. Artin’s induction identity preserves their L-functions when the base changes to the field fixed by H. Class field reciprocity identifies these functions with Hecke L-functions over that field.

**Paper or page:** [A new bound on the relative error in the Chebotarev density theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01802v2). It says: “If $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ and $\\chi $ is a representation of $H$, then $L(s,\\operatorname{Ind} \_H<sup>G\\chi</sup> ,L/K)=L(s,\\chi ,L/L<sup>H</sup>)$.”

**Sources:**

- [Jesse Thorner and Zhuo Zhang, A new bound on the relative error in the Chebotarev density theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01802v2)
- [Henryk Iwaniec and Emmanuel Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/053)

### Liouville weights reduce Landau’s theorem

**Remember:** Balanced factor parity is enough for Landau’s theorem.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a number field K, factor each nonzero integral ideal into prime ideals. Give it weight 1 for an even number of factors and −1 for an odd number, counting repeats.

**Problem.** Sum these weights over ideals of norm at most x, where the norm counts residue classes modulo the ideal. If the sum divided by x tends to zero, the number of prime ideals up to norm x is asymptotic to x/log x.

**How the definition helps.** In our own formulation, the sign turns balance between even and odd factor counts into cancellation in one sum. Burgin proves that this cancellation implies the prime ideal theorem and establishes the required cancellation.

### Null boundaries permit infinite Chebotarev

**Remember:** A boundary of measure zero lets finite quotients approximate the prime density.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Galois group G of an infinite Galois extension is the inverse limit of its finite Galois groups. Give G its translation-invariant probability measure, called Haar measure. Choose a set X stable under conjugation whose boundary has measure zero.

**Problem.** Let L be a possibly infinite Galois extension of a number field K, ramified at only finitely many primes. The proportion of primes with Frobenius in X tends to its Haar measure as the residue field size bound grows.

**How the definition helps.** A boundary of measure zero lets finite quotient conditions approximate X from inside and outside with arbitrarily small differences in measure. Our own argument applies finite Chebotarev to both approximations. In our own counterexample, the cyclotomic ℤ₃-extension of ℚ has Galois group the additive group of 3-adic integers. The countable set of prime Frobenius elements has measure zero but contains the Frobenius of every unramified prime.

**Wikipedia:** [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem). It says: “Let X be a subset of G that is stable under conjugation and whose boundary has Haar measure zero.”

### Signed corrections stabilize Chebotarev counts

**Remember:** Subtract the exceptional contribution before measuring relative error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let C be a conjugacy class in the group G of a finite Galois extension L/K of number fields. Write Li for the logarithmic integral and set M(x) = \|C\|Li(x)/\|G\|. **Problem.** Count unramified primes of K up to residue field size x whose Frobenius belongs to C, obtaining π(x). For L ≠ ℚ, π(x)/M(x) tends to one whenever log x/log(D exp(n log n)) tends to infinity. Here D is the absolute discriminant of L and n its degree over ℚ.

**How the definition helps.** Including the exceptional zero in M measures the error against the prime count predicted for that particular class. Frobenius records how raising residues to the base residue field size acts above the prime. When χ(C) = 1, the correction can nearly cancel the first term. Thorner and Zaman bound the remaining contributions relative to this smaller quantity.

**Paper or page:** [A new bound on the relative error in the Chebotarev density theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01802v2). It says: “\\frac {\|C\|}{\|G\|}(\\operatorname{Li} (x)-\\chi \_1(C)\\operatorname{Li} (x<sup>\\beta \_1</sup>))”

**Remember:** Complete at a rational point, then read off the degree.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An exceptional cover of curves over 𝔽q is a bijection on points over the field with qᵏ elements, for infinitely many k. The paper defines a matching notion, an exceptional extension of local fields. For a totally ramified extension of degree n prime to q, Theorem 1.6 shows it is exceptional exactly when gcd(n, q − 1) = 1.

Theorem 3.3 shows that the completed extension at an 𝔽q-rational point is exceptional, and Theorem 2.1 shows that an exceptional local extension of degree n has gcd(n, q − 1) = 1. In our own words, at a rational point the residue field does not grow, so the local degree is the ramification index. The paper proves the needed local facts in three ways, with different tools.

**Remember:** A zero symbol means the norm residue action fixes the division point.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Remember:** An Artin action upstairs restricts to the action of the norm downstairs.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; \\(p\\)-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over a local field of positive characteristic, a formal Drinfeld module uses additive power series for scalar multiplication. For α in the maximal ideal, choose a division point ξ mapping to α. For nonzero β in L, the symbol subtracts ξ from its image under the automorphism assigned to β by local reciprocity.

**Problem.** Let M/L be finite separable, let α belong to the maximal ideal of L, and let β be nonzero in M. The symbol over M equals the symbol over L evaluated at α and the norm of β.

**Remember:** Remove the factor whose exponent behaves discontinuously in the p-adic distance.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S40 (Zeta functions and \\(L\\)-functions), 11M41. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Problem.** These corrected values extend continuously in the p-adic variable n away from n=0, where the extension has a pole. For p=5, the original values have no continuous extension at n=4.

**How the definition helps.** Removing the Euler factor avoids a discontinuity from taking powers of 5 (our own). Take n = 4 + 4·5ᵏ, so n tends to 4 in the 5-adic distance (our own). But 5 to the power n−1 tends to 0 along these indices (our own). The corrected values therefore force the uncorrected limit to be (1−5³)ζ(−3), not ζ(−3) (our own). The work moves to the Kubota–Leopoldt interpolation theorem, which uses Kummer’s congruences to control the corrected values (our own).

### Regularization bounds Bernoulli weights

**Remember:** Subtract the rescaled Bernoulli weight to cancel the denominator N.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, \\(p\\)-adic integration, etc.)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix an odd prime p and positive integers d and c, with c ≥ 2 coprime to dp. At modulus N = dpⁿ, give each least nonnegative representative a the weight w(a) = a/N − 1/2. Let b represent c⁻¹a modulo N in the same range. The corrected weight is w(a) − cw(b).

**Problem.** For odd p the regularized distribution is a bounded p-adic measure, even though the original Bernoulli distribution is not.

**How the definition helps.** The correction puts a multiple of N in the numerator (our own calculation). The result is (a − cb)/N + (c − 1)/2, which belongs to the p-adic integers for odd p. The original weights add correctly under subdivision of residue classes, and multiplication by c permutes those subdivisions. The corrected weights therefore still add correctly and define a bounded measure (our own argument). With d = a = 1, the original weights have unbounded p-adic absolute value as n grows.

**Definition.** Take a list of fractional linear maps over 𝔽ₚ, meaning invertible changes of variable x ↦ (ax + b)/(cx + d). Call the list normal if some map occurs an odd number of times.

**Problem.** Let F be a middle extension over 𝔽ₚ, a coefficient system extended across singularities by local invariant vectors, with Frobenius eigenvalues of modulus one at regular points. Suppose its geometric symmetry group is the full symplectic group in its standard representation and only the identity preserves F up to scalar twist; then for a normal list, the sum of products of the transformed traces over common finite inputs avoiding poles is O(√p).

**How the definition helps.** Odd multiplicity gives a factor on which the central symmetry −I negates every tensor, ruling out invariant vectors. Our own explanation uses the independence theorem for distinct transformed systems. Deligne’s bound controls the remaining sum in terms of list length and the rank and ramification of F.

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “where the cohomology groups are replaced by cohomology with coefficients in the sheaf.”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel, A study in sums of products](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/sums-of-products.pdf)

### Signed multiplicities force special linear cancellation

**Remember:** Count ordinary factors positively and conjugate factors negatively, modulo the rank.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Give each occurrence of a fractional linear map x ↦ (ax + b)/(cx + d) a sign, with ad − bc ≠ 0. Its signed multiplicity counts positive occurrences minus negative occurrences. Call the list r-normal if some map has signed multiplicity indivisible by r.

**Problem.** Take a middle extension F over 𝔽ₚ with weight zero and geometric symmetry group SL(r) in its standard representation, where p &gt; r ≥ 3. Geometrically, only the identity preserves F up to scalar twist, and no fractional linear map carries F to its dual up to twist. For an r-normal list over 𝔽ₚ, the complete trace product summed away from poles is O(√p), conjugating traces with negative signs.

**How the definition helps.** Signed multiplicity gives the exponent by which scalar matrices in SL(r), the determinant-one group, act on each tensor factor, and a nonzero exponent modulo r prevents invariant vectors. Our own explanation uses independence of distinct transformed systems and Deligne’s bound. The bound depends on the list length and the rank and ramification of F.

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “where the cohomology groups are replaced by cohomology with coefficients in the sheaf.”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel, A study in sums of products](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/sums-of-products.pdf)

### Character spaces isolate Jacobi factors

**Remember:** Each character pair labels its own Frobenius eigenvalue.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11T24 (Other character sums and Gauss sums), 14G10. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take the smooth projective Fermat curve with affine equation xᵐ + yᵐ = 1, where m is a prime power dividing q − 1. Multiplying either coordinate by an mth root of unity preserves the curve. Split its first étale cohomology, the vector space recording its zeta numerator, into spaces where these scalings act by fixed characters.

**Problem.** Each pair χ, ψ of nontrivial multiplicative characters of 𝔽q with orders dividing m and nontrivial product labels a one-dimensional space. Frobenius acts there by −∑χ(x)ψ(1 − x), summing over 𝔽q and extending the characters by zero at zero.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, splitting by characters lets us specify which Jacobi sum belongs to each Frobenius eigenvalue. Frobenius preserves the spaces because all the scalings are defined over the base field. Computing their dimensions and identifying their eigenvalues with character sums still requires the cohomological point-count formula.

**Paper or page:** [On the variation of the Frobenius in a non abelian Iwasawa tower](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16774). It says: “The eigenvalues of $\\sigma \_q$ on the eigenspace $M<sub>n</sub>(\\eta )$ are given by the Jacobi sum 

\\\[ -J<sub>q</sub>(\\chi \_1,\\chi \_2) = -\\sum <sub>x \\in \\mathbb F<sub>q</sub></sub>\\chi \_1(x)\\chi \_2(1-x). \\\]”

**Sources:**

- [Asvin G, On the variation of the Frobenius in a non abelian Iwasawa tower](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16774)

### Frobenius preserves strict Waring numbers

**Remember:** Strip off Frobenius before counting the needed powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11T55 (Arithmetic theory of polynomial rings over finite fields), 11P05, 11P55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For polynomials over a finite field of characteristic p, let J(k) contain all finite sums of kth powers. For nonzero m in J(k), bound each base degree by ⌈deg(m)/k⌉. Increase this bound by one if k divides deg(m) and its leading coefficient lies outside the sums of kth powers in the field. Define G(k) as the least summand count sufficient under this bound for every m in J(k) of sufficiently large degree.

**Problem.** For a positive integer k divisible by p, G(k) = G(k/p), with G(1) = 1.

**How the definition helps.** In our own explanation, taking pth powers maps exactly the allowed targets for k/p onto those for k while preserving the base-degree bound. In characteristic p the pth power of a sum is the sum of the pth powers, and the polynomial ring has no nonzero element with pth power zero, so representations correspond in both directions. This map multiplies target degrees by p and permutes the coefficient field, so the exceptional leading-coefficient test also agrees. Using all polynomials as targets would include powers of the variable whose degrees are not divisible by p.

**nLab:** [Frobenius morphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Frobenius+morphism). It says: “the characteristic of the field is used to show (a + b)ᵖ = aᵖ + bᵖ.”

**Sources:**

- [Y.-R. Liu and T. D. Wooley, Waring’s problem in function fields, §1](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~twooley/publ/wpfqt110809.pdf)
